record.title: Absent contractions with upper-normal relaxation pressure
fairness: The resident must interpret universal failed contractions with relaxation measurements at the laboratory's upper normal boundary rather than accept the normal flag as exclusion of obstruction, then select an independent supportive emptying assessment. Timed barium with tablet passage is the best offered study.

Further manometric provocation is a credible near-miss but does not offer the same independent demonstration of passage. Reflux monitoring can address reflux physiology but does not resolve whether these swallowing findings represent an outflow problem. The explanation appropriately withholds a definitive diagnosis.

The laboratory-relative description avoids an unsupported device-independent threshold. The complete acquisition and alternate-position findings are relevant to uncertainty; the word 'every' reports the observed series rather than functioning as a rhetorical absolute. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.

This standalone node supplies a consistent patient, complete task and necessary workup context. No prior feedback supplies the answer. The study labels are parallel and the correct option has no material length or wording advantage.

Recognizing that an apparently normal relaxation metric does not settle profound dysmotility is relevant board-level interpretation. The boundary-case application makes this moderate, with two consequential steps, rather than simple recall of a numeric cutoff.
suggestions: Preserve the inconclusive interpretation and laboratory-relative measurements; do not rewrite the explanation to diagnose achalasia definitively from these fields.

Keep this distinct from the preserved-peristalsis item: the learning point here is all-failed contractions despite an upper-normal relaxation measurement, not simply another repetition of the same keyed test.

fairness: The failed contractions, impaired relaxation and retained contrast support the motor/outflow disorder. The resident must then apply both anesthesia and rescue constraints: an endoscopic approach is not automatically suitable merely because it avoids a planned operation.

Pneumatic dilation is the meaningful near-miss because the patient cannot tolerate major rescue if perforation occurs. The myotomy alternative requires a different anesthesia burden. cues.phrase: no mass or focal wall abnormality / Endoscopic ultrasound of the cardia and junction wall

fairness: The acquisition history makes clear that crossing the junction was achieved but did not yield usable swallow recordings. question.stem: Which investigation should next inform care for {patientName}'s continuing dysphagia?

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound of the cardia and junction wall
answerChoices.rationale: An infiltrative junction process can mimic a motor disorder despite an unrevealing mucosal examination. EUS is useful when clinical or imaging findings raise that concern. The represented gradual, weight-stable course and prior structural assessment provide no new wall target; the outstanding gap is usable physiology after failed assisted manometry.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An infiltrative junction process can mimic a motor disorder despite an unrevealing mucosal examination. EUS is useful when clinical or imaging findings raise that concern. The represented gradual, weight-stable course and prior structural assessment provide no new wall target; the outstanding gap is usable physiology after failed assisted manometry.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic FLIP topography and junction distensibility
answerChoices.rationale: Retention has been documented but usable pressure physiology has not been acquired despite assisted placement. FLIP is a supported complementary assessment of junction opening and motor response in this circumstance. It neither supplies a complete manometric subtype nor by itself authorizes myotomy.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory esophageal pH-impedance reflux monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Regurgitation can reflect reflux, but the acquired retained-column pattern and incomplete motor assessment leave obstructive physiology unresolved. Reflux burden and symptom association do not characterize that opening problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Regurgitation can reflect reflux, but the acquired retained-column pattern and incomplete motor assessment leave obstructive physiology unresolved. Reflux burden and symptom association do not characterize that opening problem.

question.explanation: The contrast record demonstrates retention, while even assisted manometry has not produced usable physiology. With no represented new structural concern, FLIP is a supported complementary way to assess junction opening and motor response. EUS targets a suspected wall process, and pH-impedance targets reflux. FLIP does not establish a complete pressure subtype or automatically justify irreversible treatment.

concept.displayName: flip after failed assistance
concept.learningObjective: Choose complementary distensibility assessment after genuine repeated inability to complete pressure testing.
concept.identityDecision: new_meaning
concept.identityReason: The live acquisition questions favor assisted completion. This new boundary asks what to do after assistance has also failed to produce usable measurements.
concept.historyMigration: Retain prior definitions and histories on their existing identities.

record.title: Physiologic assessment after unusable assisted manometry

cues.phrase: no mass or focal wall abnormality / Endoscopic ultrasound of the cardia and junction wall
cues.why: The negative wall finding lexically weakens the wall-imaging option. This is a residual elimination cue, but structural observations and the gradual stable-weight course are needed to rank further structural evaluation fairly. They do not exclude occult infiltration with certainty, and the final choice still requires understanding which physiologic assessment is feasible after failed manometry.

fairness: The acquisition history makes clear that crossing the junction was achieved but did not yield usable swallow recordings. The resident must avoid treating attempted placement as a completed physiologic test, then select FLIP to assess junction opening and motor response in the setting of demonstrated retention.

FLIP is the best offered next test. EUS remains plausible when occult secondary obstruction is suspected, but the gradual course, stable weight and described structural assessment lower that priority here. They do not prove that every infiltrative process has been excluded. Reflux monitoring does not resolve the demonstrated retention and missing motor assessment.

The explanation appropriately limits FLIP: it does not supply a complete pressure-based subtype or independently authorize irreversible treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Exact test-priority verification was not performed because network and source review are outside this task.

The standalone node gives sufficient chronology and a complete task. No prior answer is needed. The present diagnostic competitors are different investigations, and the key is not merely the only untried test.

This is a useful advanced niche within a high-yield disease area. The precise FLIP-after-failed-assisted-manometry decision is narrower than commonly tested achalasia diagnosis and treatment; unfamiliarity with FLIP should not be mistaken for hard reasoning.
suggestions: Retain as optional advanced coverage rather than use it to satisfy core high-yield or hard-item targets.
Preserve the distinction between lower suspicion for a wall lesion and exclusion of secondary disease. Keep the failed acquisition observations and FLIP limitations explicit.

record.title: Absent contractions with upper-normal relaxation pressure
fairness: The resident must interpret universal failed contractions with relaxation measurements at the laboratory's upper normal boundary rather than accept the normal flag as exclusion of obstruction, then select an independent supportive emptying assessment. Timed barium with tablet passage is the best offered study.

Further manometric provocation is a credible near-miss but does not offer the same independent demonstration of passage. Reflux monitoring can address reflux physiology but does not resolve whether these swallowing findings represent an outflow problem. The explanation appropriately withholds a definitive diagnosis.

The laboratory-relative description avoids an unsupported device-independent threshold. The complete acquisition and alternate-position findings are relevant to uncertainty; the word 'every' reports the observed series rather than functioning as a rhetorical absolute. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.

This standalone node supplies a consistent patient, complete task and necessary workup context. No prior feedback supplies the answer. The study labels are parallel and the correct option has no material length or wording advantage.

Recognizing that an apparently normal relaxation metric does not settle profound dysmotility is relevant board-level interpretation. The boundary-case application makes this moderate, with two consequential steps, rather than simple recall of a numeric cutoff.
suggestions: Preserve the inconclusive interpretation and laboratory-relative measurements; do not rewrite the explanation to diagnose achalasia definitively from these fields.

Keep this distinct from the preserved-peristalsis item: the learning point here is all-failed contractions despite an upper-normal relaxation measurement, not simply another repetition of the same keyed test.

record.title: Additional investigation after inconclusive wireless monitoring
fairness: Off-PPI catheter impedance-pH is the best of these investigations for the unresolved reflux assessment: the multiday record is neither uniformly physiological nor conclusively pathological, and nonpositive symptom association does not resolve that uncertainty.

On-treatment testing assumes a different diagnostic starting point; manometry can serve motor assessment but does not answer the remaining reflux-evidence question. The explanation appropriately says impedance-pH 'can add' evidence rather than guarantee a diagnosis.

Two steps are present: interpret an intermediate, variable multiday result, then choose an adjunct investigation under appropriate treatment conditions. This is clinically relevant, high-yield preintervention evidence assessment; exact adjunct thresholds are not tested here.

The options are parallel investigations. Neither the task nor the exhibit names the keyed modality, and no nonmedical overlap or outlier selects it. The single-node case stands alone with a consistent patient and completed diagnostic history.
This offline judgment does not independently verify the current numerical diagnostic criteria or establish that this is the only acceptable real-world pathway beyond the offered options.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between inconclusive and normal testing, and the limited 'can add' explanation. Avoid turning the adjunct investigation into a universal mandate or a promise of conclusive results.

record.title: Indefinite dysplasia in inflamed tissue
clarityIssues: Optimize PPI is less concrete than the owner's requested medication-plan style; the drug and administration plan are not specified in this node.
fairness: Expert-confirmed indefinite dysplasia with marked inflammation requires interpreting the uncertainty before choosing reassessment rather than routine nondysplastic surveillance or ablation. The routine-surveillance option is a credible underreaction.
The update establishes adequate sampling and intestinal metaplasia, resolving the earlier diagnostic uncertainty. It stands alone with the presentation and does not rely on the preceding answer.
The explanation does not falsely equate indefinite dysplasia with confirmed neoplasia or set an unsupported repeat interval.
suggestions: Make the intended acid-suppression optimization concrete using the verified drug and regimen from the authoring evidence; do not invent a dose or interval. This wording refinement does not change the defensible sequencing key.

record.title: Meal-related breathlessness with an apparent incidental hiatal hernia
fairness: Offering elective anatomical repair is defensibly best among the choices. Meal limitation and reproducible postprandial breathlessness, substantial intrathoracic stomach with adjacent lung compression, unrevealing competing cardiopulmonary studies and preserved independence support a symptomatic hernia rather than an incidental heartburn-negative finding.

Continued observation remains a possible informed patient preference, but the task asks what is most appropriate to offer, not what operation must be performed. Limited fixation has no supplied high-risk or emergency justification. This conditional ranking is fair within the stated choices.

Two steps are present: reassess symptom attribution using chronology, anatomy and competing assessment, then choose the appropriate management offer. Symptomatic paraesophageal-hernia indications are high-yield.

The referral's 'asymptomatic' assertion is attributed to an outside source and contested by actual observations. It does not itself name the operation, and choosing anatomical repair over limited fixation still requires clinical interpretation. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

The single-node case stands alone and has a consistent named 74-year-old patient. The explanation appropriately says that a symptomatic hernia is plausible and repair can be offered; it does not claim that causation is proven or every such patient must undergo surgery.
suggestions: Optional tightening: remove the referral's 'because he denies heartburn' rationale, which adds a teaching hint without changing the decision. Keep the actual denial of heartburn only if it serves the intended misconception, and retain the symptom pattern, anatomy and competing assessment.

record.title: Junctional metaplasia and surveillance eligibility
fairness: Symptom care without Barrett surveillance is the best answer from the described landmarks and junctional biopsy. The learner must calculate the short displacement and distinguish junctional intestinal metaplasia from an established esophageal Barrett segment.

The outside pathology label is a legitimate competing interpretation, not a supplied answer to the follow-up task. No key-only lexical match or convergence selects the answer without interpreting anatomy.

The ablation option is a weak competitor in a patient without dysplasia or a focal lesion. The surveillance versus no-surveillance distinction remains a credible, consequential high-yield error and supports a moderate judgment, near the easier end.
This is a self-contained single-node case with consistent age, sex and endoscopy history. No prior feedback is required.
suggestions: Preserve measured landmarks and biopsy location. Any future replacement for the weak ablation distractor should be a genuinely plausible follow-up error, with clinical review confirming that it does not create a second defensible key.

record.title: Negative distal fragments from a longer columnar segment
fairness: Repeat endoscopy with multilevel biopsies is the best offered strategy. The negative fragments cover a small distal part of a longer observed segment, so rereviewing or sectioning the same sampled territory cannot substitute for acquisition from unrepresented territory.

The negative histology remains valid for the submitted fragments; the explanation does not call the specimen useless or assert a confirmed Barrett diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two consequential steps are present: identify a spatial sampling limitation rather than a grading dispute, then choose acquisition rather than further interpretation of the same tissue. Expert review and deeper sections are credible neighboring pathology-workflow errors.

The exhibit does not name the keyed procedure or label the sample inadequate. A reader must interpret coverage and the relevance of patchy histology; the differently worded strategies have comparable specificity. This is high-yield diagnostic sampling reasoning.
This version is a single-node case with consistent landmarks and an unresolved diagnosis. It does not depend on the separate frozen inflammation case or its feedback.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between tissue not sampled and a pathologist's uncertainty in adequately sampled tissue. Do not add a predetermined Barrett diagnosis to the presentation or caption.

record.title: Medication decision after negative reflux evaluation
fairness: Discontinuing empiric PPI is the defensible best answer among these plans: the four complete off-treatment days show low acid exposure, typical symptoms were captured without positive association, symptoms did not improve on the resumed regimen, and no independent PPI indication is supplied.
The separate-indication check is decision-critical rather than an arbitrary set of distractor-eliminating negatives. No confident clinical error or nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

Two steps are present: interpret reflux burden together with symptom association, then apply that result to medication use while checking independent indications. This is a high-yield refractory-symptom error.

The chronology coherently follows the first node, and the current update plus presentation identify the resumed medication. The first explanation supplies the reason for off-treatment testing but not this result or its management. The later task is complete when shown separately from the presentation.
suggestions: Retain the symptom capture and independent-indication findings. Feedback could explicitly say that persistent symptoms still warrant appropriate evaluation; this result does not establish a particular alternative diagnosis.

record.title: Reflux confirmation after normal off-treatment endoscopy
fairness: Off-PPI ambulatory reflux monitoring is the best of the offered investigations: the completed mucosal assessment does not establish GERD, and persistent symptoms despite treatment do not supply that diagnosis. Repeating an adequate examination has no stated new indication.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish treatment failure from objective proof of reflux, then choose diagnostic testing conditions. The on-treatment alternative represents a credible resident error. This is high-yield preintervention workup.

The named 52-year-old woman's presentation and complete task are coherent. The later medication decision follows a completed outside study; this explanation does not disclose that later result or medication answer.

Offline editorial review only: no external source, current numerical criterion, or clinical approval was independently verified. PASS in this report does not change needs_clinician_review; difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments.
suggestions: Optional clarity improvement in a future version: replace 'No ambulatory reflux study appears in the outside records' with the actual verified prior testing history. Absence from a transferred record is not proof that testing never occurred. Both monitoring choices remain plausible from the wording alone, so this is not a key-only omission cue.

record.title: On-treatment testing in established GERD
fairness: Prior LA grade C disease supplies objective GERD evidence despite subsequent mucosal healing. Persistent regurgitation after an actual optimized course makes on-PPI impedance-pH the best offered test of ongoing reflux and symptom relationship.
Off-treatment testing is a credible error if healing is mistaken for loss of the prior diagnosis. HRM has a different role and does not answer this reflux-response question.

The word now in the medication follow-up clearly supersedes the baseline administration error. Previous feedback teaches optimization without naming this node's testing answer. The record stands alone.
suggestions: Preserve the prior severe disease and actual optimized follow-up. Verify the specific treatment-duration claim through the existing evidence process; it was not independently checked during this offline review.

record.title: Reconstruction and reflux control after physiological assessment
fairness: Reduction, hiatal closure and addition of fundoplication is the best-supported offered plan with documented pathological reflux, preserved relaxation and peristalsis, contractile augmentation and no swallowing limitation.

The explanation appropriately describes conditional benefit and dysphagia tradeoffs without asserting that this record mandates a particular wrap or mesh technique. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two steps are present: interpret reflux and motor findings, then integrate them into the reconstruction. The prior decision to offer repair does not settle the antireflux component. The choices represent distinguishable operations rather than grammatical or label-matching alternatives.

This later node follows the anemia case coherently, provides the current physiological assessment and states its preoperative decision stage. It needs the shared presentation but does not require remembering a previous answer. This is high-yield operative planning.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between supporting a fundoplication and mandating a specific wrap. Preserve the motor findings and swallowing history when composing the case.

record.title: Residual Barrett after curative lesion resection
fairness: Favorable intramucosal pathology with clear margins and no lymphovascular invasion must be integrated with the remaining nondysplastic Barrett field. The credible error is treating the residual samples as ordinary nondysplastic Barrett and selecting surveillance alone.
Ablation of remaining Barrett is the best offered next plan; complete field resection is not the preferred routine alternative in this flat residual field.

The new carcinoma diagnosis is a plausible upstage after resection of a lesion initially sampled as HGD. The current pathology and residual map stand alone. Prior feedback anticipates subsequent treatment selection but does not name ablation.
suggestions: Preserve the favorable pathology and residual-field findings; they supply both consequential decisions. Avoid adding a prior explanation that explicitly names the residual-field ablation answer.

record.title: Surveillance adequacy when negative jars miss the esophageal segment
fairness: Repeating structured sampling of the established esophageal segment is the defensible best answer. The complete collection log and matching accession represent cardia and junction, not the persistent tubular-esophageal columnar segment; the negative jars therefore cannot support stopping surveillance or treating this as an adequate segment assessment.

The completeness statement has a necessary evidentiary role: it distinguishes tissue never collected from an incompletely transferred report. The outside conclusion is explicitly attributed and is a claim to assess rather than a narrator-supplied diagnosis.

Two consequential steps are present: determine the territory represented by the specimens, then decide whether the examination can start a routine surveillance interval or needs completion. This applies high-yield Barrett surveillance and sampling principles.

No key-only phrase or nonmedical option outlier establishes which tissue territory requires sampling. The task and named patient's single-node presentation are coherent and independent of the other Barrett cases.
The explanation appropriately limits the current specimen evidence rather than calling the old diagnosis disproven. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the complete collection/accession record and the previously established esophageal diagnosis. The distinction between repeating an inadequate examination and restarting routine surveillance from it is the valuable competing decision.

record.title: Recurrent anemia and meal limitation with hiatal hernia
fairness: Offering elective anatomical repair is defensibly best among these plans given the hernia anatomy, contact-site erosions, recurrent deficiency despite treatment, persistent meal limitation, alternative-source assessment and absence of prohibitive operative disease.

The inference is attribution of a clinically important symptom complex to the hernia, followed by treatment selection after medical treatment has not maintained control. Continued medical care is a credible competitor; limited fixation is less compelling for this described operative candidate.

No nonmedical wording attack uniquely identifies the answer. The operative-risk information has a real role in distinguishing definitive repair from limited intervention. This is high-yield paraesophageal-hernia management.

The next node coherently assumes that repair is planned and adds physiological findings. This explanation does not disclose the later fundoplication decision. The current question is complete within the named patient's case.
suggestions: Retain the conditional 'offer' framing and the treatment trajectory; do not turn this into a universal repair mandate for incidentally detected hernias.

record.title: Selecting reflux-monitoring conditions before a procedure
fairness: Wireless distal pH monitoring off PPI is the defensible best offered strategy when the supplied record contains a normal adequate endoscopy and symptom response but no objective reflux diagnosis. On-treatment strategies answer a different clinical question.

The learner must recognize that partial response to medication and persistent regurgitation do not establish GERD, then select testing conditions that establish untreated reflux burden. This is a narrow but consequential high-yield application.

The key is the sole off-treatment choice, but that distinction is the clinical variable being tested, not a standalone nonmedical clue. Option length and grammar are comparable; the task does not state that testing must be off treatment.

The next node supplies a later completed outside study. This explanation does not disclose its daily values, their interpretation or the motor assessment answer. The patient's presentation and task are self-contained for this stage.
suggestions: A shorter lead-in such as asking which reflux study should precede the procedural decision would read more naturally. Preserve the actual diagnostic-history boundary; do not describe the patient as 'unproven GERD' in visible text.

record.title: Visible Barrett lesion before ablation
fairness: The visible abnormality and limited forceps tissue require recognizing unresolved depth/staging before choosing resection rather than ablation. EUS first is a credible staging misconception.
Missing submucosa in a forceps specimen is not evidence that submucosal invasion is absent; the explanation correctly seeks a resection specimen rather than making that claim.
The description supports resection as the next step without forcing an unsupported EMR-versus-ESD ranking. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified offline.
suggestions: Retain the specimen-depth information and generic endoscopic-resection scope. If the lesion description later implies deeper invasion or a specific technique is keyed, verify the corresponding staging and resectability criteria before release.

fairness: Symptom care without Barrett surveillance is the best answer from the described landmarks and junctional biopsy. The learner must calculate the short displacement and distinguish junctional intestinal metaplasia from an established esophageal Barrett segment.

The outside pathology label is a legitimate competing interpretation, not a supplied answer to the follow-up task. No key-only lexical match or convergence selects the answer without interpreting anatomy.

The ablation option is a weak competitor in a patient without dysplasia or a focal lesion. The surveillance versus no-surveillance distinction remains a credible, consequential high-yield error and supports a moderate judgment, near the easier end.

record.title: Additional investigation after inconclusive wireless monitoring
fairness: Off-PPI catheter impedance-pH is the best of these investigations for the unresolved reflux assessment: the multiday record is neither uniformly physiological nor conclusively pathological, and nonpositive symptom association does not resolve that uncertainty.

On-treatment testing assumes a different diagnostic starting point; manometry can serve motor assessment but does not answer the remaining reflux-evidence question. The explanation appropriately says impedance-pH 'can add' evidence rather than guarantee a diagnosis.

Two steps are present: interpret an intermediate, variable multiday result, then choose an adjunct investigation under appropriate treatment conditions. This is clinically relevant, high-yield preintervention evidence assessment; exact adjunct thresholds are not tested here.

The options are parallel investigations. Neither the task nor the exhibit names the keyed modality, and no nonmedical overlap or outlier selects it. The single-node case stands alone with a consistent patient and completed diagnostic history.
This offline judgment does not independently verify the current numerical diagnostic criteria or establish that this is the only acceptable real-world pathway beyond the offered options.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between inconclusive and normal testing, and the limited 'can add' explanation. Avoid turning the adjunct investigation into a universal mandate or a promise of conclusive results.

record.title: Surveillance adequacy when negative jars miss the esophageal segment
fairness: Repeating structured sampling of the established esophageal segment is the defensible best answer. The complete collection log and matching accession represent cardia and junction, not the persistent tubular-esophageal columnar segment; the negative jars therefore cannot support stopping surveillance or treating this as an adequate segment assessment.

The completeness statement has a necessary evidentiary role: it distinguishes tissue never collected from an incompletely transferred report. The outside conclusion is explicitly attributed and is a claim to assess rather than a narrator-supplied diagnosis.

Two consequential steps are present: determine the territory represented by the specimens, then decide whether the examination can start a routine surveillance interval or needs completion. This applies high-yield Barrett surveillance and sampling principles.

No key-only phrase or nonmedical option outlier establishes which tissue territory requires sampling. The task and named patient's single-node presentation are coherent and independent of the other Barrett cases.
The explanation appropriately limits the current specimen evidence rather than calling the old diagnosis disproven. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the complete collection/accession record and the previously established esophageal diagnosis. The distinction between repeating an inadequate examination and restarting routine surveillance from it is the valuable competing decision.

record.title: Negative distal fragments from a longer columnar segment
fairness: Repeat endoscopy with multilevel biopsies is the best offered strategy. The negative fragments cover a small distal part of a longer observed segment, so rereviewing or sectioning the same sampled territory cannot substitute for acquisition from unrepresented territory.

The negative histology remains valid for the submitted fragments; the explanation does not call the specimen useless or assert a confirmed Barrett diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two consequential steps are present: identify a spatial sampling limitation rather than a grading dispute, then choose acquisition rather than further interpretation of the same tissue. Expert review and deeper sections are credible neighboring pathology-workflow errors.

The exhibit does not name the keyed procedure or label the sample inadequate. A reader must interpret coverage and the relevance of patchy histology; the differently worded strategies have comparable specificity. This is high-yield diagnostic sampling reasoning.
This version is a single-node case with consistent landmarks and an unresolved diagnosis. It does not depend on the separate frozen inflammation case or its feedback.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between tissue not sampled and a pathologist's uncertainty in adequately sampled tissue. Do not add a predetermined Barrett diagnosis to the presentation or caption.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management option is most appropriate to offer {patientName} from this completed assessment?

answerChoices.label: Offer elective anatomical hiatal hernia repair
answerChoices.rationale: No heartburn does not establish an asymptomatic hernia. Meal limitation, meal-related breathlessness and the anatomy, with an unrevealing competing cardiopulmonary assessment, make symptomatic hernia plausible. Repair can be offered rather than treating the finding as incidental.

answerChoices.label: Offer continued observation with return precautions
answerChoices.rationale: Observation is reasonable for truly asymptomatic patients, but the referral label overlooks meal-related functional limitation. Acid-symptom history does not resolve that attribution.

answerChoices.label: Offer limited reduction and gastric fixation
answerChoices.rationale: Limited fixation may reduce burden when definitive reconstruction cannot be tolerated; this functional and cardiopulmonary assessment does not provide that risk constraint.

Meal limitation, meal-related breathlessness and the anatomy, with an unrevealing competing cardiopulmonary assessment, make symptomatic hernia plausible. Repair can be offered rather than treating the finding as incidental.

record.title: Meal-related breathlessness with an apparent incidental hiatal hernia
fairness: Offering elective anatomical repair is defensibly best among the choices. Meal limitation and reproducible postprandial breathlessness, substantial intrathoracic stomach with adjacent lung compression, unrevealing competing cardiopulmonary studies and preserved independence support a symptomatic hernia rather than an incidental heartburn-negative finding.

Continued observation remains a possible informed patient preference, but the task asks what is most appropriate to offer, not what operation must be performed. Limited fixation has no supplied high-risk or emergency justification. This conditional ranking is fair within the stated choices.

Two steps are present: reassess symptom attribution using chronology, anatomy and competing assessment, then choose the appropriate management offer. Symptomatic paraesophageal-hernia indications are high-yield.

The referral's 'asymptomatic' assertion is attributed to an outside source and contested by actual observations. It does not itself name the operation, and choosing anatomical repair over limited fixation still requires clinical interpretation. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

The single-node case stands alone and has a consistent named 74-year-old patient. The explanation appropriately says that a symptomatic hernia is plausible and repair can be offered; it does not claim that causation is proven or every such patient must undergo surgery.
suggestions: Optional tightening: remove the referral's 'because he denies heartburn' rationale, which adds a teaching hint without changing the decision. Keep the actual denial of heartburn only if it serves the intended misconception, and retain the symptom pattern, anatomy and competing assessment.

choices.choiceLabel: Offer elective anatomical hiatal hernia repair
Offer continued observation with return precautions
Offer limited reduction and gastric fixation

record.title: Antibacterial endpoint after pelvic source control
fairness: Stopping is the single best offered endpoint in this explicitly recovered patient after four full active post-control days, with no residual fluid cavity, continuing communication, bloodstream infection or other treatment indication. This conclusion is conditional on the stated adequacy of source control and is not a universal four-day rule for every abdominal infection.

The learner must distinguish persistent fat stranding and a retained drain from evidence of an uncontrolled fluid source, then choose a treatment endpoint. Extending therapy to drain removal is a recognizable clinical error. Waiting for disappearance of stranding is the weaker competitor, but still targets a distinct clinical-versus-radiographic endpoint error.

The recovery findings are necessary to make stopping fair. The options are parallel endpoints; neither option length nor a uniquely explanatory phrase identifies the key. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the supplied conditional explanation. Predicted difficulty is at the easier end of moderate.

The full update restates the procedure, completed treatment, source findings and present status, so it stands alone. It follows the day-2 specimen node coherently. Prior feedback discusses source validity, not the four-day stopping answer. The retrospective presentation keeps this hospital-stage imaging separate from an unannounced new clinic order.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between absent fluid cavity and residual inflammatory stranding. Preserve the explicit absence of another treatment indication and the separate drain-management plan.

record.title: Enteric coverage and a concurrent antiarrhythmic
fairness: Cefepime plus metronidazole is the single best offered regimen. Aerobic-only processing cannot establish absence of anaerobes from the leaking enteric source, while ongoing sotalol makes the otherwise active ciprofloxacin-containing option less appropriate because of additive arrhythmic risk. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the precise labeling claim in the explanation was not freshly verified offline.

Both axes are consequential: interpret the microbiology's sampling/processing limit to preserve anaerobic coverage, then account for the medication interaction when choosing between susceptible antipseudomonal agents. Solving only one axis leaves two options.

The four labels form a balanced component set. Each antipseudomonal drug occurs twice and metronidazole occurs twice; there is no convergence advantage. Susceptibility is supplied for both antipseudomonal choices. No option contains a rationale or an absolute, and the source/medication task does not name the interaction.

The question is hard because a resident must combine antimicrobial spectrum with a medication-specific safety constraint, not because of missing data. The source-control timing and current medication are clear within a standalone retrospective hospital decision. This is clinically relevant surgical antimicrobial selection, although exact exam frequency is not asserted.
suggestions: Keep the balanced four-option structure and both susceptible agents. Do not add a pre-answer QT warning, which would supply the second inference.

record.title: Postoperative prescription and drain-culture reconciliation
fairness: Discontinuing the carried-forward cefazolin is the single best offered medication plan. The operative chronology supports a prophylactic origin, while the benign clinical course and indwelling-port culture do not independently establish an infection needing treatment. Mesh and a retained drain do not by themselves supply that indication.

The added MSSA report creates a consequential second judgment: reconstruct the original antibiotic indication, then decide whether the subsequent culture supplies a new treatment indication. Oral cephalexin is a credible attempted conversion for someone who mistakes susceptibility for a need to treat.

The task uses a somewhat artificial 'cefazolin-related' phrase, but the exact medication decision is clear. All choices refer to that same medication plan, so the overlap does not uniquely favor the key. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The discharge prescription's route is not stated explicitly, although cefazolin implies parenteral administration. This does not change the offered decision, but a medication-reconciliation record could label the route for realism. The named patient, age/sex, complaint and standalone chronology are consistent.
suggestions: Optional polish: ask which medication plan is appropriate and label the carried-forward cefazolin route in the medication record. Preserve the new device-culture conflict and clinical reassessment findings.

record.title: Narrowing a remaining post-control antibiotic course
fairness: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole is the best offered stewardship choice when the reliable first-entry specimen identifies these susceptible organisms, the source is controlled and the patient is improving. Meropenem and cefepime plus metronidazole are active, but their additional spectrum is not justified by the supplied findings. This is a best-choice ranking, not a claim that those drugs would fail microbiologically.

The resident must assemble coverage for both organisms, then use specimen reliability, response and remaining-course context to choose the narrower adequate regimen. The table deliberately leaves all offered regimens active, preserving a real de-escalation decision.

No unique label overlap, majority-component convergence or explanatory option identifies the key. Meropenem's shorter single-drug label reflects a genuine regimen difference rather than an artificial cue. The task does not explicitly instruct the learner to select the narrowest drug.

Day 2 and ongoing remaining treatment distinguish this from a completed-course stopping decision. That makes the choice fair without pretending this report alone proves a universally required duration. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The retrospective stage, source, timing and specimen history are stated within this standalone node. Patient age/sex and complaint are consistent.
suggestions: Retain the all-active comparator set and the clear course stage. The explanation can be shortened by deleting repeated contrasts with a hypothetical completed four-day course.

record.title: Treating Candida from a newly accessed abdominal source
fairness: Adding micafungin while continuing the active antibacterial regimen is the best offered plan for Candida recovered from direct initial access to the infected cavity in this persistently severely ill patient. C. glabrata, pending susceptibility and recent azole exposure make empiric fluconazole a less appropriate offered choice. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The first consequential judgment is whether this source isolate warrants antifungal treatment rather than dismissal as a device isolate. The second is selection of the initial antifungal class using severity, species and prior exposure. The latter is strongly supported by several concordant findings, so this is moderate rather than hard.

The shared piperacillin-tazobactam component is balanced across all plans. The no-antifungal option names an actual alternative, and neither antifungal label contains an embedded explanation. Candida identification is legitimate microbiology for a treatment question. Repetition of fluconazole between prior exposure and an option is a clinical association requiring knowledge, not a sufficient nonmedical giveaway.

The specimen is explicitly from first access to a previously undrained cavity; it does not silently inherit the interpretation of an old drain sample. Continued source follow-up prevents the task from implying that antifungal addition replaces source assessment. The hospital-stage chronology is clear and standalone.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between a direct source specimen and a longstanding device culture, and keep susceptibility pending. Do not generalize the explanation to every postoperative Candida isolate.

record.title: Procedure-specific prophylaxis with MRSA carriage
fairness: Cefazolin plus vancomycin is the best offered regimen for the stated mesh procedure, documented MRSA carriage and beta-lactam tolerance. Gentamicin does not replace the required MRSA-directed component or the preferred routine prophylactic component in this comparison. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the limited offered ranking.

The two consequential judgments are the procedure's baseline prophylactic coverage and how documented carriage modifies it. The error is substituting or adding the wrong component rather than forgetting that prophylaxis is needed.

Every option contains two drugs, and each drug appears in two options. There is no majority-component convergence, uniquely long key, or rationale embedded in an option. MRSA is legitimate known microbiology for this management task, not a supplied diagnosis answering a diagnosis question.

The historical preoperative stage is clear despite the present clinic frame. The next node concerns redosing, and this explanation does not disclose its clock or interval. The planned decolonization does not claim proven eradication.
suggestions: Retain balanced two-drug labels and the procedure, allergy/tolerance and carriage information. Keep redosing instructions out of this node's feedback.

record.title: A new drain isolate after a completed treatment course
fairness: Not restarting therapy is the best offered plan given the completed course, documented control, recovery and provenance of the new isolate. A falling but still elevated leukocyte count does not independently establish treatment failure. Neither active antipseudomonal drug acquires an indication merely because the device sample reports susceptibility. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this conditional conclusion.

The two judgments are the significance of a disinfected-port isolate from a catheter present throughout recovery and whether the clinical trajectory justifies restarting a completed course. Persistent leukocytosis supplies a real competing concern rather than an entirely normalized recovery vignette.

The no-treatment choice differs from the two restart choices because that is the decision being tested. There is no independent grammatical, length or rationale cue selecting it. Cefepime is the stronger overtreatment temptation; meropenem additionally represents unnecessarily broad escalation, so this is moderate at most.

The update establishes catheter persistence through a completed four-day course and later recovery; an invented exact catheter-age threshold is unnecessary. The standalone clinic narrative, patient details and task are coherent. The explanation appropriately requires reassessment for new illness rather than treating all future drain cultures as harmless.
suggestions: Optional concision: remove 'no blood cultures were obtained' unless a blood-culture decision is added; its absence does not distinguish any current option and could distract from the actual specimen and clinical trajectory.
Retain the falling leukocyte-count trend and the disinfected-port detail because they make the treatment-indication judgment consequential.

record.title: Source control for a localized postoperative pelvic collection
fairness: Image-guided catheter drainage is the best offered action for the substantial confined collection, persistent focal illness and described access corridor. Continued medical treatment fails to address the collection; exploration is less appropriate than the available less invasive source-control route in this stated stable, localized presentation.

Two judgments remain: recognize the need for source control despite active antibiotics, then use distribution, access anatomy and examination to choose its route. These are common general-surgery decisions, although this is at the easier end of moderate rather than a stretch item.

The corridor and examination are decision-critical observations. They should not be deleted as alleged cues: without them exploration could become more defensible. No option uniquely repeats a diagnostic label or rationale sentence. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the explanation appropriately avoids equating absent contrast escape with proof that every leak is excluded.

The retrospective hospital decision is clearly distinguished from the current clinic visit. It precedes drainage, specimen interpretation and duration decisions coherently. Later results were not used to solve this node.
suggestions: Retain the explicit access anatomy and localized examination. Do not advertise this straightforward source-control comparison as hard.

record.title: Systemic treatment after incisional drainage
fairness: Review scope for this array: all 13 current executable proposedQuestions, comprising two rewrites and eleven new candidates, including the two pass-preserved new candidates. The two original Keep records, twenty retirement proposals, two parked repairs, parked retained replacement, inherited held versions/recorded holds/withheld points and unkeyed material were noted but not adjudicated. No prior verdict or author self-assessment determined these judgments.

Offline editorial review of Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task, option labels and Explanation under question-authoring.2026-11-08.v15 and AGENTS.md presentation guidance. Input JSON SHA256: ac6199fa217d2159c037274d42c432055022ba7748a67c6d9796df965ae7c838. No network or fresh source verification was performed. PASS is not clinical approval; drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative resident-level judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies. Runtime rendering, randomization, wait metadata and source-ledger completeness are outside this text-only review.

Not starting a systemic antibiotic is the single best offered plan for the decompressed, improving superficial wound without spreading cellulitis, systemic illness or immunocompromise. Neither susceptible organism identity nor availability of an active oral agent creates a treatment indication. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The resident must reconcile a positive MSSA culture with the postdrainage response, then decide whether either active drug is indicated. Cephalexin is a credible overtreatment temptation; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole supplies another active oral prescription rather than the former unrelated escalation in route.

The negative-treatment option is necessarily different from the two treatment options, but its wording does not independently disclose correctness. Improvement and host findings are necessary clinical evidence, not a nonmedical wording shortcut. Name, age/sex, short complaint and complete standalone task are present.
suggestions: Retain the positive culture and both active oral alternatives. Do not remove the source-control, response or host findings in pursuit of difficulty.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At today's visit, Nora Ellis's opened subcutaneous cavity is fully decompressed. Pain and surrounding redness have receded since drainage without systemic antibiotics. She is afebrile, has no spreading cellulitis and is not immunocompromised. The original cavity culture reports MSSA susceptible to cephalexin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Dressings and clinical reassessment will continue with every plan.

answerChoices.label: Do not start a systemic antibiotic
answerChoices.rationale: The improving, drained superficial infection has no remaining systemic-treatment indication; a susceptible isolate identifies an option if treatment is needed, not a reason to prescribe it.

answerChoices.label: Start oral cephalexin
answerChoices.rationale: This is a plausible MSSA-directed outpatient agent, but the current local response and host findings do not justify systemic treatment.

answerChoices.label: Start oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
answerChoices.rationale: Susceptibility makes this a real oral alternative; it still exposes Nora to a drug without establishing that systemic treatment adds benefit after this drainage.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Tessa Lane's operative record describes elective mesh abdominal-wall repair without bowel entry or infected tissue. Cefazolin was first given before incision, repeated during the operation and then carried onto the discharge medication list. She now has an intact incision, expected mild tenderness, no spreading erythema and no fever. A drain retained for a postoperative seroma has been present since surgery. A specimen from its disinfected port now reports MSSA susceptible to cefazolin and cephalexin; no new cavity was accessed. Wound and drain reassessment will continue with every medication plan.
decisionNodes.stem: Which cefazolin-related medication plan is most appropriate for Tessa Lane at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the cefazolin prescription
answerChoices.rationale: The operative/dose chronology supplies an incision-related indication, not a current infection. A positive longstanding-drain report without clinical infection does not create a new treatment indication.

answerChoices.label: Continue the cefazolin prescription
answerChoices.rationale: Cefazolin is active against the isolate, but neither the carried-forward operative doses nor this drain report establishes an infection requiring an ongoing IV course.

answerChoices.label: Replace cefazolin with oral cephalexin
answerChoices.rationale: Changing route reduces IV burden but still treats a laboratory result without establishing a postoperative infection.

decisionNodes.explanation: The medication timing and operative findings explain why cefazolin appeared in the record. They do not establish treatment of an infection, and prophylaxis does not need continuation after closure because a drain remains. The new port isolate must be interpreted as an indwelling-device sample alongside the benign clinical course; it does not justify IV continuation or oral conversion.

record.title: Narrowing a remaining post-control antibiotic course
fairness: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole is the best offered stewardship choice when the reliable first-entry specimen identifies these susceptible organisms, the source is controlled and the patient is improving. Meropenem and cefepime plus metronidazole are active, but their additional spectrum is not justified by the supplied findings. This is a best-choice ranking, not a claim that those drugs would fail microbiologically.

The resident must assemble coverage for both organisms, then use specimen reliability, response and remaining-course context to choose the narrower adequate regimen. The table deliberately leaves all offered regimens active, preserving a real de-escalation decision.

No unique label overlap, majority-component convergence or explanatory option identifies the key. Meropenem's shorter single-drug label reflects a genuine regimen difference rather than an artificial cue. The task does not explicitly instruct the learner to select the narrowest drug.

Day 2 and ongoing remaining treatment distinguish this from a completed-course stopping decision. That makes the choice fair without pretending this report alone proves a universally required duration. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The retrospective stage, source, timing and specimen history are stated within this standalone node. Patient age/sex and complaint are consistent.
suggestions: Retain the all-active comparator set and the clear course stage. The explanation can be shortened by deleting repeated contrasts with a hypothetical completed four-day course.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: In the outside record, Dana Mercer is on post-control day 2 after drainage and closure of a leaking small-bowel source. Fever and pain are improving. The cavity specimen was processed for aerobic culture only; it grew Pseudomonas susceptible to cefepime and ciprofloxacin. The inpatient medication list includes ongoing sotalol for a prior arrhythmia. Renal function permits the offered drugs. The team is choosing an IV regimen for the remaining post-control treatment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which IV antibacterial regimen best fits Dana Mercer's source, available microbiology and current medication list?

answerChoices.label: Cefepime plus metronidazole
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the susceptible aerobic isolate and retains enteric anaerobic coverage without adding the ciprofloxacin-sotalol QT interaction.

answerChoices.label: Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole
answerChoices.rationale: The combination can cover susceptible complicated intra-abdominal pathogens, but the concurrent sotalol makes ciprofloxacin an avoidable QT-risk choice here.

answerChoices.label: Cefepime
answerChoices.rationale: It avoids the ciprofloxacin interaction and covers the recovered Pseudomonas, but it does not supply the anaerobic component required by this enteric source.

answerChoices.label: Ciprofloxacin
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the susceptible Pseudomonas but omits the enteric anaerobic component and adds the concurrent-sotalol safety problem.

decisionNodes.explanation: The culture-processing history cannot exclude anaerobes from a leaking enteric source; cefepime needs an anaerobic partner here. Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole is a real active alternative in susceptible intra-abdominal infection, but the ciprofloxacin label advises avoidance with sotalol because of QT/torsades risk. Combining the source interpretation with the medication list selects cefepime plus metronidazole.

concept.displayName: Integrate incomplete enteric culture processing and a QT-related drug interaction when choosing among active regimens.
concept.learningObjective: Integrate incomplete enteric culture processing and a QT-related drug interaction when choosing among active regimens.
concept.historyDecision: Explicit changed-meaning concept version. Preserve the v1 definition and every prior FSRS/frozen encounter; do not transfer review history.
concept.newMeaningDecision: Removed preselection, redundant processing clue and resistant throwaway. Added a directly label-supported patient-specific interaction to distinguish two microbiologically credible complete regimens. This broadens the scored construct and requires a new concept version.

record.title: Enteric coverage and a concurrent antiarrhythmic
fairness: Cefepime plus metronidazole is the single best offered regimen. Aerobic-only processing cannot establish absence of anaerobes from the leaking enteric source, while ongoing sotalol makes the otherwise active ciprofloxacin-containing option less appropriate because of additive arrhythmic risk. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the precise labeling claim in the explanation was not freshly verified offline.

Both axes are consequential: interpret the microbiology's sampling/processing limit to preserve anaerobic coverage, then account for the medication interaction when choosing between susceptible antipseudomonal agents. Solving only one axis leaves two options.

The four labels form a balanced component set. Each antipseudomonal drug occurs twice and metronidazole occurs twice; there is no convergence advantage. Susceptibility is supplied for both antipseudomonal choices. No option contains a rationale or an absolute, and the source/medication task does not name the interaction.

The question is hard because a resident must combine antimicrobial spectrum with a medication-specific safety constraint, not because of missing data. The source-control timing and current medication are clear within a standalone retrospective hospital decision. This is clinically relevant surgical antimicrobial selection, although exact exam frequency is not asserted.
suggestions: Keep the balanced four-option structure and both susceptible agents. Do not add a pre-answer QT warning, which would supply the second inference.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: In the outside record, Adrian Cole has undergone operative closure of a postoperative bowel leak and drainage of an abdominal collection. Piperacillin-tazobactam is active against the recovered bacteria. He remains febrile and requires norepinephrine after fluid resuscitation. The specimen obtained by direct needle entry into the previously undrained cavity, before any catheter was placed, grows C. glabrata; antifungal susceptibilities are pending. He recently received fluconazole during this admission. The team is reassessing the current antimicrobial plan while continuing source follow-up.
decisionNodes.stem: Which antimicrobial plan is most appropriate now for Adrian Cole at this recorded stage?

answerChoices.label: Continue piperacillin-tazobactam and add micafungin
answerChoices.rationale: The fresh normally sterile cavity isolate in a patient with persistent severe infection warrants antifungal treatment. An echinocandin is the preferred offered initial choice with pending susceptibility, recent azole exposure and current vasopressor requirement.

answerChoices.label: Continue piperacillin-tazobactam without an antifungal
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the bacteria but dismisses yeast recovered directly from a previously undrained infected cavity while severe illness persists. This is not a longstanding drain-isolate scenario.

answerChoices.label: Continue piperacillin-tazobactam and add fluconazole
answerChoices.rationale: Antifungal treatment is justified, but initial fluconazole is less appropriate with C. glabrata susceptibility still unknown, recent azole exposure and ongoing vasopressor requirement.

decisionNodes.explanation: The decisive source fact is direct first access to a previously undrained infected cavity, rather than a device culture. Together with persistent severe illness, that supports treatment of intra-abdominal Candida. Among these plans, micafungin supplies the preferred initial class for this C. glabrata/azole-exposure/pending-susceptibility context. Fluconazole is conditional on a different susceptibility and clinical setting; piperacillin-tazobactam has no antifungal role.

concept.displayName: Distinguish fresh-cavity Candida from device colonization, then select an initial regimen under severe illness and uncertain susceptibility.
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish fresh-cavity Candida from device colonization, then select an initial regimen under severe illness and uncertain susceptibility.
concept.historyDecision: Explicit changed-meaning concept version. Preserve the v1 definition and every prior FSRS/frozen encounter; do not transfer review history.
concept.newMeaningDecision: Constructed a new version without the redundant bloodstream proof, explicitly recording that change from the archived reviewed case. Replaced amphotericin with the credible colonization decision, so no unsupported toxicity ranking of an otherwise active drug is taught. This adds source-significance assessment and receives a new concept version.

record.title: Treating Candida from a newly accessed abdominal source
fairness: Adding micafungin while continuing the active antibacterial regimen is the best offered plan for Candida recovered from direct initial access to the infected cavity in this persistently severely ill patient. C. glabrata, pending susceptibility and recent azole exposure make empiric fluconazole a less appropriate offered choice. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The first consequential judgment is whether this source isolate warrants antifungal treatment rather than dismissal as a device isolate. The second is selection of the initial antifungal class using severity, species and prior exposure. The latter is strongly supported by several concordant findings, so this is moderate rather than hard.

The shared piperacillin-tazobactam component is balanced across all plans. The no-antifungal option names an actual alternative, and neither antifungal label contains an embedded explanation. Candida identification is legitimate microbiology for a treatment question. Repetition of fluconazole between prior exposure and an option is a clinical association requiring knowledge, not a sufficient nonmedical giveaway.

The specimen is explicitly from first access to a previously undrained cavity; it does not silently inherit the interpretation of an old drain sample. Continued source follow-up prevents the task from implying that antifungal addition replaces source assessment. The hospital-stage chronology is clear and standalone.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between a direct source specimen and a longstanding device culture, and keep susceptibility pending. Do not generalize the explanation to every postoperative Candida isolate.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Maya Grant completed four full days of active antibacterial treatment after drainage of her postoperative collection and has been off treatment since then.
