record.title: A new drain isolate after a completed treatment course
fairness: Not restarting therapy is the best offered plan given the completed course, documented control, recovery and provenance of the new isolate. A falling but still elevated leukocyte count does not independently establish treatment failure. Neither active antipseudomonal drug acquires an indication merely because the device sample reports susceptibility. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this conditional conclusion.

The two judgments are the significance of a disinfected-port isolate from a catheter present throughout recovery and whether the clinical trajectory justifies restarting a completed course. Persistent leukocytosis supplies a real competing concern rather than an entirely normalized recovery vignette.

The no-treatment choice differs from the two restart choices because that is the decision being tested. There is no independent grammatical, length or rationale cue selecting it. Cefepime is the stronger overtreatment temptation; meropenem additionally represents unnecessarily broad escalation, so this is moderate at most.

The update establishes catheter persistence through a completed four-day course and later recovery; an invented exact catheter-age threshold is unnecessary. The standalone clinic narrative, patient details and task are coherent. The explanation appropriately requires reassessment for new illness rather than treating all future drain cultures as harmless.
suggestions: Optional concision: remove 'no blood cultures were obtained' unless a blood-culture decision is added; its absence does not distinguish any current option and could distract from the actual specimen and clinical trajectory.
Retain the falling leukocyte-count trend and the disinfected-port detail because they make the treatment-indication judgment consequential.

record.title: Secondary-prevention aspirin versus nonaspirin NSAID
fairness: Continue aspirin and discontinue naproxen is the best offered discharge plan after controlled diverticular hemorrhage with a documented prior myocardial infarction.

Two consequential judgments remain: infer the secondary-prevention role rather than treating all bleeding-risk drugs alike, then distinguish the continuing cardiovascular benefit from the avoidable nonaspirin NSAID exposure.
The full two-by-two option matrix has no convergence or uniquely comprehensive key. Indications, bleeding control and absence of additional antithrombotic drugs are explicit.
Standalone and high yield. The explanation appropriately uses generally and when feasible rather than asserting an absolute medication rule. No dose or exact resumption interval is claimed.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve the indication-specific rationale and avoid expanding this simple aspirin-only decision into a dual-antiplatelet timing rule.

record.title: Worsening after drainage: a separate undrained compartment
fairness: Sigmoid resection with abdominal drainage is the best offered escalation for clinical deterioration and an enlarging inaccessible separate collection after antibiotics and drainage.

Two consequential inferences remain: falling drain output does not establish overall source control, and enlarging the catheter in a collapsed different cavity will not drain the new compartment. The anatomy defeats a credible catheter-exchange error.

The shared presentation and update establish the problem without requiring recall of the previous correct choice. Earlier feedback teaches initial drainage but not the changed compartment anatomy. High-yield failure of nonoperative source control.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve the nearly collapsed cavity and separate-compartment observations; they earn the reasoning step.

record.title: Initial investigation of suspected bowel-bladder communication
fairness: Interpret recurrent infections and pneumaturia without instrumentation as possible bowel-bladder communication, then choose cross-sectional evaluation of cause and extent. Cystoscopy is a credible narrower alternative; CT best addresses the combined abdominal and urinary findings.
Absence of catheterization is decision-critical context rather than improper distractor deletion. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The explanation supports the diagnostic inference without prescribing the later operation. Subsequent CT and treatment follow-up are coherent.
This is high-yield moderate application; the classic symptom pattern does not justify a hard rating.

record.title: First episode: urinary findings versus colonic imaging
fairness: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT is the best offered investigation: the resident must interpret nonspecific urinary findings alongside focal febrile abdominal pain, then choose the examination that evaluates the suspected bowel process and complications. Stone-protocol CT is a plausible competing error; acute colonoscopy is less appropriate.

The task is complete, patient identity and demographics are clear, and the subsequent CT-treatment node follows coherently. The current explanation does not reveal whether antibiotics should be prescribed.
High-yield initial diverticulitis assessment. Difficulty and testability are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or independently verified exam frequency.

Review scope: all 19 previewAssembled current after nodes, including nine pass-preserved executable rewritten/new candidates; historical before versions were not scored. Five parked candidates and one deferred candidate were excluded. No kept-unchanged, retired or held record was promoted into this review.

Offline editorial review of supplied visible text only; no network or fresh guideline verification. PASS is not clinical approval; every version remains needs_clinician_review. Runtime waits and rendering were outside this text-only review.
suggestions: No required content repair. Preserve the distinction between nonspecific urinary abnormalities and a confirmed urinary diagnosis.

Excluded candidates noted only: post-abscess-colonoscopy.v2, elective-burden-after-abscess.v2, symptomatic-colovesical-fistula.v2, gross-perforation-source-control.v2, high-risk-recovered-observation.v2 (parked); first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.v1 (deferred). Retained hold review.n3.postdiverticulitis-examination-extent.v2 and unkeyed boundaries were not scored. Historical PASS records remain historical exact-version decisions.

record.title: Residual oozing vascular patch after focal clipping
fairness: APC is the best offered next treatment for residual distributed oozing from the flat branching cecal vascular patch after focal clipping. The resident must recognize the remaining mucosal vascular target, then match treatment to the residual distribution rather than equating one controlled point with complete hemostasis.

Further clips are a plausible competing error; epinephrine does not supply a comparable definitive treatment plan. The explanation appropriately describes APC as accepted rather than claiming all mechanical or other thermal approaches are inferior.

The morphology and residual distribution favor APC, but exact endoscopic technique ranking still requires clinician judgment. No confident inaccuracy is identified, and the supplied text does not justify a universal superiority claim or settings recommendation.

The common availability of all device classes does not single out the key. The local update is self-contained and follows a coherent partial-response sequence. High-yield angioectasia treatment and reassessment after hemostasis.
suggestions: No required editorial repair. Retain the residual distributed-oozing discriminator and qualified explanation; have Melissa confirm the offered clips-versus-APC ranking for this exact description.

record.title: High-risk host: reconstruction after emergency resection
fairness: Rectal-stump closure with end colostomy is the best offered definitive reconstruction with continuing vasopressor requirement, chronic corticosteroid exposure and edematous bowel.

The learner must synthesize host and physiologic risk, then recognize that proximal diversion does not make an otherwise high-risk anastomosis equivalent to avoiding it. The two anastomotic choices test a credible resident misconception.

Definitive abdominal closure is explicitly common background, delimiting the question rather than silently ruling out an unoffered damage-control decision. The explanation acknowledges that separate judgment.
Standalone operative chronology is sufficient. High-yield reconstruction selection; no assertion that Hartmann is mandatory in every contaminated abdomen.
suggestions: No required repair. Retain the actual vasopressor, medication and bowel observations and the limitation to offered definitive reconstructions.

record.title: Immunosuppression and oral antibiotic coverage
fairness: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the best offered oral plan. Immune suppression defeats omission despite mild uncomplicated findings; ciprofloxacin without an anaerobic partner is an incomplete offered diverticulitis regimen.

Two consequential decisions remain: apply host risk despite a reassuring trajectory, then choose appropriate coverage. The ward setting and oral route are explicitly fixed, so this is not an underspecified admission-versus-discharge or oral-versus-IV contest.

No dose, duration or renal threshold is invented. The explanation correctly limits what the question decides. The named transplant drugs, oral tolerance, allergy and renal information support the offered-plan comparison.
Standalone chronology is clear. High-yield antibiotic indication and spectrum, with no unique length, wording-match or convergence shortcut identified.
suggestions: No required repair. The home-oxygen history and repeated statement that observation is common could be shortened if they are not needed elsewhere in the case.

record.title: Large localized diverticular abscess: initial source control
fairness: Image-guided drainage with antibiotics is the best offered initial plan. The resident must integrate the large localized collection with stable physiology and access anatomy, then choose drainage over antibiotics alone or immediate resection.

The percutaneous route is decision-critical feasibility information, not an unfair permission cue: omitting it could make the drainage-versus-surgery comparison underdetermined. It names access but does not establish that drainage is indicated without interpreting the collection and clinical condition.

No exact cutoff is required to distinguish this clearly large collection. The follow-up supplies a different residual-compartment problem; this explanation does not reveal that answer. High-yield abscess management.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve the access and peritonitis observations rather than deleting necessary information merely to make the question harder.

record.title: Discordant localization before surgical rescue
fairness: Right colectomy is the best offered extent after surgery has been selected: current dynamic CTA and selective angiographic extravasation identify an ascending-colon source, whereas left-pelvic activity occurs only on delayed tagged-cell images.

The resident must rank localization reliability and timing, then select segmental rather than blind sigmoid or subtotal resection. Concordant current studies are legitimate clinical evidence, not arbitrary option-component convergence.

The prior node already located a right-sided bleed, which lowers surprise and prevents a hard rating. Nevertheless, the new apparently discordant study creates a meaningful subtotal-versus-targeted-resection error; the explanation does not treat the earlier history alone as sufficient.

The update supplies prior treatment failure, the surgical decision and both current studies, so it stands alone. High-yield requirement for reliable localization before segmental resection. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this is not fresh verification of operative-guideline wording.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve the distinction between delayed-only tracer position and current direct extravasation; do not teach that every positive tagged-cell scan is unusable.
Keep the explanation conditional on the supplied concordant current localization and failed hemostatic attempts.

record.title: Ongoing significant lower-GI bleeding: localization
fairness: CTA is the best offered localization study during ongoing significant bleeding after a negative upper examination and unsuccessful preparation. The resident must interpret continued blood loss and circulatory response, then select the modality suited to the current bleeding phase.

Tagged-cell scintigraphy remains a recognizable competing localization technique; another full preparation delays assessment in the supplied continuing course. The preparation failure is necessary decision information, not a gratuitous exclusion.
The question is a retrospective hospital-record review, and resuscitation explicitly continues. No implication that diagnostic testing replaces resuscitation. High-yield acute bleeding pathway.
The subsequent CTA node introduces raw contrast-phase findings. This explanation does not name its angiographic treatment answer.
suggestions: No required repair. Optional style improvement: remove the sentence about the founder reviewing decisions, which adds no clinical information.

record.title: Dynamic CTA extravasation and angiographic treatment
fairness: Selective angiography with possible embolization is the best offered next route for continuing significant hemorrhage with dynamic CTA extravasation and failed preparation.

The learner must interpret new arterial-phase contrast that enlarges in the lumen, then apply the continuing bleeding and preparation constraints to choose treatment. CTA is not merely labelled positive in the visible update.

The node includes current physiology and prior preparation status locally. It follows coherently from the localization node without its explanation supplying embolization. Urgent colectomy is premature relative to the offered radiologic route.
High-yield interpretation-to-management decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical wording shortcut identified.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve the unenhanced, arterial and later-phase observations rather than replacing them with a diagnostic label.

record.title: Alarm symptoms despite a recent adequate colonoscopy
fairness: Optical colonoscopy is the best offered next evaluation after resolution of acute inflammation: persistent caliber change, weight loss and focal thickening warrant diagnostic luminal assessment despite a recent adequate examination. The second inference is that the previous reassuring examination does not settle a newly symptomatic focal abnormality.

CT colonography is a credible modality competitor but cannot provide tissue sampling; repeating conventional CT is less useful after the already documented persistent lesion. The choices remain distinguishable without assuming a new numerical interval rule.

The recent examination and current course are explicit. The next node provides its own colonoscopy findings and mechanical symptoms; this explanation does not disclose resection. High-yield alarm-feature assessment.
suggestions: No required repair. In feedback, consider briefly explaining the tissue-sampling advantage over CT colonography so the closest alternative teaches a reusable distinction.
The sentence about prior procedural tolerance adds little to the new alarm-feature decision and could be shortened in a future authorized version.

record.title: Significant recurrent bleeding after endoscopic clipping
fairness: Selective angiography with possible embolization is the best offered escalation after recurrent hemodynamically significant bleeding, failed endoscopic control and current CTA localization.
The reasoning is consequential: recurrence does not automatically mean either repeat endoscopy or surgery. Its severity, visualization problem and current arterial target select the radiologic route.
The previous clipping is stated in this node, so it stands alone. Its explanation establishes why angiography is next but does not resolve the later discordant-localization resection question.
High-yield escalation pathway. No confident clinical error or nonmedical unique-label cue identified.
suggestions: No required repair. Preserve current localization and bleeding severity rather than relying on a historical clipping site alone.

record.title: Reconstruction after perforation in a stable low-risk host
fairness: Primary colorectal anastomosis with diversion is the best offered selected reconstruction given stable physiology, favorable host factors and viable tension-free ends despite fecal contamination.

Hartmann reconstruction is a clinically real alternative, not an inherently incorrect operation. The observations support preferring the offered diverted anastomosis in this constructed case; the explanation appropriately does not claim it is obligatory. Exact comparative ranking remains for clinician sign-off, not a claim of universal superiority.

The resident must weigh contamination against host and post-resection physiology, then choose reconstruction rather than equating fecal contamination with mandatory Hartmann surgery. Staged reconstruction is less persuasive without continuing instability.
The previously paired source-control question is absent, but the current standalone operative record supplies the perforation and resection context. High-yield operative decision.
suggestions: No required editorial repair. Retain the qualified explanation and have Melissa confirm the exact reconstruction ranking; do not turn this selected-case answer into a universal rule.

answerChoices.label: Continue antibiotics with serial inpatient reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Antibiotics are required, but this large collection and feasible route support adding drainage. Antibiotics without drainage remain an option when access is unsafe and the clinical course permits close observation.

answerChoices.label: Perform sigmoid resection during the initial admission assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate resection can control a failed or uncontained process. Stable physiology, a localized collection and a safe drainage route support an initial less invasive source-control approach here.

answerChoices.label: Add image-guided percutaneous drainage to the antibiotics
answerChoices.rationale: The collection is beyond both retrieved guideline size boundaries and has an assessed safe route. Drainage adds source control while antibiotics continue.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After drainage and antibiotics she developed increasing fever, tachycardia and broader abdominal tenderness. Drain output had fallen. CT showed the catheter tip in a nearly collapsed cavity and an enlarging rim-enhancing collection between bowel loops in a separate compartment. decisionNodes.stem: Which next hospital plan best fits {patientName}'s changed course?

answerChoices.label: Change antibiotics and continue the existing drain
answerChoices.rationale: Medication changes do not drain the separate enlarging collection during clinical worsening. Monitored nonoperative care can remain reasonable when the course improves.

answerChoices.label: Exchange and enlarge the existing drain catheter
answerChoices.rationale: The catheter ends in the collapsed compartment, not the enlarging source; its exchange does not correct that mismatch.

answerChoices.label: Perform sigmoid resection and abdominal drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Deterioration with an enlarging separate collection and no safe percutaneous route supports operative source control. Reconstruction is a separate decision.

record.title: Sequence reperfusion and fracture stabilization for a threatened limb
fairness: The learner must recognize that the interval perfusion loss requires prompt flow restoration while the viable limb remains salvageable, then reconcile that priority with gross skeletal instability that can compromise a definitive repair. Temporary shunting resolves two consequential sequencing problems.

Shunt, fixation, then definitive repair is the defensible best sequence among the offered plans with control already obtained and the limb still poorly perfused. Fixation first prolongs the present ischemia; definitive reconstruction before stabilizing the grossly unstable injury exposes it to subsequent manipulation.

All options compare actual operative sequences, and the extra shunt component is the clinical construct rather than an appended generic safety qualification. The labels are sufficiently comparable in length and specificity; there is no strong nonmedical wording shortcut.

Sequence: the warm foot in the prior node becomes cool with absent Doppler signals here. The new CTA and operative findings explain the change and provide the fracture, perfusion and viability information needed without recalling the prior ABI. No earlier explanation supplies the sequence.

Hard is a qualitative prediction based on competing operative priorities, not a claim about resident success rates. No confident clinical inaccuracy or unresolved competing best answer was identified in the stated scenario.
suggestions: Preserve the already-obtained arterial control, gross instability and ongoing perfusion deficit. Those details make the sequence specific; do not generalize the feedback into a universal requirement to shunt every combined fracture and arterial injury.

record.title: Use reliable vascular findings and ABI to decide imaging versus follow-up
fairness: Recalculation gives 120/150 = 0.80, whereas 1.25 is the inverted ratio. The learner must first reject the worksheet's reassuring summary, then use the abnormal vascular index to select imaging despite the reassuring examination. The arithmetic was independently re-solved.

CTA is the defensible best offered plan. The repeated raw pressures make simple measurement error less persuasive, while discharge based on the reported ratio misses the consequential calculation error. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The second operator and equal ankle measurements establish the intended measurement reliability; they do not identify a correct option by wording alone. Common wound care and follow-up prevent a uniquely comprehensive discharge option.

Single-node case: all numerator, denominator, reliability and limb-examination information is present. The task is complete without another node. This is clinical vascular assessment with a consequential calculation, not a statistics item requiring removal of the second step.
suggestions: Retain the raw pressures and the incorrect recorded ratio without announcing the inversion before answering. Preserve the short worked calculation in feedback.

record.title: Recognize cumulative false-positive risk
fairness: For independent true-null tests at alpha 0.05, the familywise probability is 1-0.95^10, approximately 0.401, compared with 0.05 for one test. Thus it increases.

decisionNodes.stem: Which pattern explains the crude pathway difference in this constructed comparison?

answerChoices.label: Confounding by baseline severity
answerChoices.rationale: Within each baseline stratum the pathway risks match, while A includes more high-severity participants. That mix produces the crude difference in this constructed comparison.

answerChoices.label: Effect modification by baseline severity
answerChoices.rationale: Both stratum-specific pathway risk ratios are one. Severity changes event risk, but it does not change the displayed pathway association on the risk-ratio scale.

answerChoices.label: No confounding or effect modification
answerChoices.rationale: The equal stratum-specific ratios exclude the displayed ratio-scale modification, but they do not erase the crude difference caused by the unequal baseline mix.

decisionNodes.explanation:
Compare risks within baseline strata: low 2/10 = 18/90 = 20%; high 54/90 = 6/10 = 60%.
Crude risks are 56/100 = 56% for A and 24/100 = 24% for B.
The unequal baseline mix explains this constructed difference, consistent with confounding here.
Equal stratum risk ratios do not show effect modification; crude/adjusted disagreement alone does not prove confounding.

record.title: Recognize preferential detection of slow disease
fairness: Length-time bias is the best answer for preferential screening detection of slow-growing tumors while faster tumors become symptomatic between screens. Lead-time bias can coexist, but does not describe this selection mechanism; recall bias is unsupported.

The task specifically asks about the detection pattern, so coexistence does not create a second best answer. The explanation explicitly preserves that distinction. Growth-related capture is the data the learner must classify.

record.title: Source control before encapsulation during deterioration
fairness: Percutaneous catheter drainage now is the best offered plan. Escalating support despite active antibiotics and resuscitation makes continued waiting inappropriate; the liquid lateral target and surrounding anatomy then support catheter access rather than primary open necrosectomy.

Waiting for encapsulation and operating because infection is uncontrolled are both recognizable competing errors. The bowel-enhancement and bleeding observations help avoid confusing this presentation with a separate operative catastrophe; they should not be deleted merely as negatives.
The explanation does not turn the calendar day into a mandatory intervention threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The current node contains the infection evidence, treatment failure and anatomy needed to stand alone. In the proposed sequence, day-17 improvement followed by day-18 deterioration is coherent. Prior feedback reduces the novelty of the timing rule, but the current anatomy still requires a new route decision; the combined sequence is not granted an independent difficulty PASS here.

record.title: Nutrition route during prolonged intestinal dysfunction
fairness: Parenteral nutrition is the best offered route for the stated required support. The resident must distinguish diffuse intestinal dysfunction from isolated gastric intolerance, then recognize why bypassing the stomach does not solve the demonstrated delivery problem.

Nasojejunal feeding is a credible competitor because enteral support is generally preferred; persistent small-bowel dilation and lack of contrast progression, alongside the clinical course, distinguish this case. Nasogastric feeding has already failed.

The task is route selection, not a universal day for initiating parenteral nutrition. 'Several days' would not independently establish an exact initiation threshold; the explanation appropriately avoids one. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified at the stated scope.

Standalone context is sufficient. In the proposed nonexecuting nutrition sequence, subsequent recovery of distal transit can coherently change the route; this explanation invites reassessment but does not reveal the later nasojejunal answer.

record.title: Step-up debridement after effective liquid drainage
fairness: Video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement is the best offered next procedure. The resident must interpret patent catheters plus collapse of the liquid spaces as achieved drainage with persistent solid burden, then choose an escalation and route compatible with the remaining anatomy.

Catheter upsizing with irrigation is a credible close alternative, not an absurd distractor. Persistence of illness despite emptied liquid spaces and bulky residual material favors debridement here. This does not establish that further catheter strategies can never work in other patients.

The intervening colon makes transgastric necrosectomy unsuitable, but that exclusion alone does not resolve VARD versus catheter optimization. The catheter study and follow-up CT therefore have a genuine consequence. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The standalone node includes the previous procedure, elapsed course, drain performance, antibiotic response and access anatomy. In the proposed drainage sequence, escalation follows actual acquired failure rather than a hypothetical result, and the preceding explanation does not name this answer.

record.title: Reduce fluid loading after new congestion
fairness: The best offered adjustment is reducing or stopping ongoing crystalloid with reassessment. New oxygen requirement, crackles, B-lines and venous congestion combined with recovered perfusion support that choice.

The two consequential steps are integrating respiratory/venous findings as congestion despite favorable BUN/urine trends, then changing the fluid plan rather than continuing the earlier appropriate treatment. B-lines alone would not establish the cause, but the combined record is sufficient for this offered adjustment.
All three options include reassessment and differ in the same immediate treatment dimension. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally best offered answer identified.

Chronology is explicit and the presentation/current update contain enough information without the earlier response. Prior feedback teaches reassessment without disclosing this specific answer. Difficulty is qualitative, not measured.

record.title: Postpyloric feeding after gastric-route failure
fairness: Nasojejunal feeding is the preferred offered temporary plan: interpret proximal compression with preserved distal passage, then bypass the failed gastric route while using the functioning intestine.

Further prokinetic escalation is a plausible competing response to gastric intolerance, but persistent vomiting after a trial and the compression findings favor changing route. Parenteral nutrition remains a fallback if enteral access or delivery fails, not the preferred first response to this supplied record.
The observations support an attempt at postpyloric delivery, not a guarantee of technical tube-placement success. The explanation retains that limit. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

This later assessment stands alone because it supplies the current feeding failure and distal transit evidence. In the proposed nutrition sequence, it can follow diffuse dysfunction resolving with residual proximal compression; the previous explanation does not specify this answer.

record.title: Persistent volume deficit after an initial bolus
fairness: An additional LR bolus followed by reassessment is the best offered response. The resident must reconcile reassuring resting pressure and positive balance with positional hypotension, oliguria and rising concentration markers, then choose further resuscitation rather than merely continuing or stopping replacement.

Oral tolerance does not establish adequate replacement, and a positive chart balance does not establish adequate intravascular volume. These are real competing interpretations, rather than an authored hypovolemia label.
The vignette does not justify a fixed bolus volume or schedule, and neither the option nor explanation prescribes one. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
This standalone node establishes its own initial bolus and response. It does not depend on the unchanged fluid-overload item or authorize combining the two exact versions without a sequence review.

record.title: Surgical decompression without premature necrosectomy
fairness: Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure is the defensible best offered procedure for sustained markedly elevated measured intra-abdominal pressure with renal/ventilatory dysfunction despite optimized medical measures and drainage of accessible fluid.

The two consequential steps are recognizing refractory abdominal compartment physiology from pressure plus organ dysfunction, then distinguishing the indication for pressure relief from an indication for pancreatic necrosectomy. The early uninfected necrosis makes the latter distinction consequential.

The remaining small fluid layer makes further fluid drainage less attractive, but that observation is necessary to establish failure of the less invasive option. It is not a reason to hide drainability information.

Parallel procedure choices preserve a credible error: combining necessary laparotomy with unnecessary early debridement. No confident clinical inaccuracy or competing equally best offered answer identified. Difficulty is an offline qualitative prediction.

record.title: Postponing intervention during a response to antibiotics
fairness: Continue antibiotics and postpone drainage with close reassessment is the best offered plan. The resident must distinguish established infection from uncontrolled infection by interpreting the acquired response, then apply that response to intervention timing before encapsulation.

Immediate percutaneous drainage is the closest credible alternative: infection is a real indication to consider intervention, but improving organ function and intake support postponement. Open necrosectomy is a weaker, historically plausible failure to apply a step-up approach.
The explanation correctly makes delay conditional and avoids requiring eventual drainage or a fixed intervention date. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The standalone node supplies infection evidence, treatment and subsequent response. The proposed day-18 deterioration can coherently follow this transient response. This feedback teaches the conditional nature of delay but does not supply the later route choice.

record.title: Gas after collection drainage and antibiotic decisions
fairness: Observation with repeat infection assessment is the best offered plan. The resident must contextualize new cavity gas after instrumentation and then use the untreated improving clinical trajectory to decide whether infection-directed treatment is warranted.

Empirical antibiotics are a credible error when gas and a transient temperature are overweighted. Aspiration is not a necessary prerequisite in this improving scenario. Negative blood cultures appropriately do not establish sterility.

The temporal information is necessary evidence, not a pre-answer diagnosis label. Options have comparable scope and all address the current infection decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
The mature collection and completed drainage are fully stated, so the node works independently of earlier imaging or drainage tasks.

case.presentation: Gabriel Reed, a 62-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside acute-pancreatitis admission. The initial record showed vomiting, thirst, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, low urine output and rising BUN. His lungs were clear. He had no cardiac or renal disease.
sourceLabels: ACG guideline highlights: acute pancreatitis

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During the next hospital interval the infusion continued and cumulative balance rose markedly. Gabriel developed new oxygen need, bibasal crackles and diffuse lung ultrasound B-lines. Blood pressure was 126/76 mmHg, urine output had recovered and BUN was falling. Bedside assessment found a plethoric vena cava.

answerChoices.rationale: New congestion with restored perfusion calls for reversing continued fluid loading and reassessing support.

case.presentation: Marcus Ellis, a 54-year-old man, attends clinic after recovery to review an outside ICU admission for necrotizing pancreatitis. After resuscitation his abdomen became tense, urine output fell and ventilator pressures rose despite stable systemic blood pressure.
sourceLabels: 2019 WSES guidelines for severe acute pancreatitis
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Repeated standardized bladder-pressure measurements were 28 and 30 mmHg. Sedation, paralysis and nasogastric/rectal decompression had been optimized. A percutaneous catheter drained the accessible ascites, but pressure and renal/ventilatory dysfunction persisted; the repeat study showed only a small residual fluid layer. Necrosis remained early and unencapsulated, without evidence of infection.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next procedure should the clinic review recommend for Marcus Ellis at that ICU decision point?

answerChoices.label: Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
answerChoices.rationale: Pressure-related organ dysfunction persists despite nonoperative and percutaneous measures, supporting operative decompression.

answerChoices.label: Additional percutaneous drainage of abdominal fluid
answerChoices.rationale: The accessible ascites has already been drained and the remaining fluid layer is small, without reversing the pressure/organ problem.

answerChoices.label: Laparotomy with immediate pancreatic necrosectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Opening the abdomen to relieve pressure does not make early sterile pancreatic debridement necessary.

decisionNodes.explanation: Combine sustained high intra-abdominal pressure with worsening organ function, then use the actual failure of medical and drain-based decompression. Surgical pressure relief is justified here. That indication does not itself justify early pancreatic necrosectomy.
sourceLabels: 2019 WSES guidelines for severe acute pancreatitis
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

concept.learningObjective: Select decompression for refractory pressure-related organ dysfunction without automatic necrosectomy.

record.title: Surgical decompression without premature necrosectomy
fairness: Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure is the defensible best offered procedure for sustained markedly elevated measured intra-abdominal pressure with renal/ventilatory dysfunction despite optimized medical measures and drainage of accessible fluid.

The two consequential steps are recognizing refractory abdominal compartment physiology from pressure plus organ dysfunction, then distinguishing the indication for pressure relief from an indication for pancreatic necrosectomy. The early uninfected necrosis makes the latter distinction consequential.

The remaining small fluid layer makes further fluid drainage less attractive, but that observation is necessary to establish failure of the less invasive option. It is not a reason to hide drainability information.

Parallel procedure choices preserve a credible error: combining necessary laparotomy with unnecessary early debridement. No confident clinical inaccuracy or competing equally best offered answer identified. Difficulty is an offline qualitative prediction.

fairness: Observation with repeat infection assessment is the best offered plan. The resident must contextualize new cavity gas after instrumentation and then use the untreated improving clinical trajectory to decide whether infection-directed treatment is warranted.

case.presentation: Owen Price, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic to review nutrition during an outside admission for necrotizing pancreatitis. Required nutritional support had not been achieved over several days.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the current review, repeated oral and low-rate gastric trials produced vomiting and distension. Serial contrast studies showed dilated stomach and small-bowel loops without a focal transition; contrast remained within the proximal loops on the later study. He had passed neither stool nor flatus for several days despite correction of electrolytes and reduction of sedating medicines. Perfusion was stable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which route should provide the required nutritional support at Owen Price's current assessment?

answerChoices.label: Central venous parenteral nutrition
answerChoices.rationale: The achieved course indicates a persistent problem involving more than the stomach; bypassing the stomach does not establish a functioning enteral route.

answerChoices.label: Continuous nasojejunal enteral feeding
answerChoices.rationale: A more distal tube bypasses the stomach but not the diffuse nonpropulsive small-bowel problem shown here.

answerChoices.label: Continuous nasogastric enteral feeding
answerChoices.rationale: This would deliver nutrients into a route that has repeatedly failed in the setting of diffuse intestinal dysfunction.

decisionNodes.explanation: The preference for enteral nutrition presupposes a usable gastrointestinal route. Here the serial distribution/progression findings and the achieved feeding course involve the small bowel as well as the stomach. Parenteral support is appropriate while the prolonged intestinal dysfunction prevents adequate enteral delivery. Reassess for enteral use as function returns.

concept.clinicalVersioningReason: Recognize prolonged intestinal dysfunction that makes enteral delivery infeasible and requires parenteral support. The scored discriminator changes from the prior item; do not transfer its FSRS history.

record.title: Nutrition route during prolonged intestinal dysfunction
fairness: Parenteral nutrition is the best offered route for the stated required support. The resident must distinguish diffuse intestinal dysfunction from isolated gastric intolerance, then recognize why bypassing the stomach does not solve the demonstrated delivery problem.

Nasojejunal feeding is a credible competitor because enteral support is generally preferred; persistent small-bowel dilation and lack of contrast progression, alongside the clinical course, distinguish this case. Nasogastric feeding has already failed.

The task is route selection, not a universal day for initiating parenteral nutrition. 'Several days' would not independently establish an exact initiation threshold; the explanation appropriately avoids one. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified at the stated scope.

Standalone context is sufficient. In the proposed nonexecuting nutrition sequence, subsequent recovery of distal transit can coherently change the route; this explanation invites reassessment but does not reveal the later nasojejunal answer.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At this review, enteral contrast passed beyond a narrowed duodenal segment into nondilated small bowel and reached the colon. A post-pancreatitis collection indented the stomach and duodenum. Low-rate continuous gastric feeding still caused repeated vomiting despite a prokinetic trial. Decompression relieved the distension; perfusion remained stable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which temporary nutrition plan is preferred for Owen Price at this assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continuous nasojejunal tube feeding
answerChoices.rationale: The downstream bowel now functions while the gastric route remains poorly tolerated; a postpyloric route can preserve enteral delivery.

answerChoices.label: Nasogastric feeding with further prokinetic escalation
answerChoices.rationale: Further gastric optimization is plausible for functional retention, but the repeated trial failure and proximal indentation favor bypassing this segment.

answerChoices.label: Central venous parenteral nutrition
answerChoices.rationale: The recovered distal passage does not establish failure of all enteral nutrition.

decisionNodes.explanation: Distal passage and nondilated small bowel make this a different route problem from diffuse intestinal dysfunction. The gastric trial remains poorly tolerated in the setting of proximal compression, so temporary postpyloric feeding is the preferred offered plan. Parenteral nutrition is appropriate if feasible enteral delivery cannot meet needs; further gastric drug optimization is more attractive when the limitation is functional and responding.

record.title: Postpyloric feeding after gastric-route failure
fairness: Nasojejunal feeding is the preferred offered temporary plan: interpret proximal compression with preserved distal passage, then bypass the failed gastric route while using the functioning intestine.

Further prokinetic escalation is a plausible competing response to gastric intolerance, but persistent vomiting after a trial and the compression findings favor changing route. Parenteral nutrition remains a fallback if enteral access or delivery fails, not the preferred first response to this supplied record.
The observations support an attempt at postpyloric delivery, not a guarantee of technical tube-placement success. The explanation retains that limit. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

This later assessment stands alone because it supplies the current feeding failure and distal transit evidence. In the proposed nutrition sequence, it can follow diffuse dysfunction resolving with residual proximal compression; the previous explanation does not specify this answer.

case.presentation: Gabriel Reed, a 62-year-old man, attends clinic to review his outside acute-pancreatitis admission. The initial record showed vomiting, thirst, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, low urine output and rising BUN. His lungs were clear. He had no cardiac or renal disease.
sourceLabels: ACG guideline highlights: acute pancreatitis
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Two hours after the initial bolus, resting blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg. On sitting up he became dizzy, pulse rose from 94 to 122/min and pressure fell to 88/56 mmHg. Urine output remained scant, BUN rose from 30 to 38 mg/dL and hematocrit from 46% to 50%. The chart balance was positive. Lungs remained clear and he had taken oral liquids without vomiting. All plans include frequent perfusion, respiratory and laboratory reassessment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which fluid strategy is supported by Gabriel Reed's two-hour hospital assessment?

answerChoices.label: Additional lactated Ringer bolus, then reassess the infusion
answerChoices.rationale: The orthostatic and renal/hemoconcentration trajectory shows persisting perfusion deficit despite an improved resting pressure and positive balance.

answerChoices.label: Continue the current lactated Ringer infusion and reassess
answerChoices.rationale: A maintenance-only response underestimates the remaining deficit shown by the current orthostatic and laboratory course.

answerChoices.label: Stop intravenous replacement and use oral fluid with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The ability to take liquid does not establish restored intravascular perfusion in the actual course.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the response across domains. A normal resting pressure and positive recorded balance do not erase the orthostatic, renal and hemoconcentration findings. Additional LR resuscitation with reassessment is the preferred offered response to this persisting deficit. Do not convert it into scheduled boluses or an invented fixed-volume target.

record.title: Persistent volume deficit after an initial bolus
fairness: An additional LR bolus followed by reassessment is the best offered response. The resident must reconcile reassuring resting pressure and positive balance with positional hypotension, oliguria and rising concentration markers, then choose further resuscitation rather than merely continuing or stopping replacement.

Oral tolerance does not establish adequate replacement, and a positive chart balance does not establish adequate intravascular volume. These are real competing interpretations, rather than an authored hypovolemia label.
The vignette does not justify a fixed bolus volume or schedule, and neither the option nor explanation prescribes one. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
This standalone node establishes its own initial bolus and response. It does not depend on the unchanged fluid-overload item or authorize combining the two exact versions without a sequence review.

case.presentation: Elena Brooks, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after recovery to review the decisions made during her outside hospital admission. On day 15 of pancreatitis, CT showed nonencapsulated pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis containing new gas. There had been no instrumentation or bowel fistula. Blood cultures grew an enteric organism.
sourceLabels: ACG guideline highlights: acute pancreatitis
2019 WSES guidelines for severe acute pancreatitis
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the day-17 review after susceptibility-guided intravenous antibiotics, fever had resolved, pain had eased and enteral intake had increased. She was alert, off vasopressors and had recovering renal function. The collection remained partly liquid with an irregular boundary rather than a complete wall.
decisionNodes.stem: Which necrosis-intervention plan is supported by Elena Brooks's day-17 hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Continue antibiotics and postpone drainage with close reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The actual clinical response permits postponement while the target organizes; infection is not an automatic immediate operation.

answerChoices.label: Continue antibiotics and place a percutaneous drain now
answerChoices.rationale: The improving course permits deferral rather than mandatory immediate access.

answerChoices.label: Continue antibiotics and perform open necrosectomy now
answerChoices.rationale: Primary open debridement bypasses successful stabilization without a supplied rescue indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: The combined gas and culture record supports infection, but the next decision depends on the observed course. Effective antibiotics and recovery can permit postponing intervention while a wall develops. Delay remains conditional on ongoing control; it is neither a mandatory eventual-drainage rule nor a universal intervention date.

record.title: Postponing intervention during a response to antibiotics
fairness: Continue antibiotics and postpone drainage with close reassessment is the best offered plan. The resident must distinguish established infection from uncontrolled infection by interpreting the acquired response, then apply that response to intervention timing before encapsulation.

Immediate percutaneous drainage is the closest credible alternative: infection is a real indication to consider intervention, but improving organ function and intake support postponement. Open necrosectomy is a weaker, historically plausible failure to apply a step-up approach.
The explanation correctly makes delay conditional and avoids requiring eventual drainage or a fixed intervention date. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The standalone node supplies infection evidence, treatment and subsequent response. The proposed day-18 deterioration can coherently follow this transient response. This feedback teaches the conditional nature of delay but does not supply the later route choice.

case.presentation: Elena Brooks, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after recovery to review the decisions made during her outside hospital admission. On day 15 of pancreatitis, CT showed nonencapsulated pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis containing new gas. There had been no instrumentation or bowel fistula. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At day 18, fever returned, lactate rose and vasopressor requirements increased despite susceptibility-active antibiotics and resuscitation. fairness: Percutaneous catheter drainage now is the best offered plan. Escalating support despite active antibiotics and resuscitation makes continued waiting inappropriate; the liquid lateral target and surrounding anatomy then support catheter access rather than primary open necrosectomy.

Waiting for encapsulation and operating because infection is uncontrolled are both recognizable competing errors. The bowel-enhancement and bleeding observations help avoid confusing this presentation with a separate operative catastrophe; they should not be deleted merely as negatives.
The explanation does not turn the calendar day into a mandatory intervention threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The current node contains the infection evidence, treatment failure and anatomy needed to stand alone. In the proposed sequence, day-17 improvement followed by day-18 deterioration is coherent. Prior feedback reduces the novelty of the timing rule, but the current anatomy still requires a new route decision; the combined sequence is not granted an independent difficulty PASS here.

case.presentation: Victor Hayes, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic to review a reassessment during week 7 of his outside necrotizing-pancreatitis admission. A completely walled left-paracolic collection contained bulky nonliquid debris. Catheter drainage had been performed several days earlier.
sourceLabels: 2019 WSES guidelines for severe acute pancreatitis
KSGE peripancreatic fluid collection guideline
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Contrast injection through both flank catheters filled the liquid spaces around the residual material, and both catheters flushed freely. Follow-up CT showed collapse of those liquid spaces around the drains but little change in the bulky nonliquid component. Fever and organ-support needs persisted despite susceptibility-active antibiotics. The flank catheter tips lay beside the residual burden; colon still separated the collection from the stomach.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next source-control procedure is preferred at Victor Hayes's current reassessment?

answerChoices.label: Video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement
answerChoices.rationale: The achieved liquid drainage and persistent bulky solid burden support removing necrosis through the existing flank approach.

answerChoices.label: Catheter upsizing with cavity irrigation
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible less invasive optimization policy, but the patent catheters and collapsed liquid spaces indicate that the remaining burden is predominantly nonliquid and the illness persists.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided transgastric necrosectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The residual burden is lateral and colon remains between it and the stomach; an endoscopic route is not established by wall maturity alone.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret what drainage achieved before calling for another step. The liquid spaces have collapsed around patent drains, while solid necrosis and clinical illness persist. That pattern favors debridement rather than simply greater liquid-drainage capacity. The existing flank approach and intervening colon support the offered retroperitoneal route over transgastric debridement.

record.title: Step-up debridement after effective liquid drainage
fairness: Video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement is the best offered next procedure. The resident must interpret patent catheters plus collapse of the liquid spaces as achieved drainage with persistent solid burden, then choose an escalation and route compatible with the remaining anatomy.

Catheter upsizing with irrigation is a credible close alternative, not an absurd distractor. Persistence of illness despite emptied liquid spaces and bulky residual material favors debridement here. This does not establish that further catheter strategies can never work in other patients.

The intervening colon makes transgastric necrosectomy unsuitable, but that exclusion alone does not resolve VARD versus catheter optimization. The catheter study and follow-up CT therefore have a genuine consequence. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The standalone node includes the previous procedure, elapsed course, drain performance, antibiotic response and access anatomy. In the proposed drainage sequence, escalation follows actual acquired failure rather than a hypothetical result, and the preceding explanation does not name this answer.

case.presentation: Marcus Ellis, a 54-year-old man, attends clinic after recovery to review an outside ICU admission for necrotizing pancreatitis. After resuscitation his abdomen became tense, urine output fell and ventilator pressures rose despite stable systemic blood pressure.
sourceLabels: 2019 WSES guidelines for severe acute pancreatitis
iLATAM-AP acute pancreatitis guideline

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Repeated standardized bladder-pressure measurements were 28 and 30 mmHg. Sedation, paralysis and nasogastric/rectal decompression had been optimized. A percutaneous catheter drained the accessible ascites, but pressure and renal/ventilatory dysfunction persisted; the repeat study showed only a small residual fluid layer. Necrosis remained early and unencapsulated, without evidence of infection.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next procedure should the clinic review recommend for Marcus Ellis at that ICU decision point?

answerChoices.label: Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
answerChoices.rationale: Pressure-related organ dysfunction persists despite nonoperative and percutaneous measures, supporting operative decompression.

answerChoices.label: Additional percutaneous drainage of abdominal fluid
answerChoices.rationale: The accessible ascites has already been drained and the remaining fluid layer is small, without reversing the pressure/organ problem.

answerChoices.label: Laparotomy with immediate pancreatic necrosectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Opening the abdomen to relieve pressure does not make early sterile pancreatic debridement necessary.

concept.displayName: Select decompression for refractory pressure-related organ dysfunction without automatic necrosectomy.
concept.learningObjective: Select decompression for refractory pressure-related organ dysfunction without automatic necrosectomy.

record.title: Surgical decompression without premature necrosectomy
fairness: Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure is the defensible best offered procedure for sustained markedly elevated measured intra-abdominal pressure with renal/ventilatory dysfunction despite optimized medical measures and drainage of accessible fluid.

The two consequential steps are recognizing refractory abdominal compartment physiology from pressure plus organ dysfunction, then distinguishing the indication for pressure relief from an indication for pancreatic necrosectomy. The early uninfected necrosis makes the latter distinction consequential.

The remaining small fluid layer makes further fluid drainage less attractive, but that observation is necessary to establish failure of the less invasive option. It is not a reason to hide drainability information.

Parallel procedure choices preserve a credible error: combining necessary laparotomy with unnecessary early debridement. No confident clinical inaccuracy or competing equally best offered answer identified. Difficulty is an offline qualitative prediction.

record.title: Selecting serology after an inadequate celiac panel
fairness: tTG-IgA is the conventional best next blood test in this gluten-exposed, IgA-sufficient adult. EMA remains a clinically useful assay; its presence is a credible sequencing distractor, not proof that EMA is diagnostically invalid.

The learner must interpret the significance of an isolated IgG result and HLA susceptibility in the stated IgA context, then choose the appropriate initial IgA-based assessment instead of another IgG assay or a confirmatory-stage assay. This is a common diagnostic-workup concept, with moderate rather than hard predicted difficulty.

The task explicitly requests a blood test, so the absence of an endoscopic biopsy option does not create a competing next-test key. The named adult, sex, gluten exposure and task are supplied without another node.

Cue attack: tTG and IgA occur in the record, but the key spells out tissue transglutaminase, and both IgA choices remain viable on a purely lexical reading. The assay names and normal total IgA are necessary data, not sufficient nonmedical answer cues.

This is an offline editorial review of the supplied visible fields, not fresh source verification or clinical approval. The same limitation applies to every entry in this report; PASS does not change needs_clinician_review. Runtime rendering and wait estimates are outside the supplied visible-field review.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the distinction between a preferred initial assay and an invalid test; do not strengthen the explanation into a claim that EMA cannot evaluate celiac disease.
Optional brevity edit: remove the announcement that the outside panel and laboratory report are available; the update already supplies them.

record.title: Initial source control of a Crohn-associated collection
fairness: The collection, accessible route, maintained circulation and localized examination support antibiotics with percutaneous drainage over immediate resection or infliximab induction into an undrained infection. No competing best answer or confident clinical inaccuracy is apparent in this record.

Interpret the focal collection as a penetrating infectious complication, then use the physiology and anatomy to select the initial source-control strategy. Immediate resection is a credible stage-of-care error. This is high-yield and moderate, although the infliximab alternative is easier to reject.

The phrase 'with an image-guided access path' favors drainage, but supplies decision-critical anatomy rather than merely announcing service availability. Removing it would weaken the ranking against surgery; retain it.

The retrospective clinic frame and task agree about the admission time point. As the first node, it needs no later findings. Its explanation teaches initial source control without naming the later node's limited-resection answer; the later fistula/stenosis decision remains distinct.

All options share antibiotics and compare specific additional treatments. No unique length, qualifier, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut selects the key without interpreting the clinical findings.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the localized examination, physiology and access anatomy; do not remove these necessary discriminators in an attempt to increase difficulty.
Keep the later persistent-fistula and obstruction results out of this node's pre-answer display.

record.title: Persistent fistula and obstructing ileal disease after source control
fairness: Persistent communication from the skin tract to ileum together with symptomatic fixed narrowing and upstream dilation supports limited resection after infection control and nutritional recovery. Strictureplasty across this fistulizing segment and balloon dilation are inferior choices for the stated combination.

The learner must distinguish resolution of the collection from persistence of penetrating and obstructive bowel disease, then choose the bowel operation appropriate to that combination. This is a high-yield surgical selection problem with plausible bowel-preservation errors.

The sequence is coherent. The update states that the collection and fever resolved and supplies persistent drainage, symptoms, imaging and optimization; the learner can answer with this presentation and update even without recalling the prior selected answer. Earlier feedback does not disclose how to treat the new fistulizing stenosis.

The first two options both use 'fistulizing', and all three address the ileal narrowing. That shared terminology does not uniquely identify the key. The alternatives have comparable scope and contain no explanatory ridicule.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the simultaneous fistula and obstruction findings and the explicit infection-control chronology.

Optional precision edit in a future version: describe the medical-treatment course more concretely than 'optimized IBD therapy' if its adequacy is to become a scored discriminator; the current operative ranking does not require an invented regimen or duration.

record.title: Bowel preservation for separated uncomplicated Crohn strictures
fairness: The short, separated jejunal strictures, prior bowel loss, inaccessible endoscopic sites and absence of penetrating or suspicious findings support strictureplasty. Separate resections remain a credible operative alternative, but would remove additional bowel; en bloc resection would also sacrifice the intervening supple segments.

The two consequential judgments are whether these sites are suitable for strictureplasty and how distribution plus remaining bowel changes the choice versus resection. This is a core operative principle and moderate predicted difficulty, not a complex strictureplasty-technique question.
The 140 cm finding is patient anatomy, not a stated universal intestinal-failure threshold. The explanation appropriately avoids promising parenteral-nutrition independence or asserting a cutoff.

The negative findings are a conspicuous eligibility checklist, but they supply genuine contraindication information rather than quote the answer. 'Three narrowed segments' occurs in two options, and the options remain parallel operations. No decisive nonmedical cue was identified.
The retrospective operative task is complete and standalone. The patient, age and sex are explicit.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Do not make the item harder by withholding fistula, collection or mass findings that determine eligibility.

record.title: Discordant postoperative markers and an incomplete endoscopic examination

cues.phrase: Continue treatment with biomarker-only monitoring
cues.why: The '-only' qualifier makes this option sound less comprehensive than the key. This is a minor stylistic cue, not a decisive shortcut: surveillance without endoscopy is an actual competing strategy, and the reader must still interpret the raised markers and examination coverage.

fairness: A distal examination ending at the splenic flexure has not assessed the ileocolic postoperative site. Repeatedly elevated stool markers despite symptomatic remission and normal CRP support completing endoscopic assessment before empiric infliximab escalation. The displayed record resolves why repeating an apparently normal examination is appropriate.

Two consequential steps remain: reject whole-disease reassurance from limited specimen/visual coverage, then choose confirmation rather than symptom-based monitoring or treatment escalation based on a nonspecific marker. Both competing plans represent plausible clinical errors. This is high-yield and moderate.

The incomplete examination is actual acquisition information, not merely a statement that a desired test has not been done. The key is allowed to be an investigation against management alternatives because the record supplies a real unresolved discrepancy.

The explanation explicitly limits its postoperative monitoring claim. I cannot independently verify the exact scope of the conditional low-calprotectin guidance offline; I identify no confident contradiction in this high-marker, incompletely assessed case and do not endorse a universal rule.
The standalone update supplies the resection, timing, treatment and current condition without requiring the earlier Crohn case. The exhibit is labeled constructed and the task is complete.
suggestions: Optional wording cleanup: name the monitoring plan concretely, such as continuing infliximab with repeat fecal calprotectin assessment, rather than advertising '-only'. Do not introduce an unsupported interval.

Remove the editorial phrase 'a universal endoscopy-for-every-normal-marker rule is withheld' from learner feedback in a future revision; state the clinical limitation directly. Retain clinician verification of the conditional guideline boundary.

record.title: Initial therapy for localized GIST threatening major bowel loss
fairness: Localized disease does not by itself make immediate surgery the best initial plan when inseparable arterial arcades supply a long length of uninvolved bowel. Controlled bleeding and maintained intake permit a neoadjuvant strategy; the KIT exon 11 result supports the conventional imatinib choice over sunitinib.

The learner must infer the functional consequence of en bloc vascular resection, then combine that consequence with molecular sensitivity and the absence of an urgent symptom driver to choose initial therapy. Immediate surgery is a credible error, and sunitinib tests treatment-line confusion. This is high-yield and moderate, not merely diagnosis recognition.

The known GIST diagnosis is appropriate for a management question. Two choices share 'Begin neoadjuvant ... therapy', so that phrasing does not uniquely identify imatinib. The vascular description supplies operative consequences without directly stating 'unresectable' or naming a desired drug.

The word 'variant' is less precise than an activating pathogenic KIT mutation. I have not verified the particular molecular result offline and am not treating every possible exon 11 variant as sensitive. This is a precision limitation, not a confident claim that the conventional keyed answer is clinically wrong.
The named patient, staging, bleeding status and vascular anatomy make the task standalone. No later surgical result is needed.
suggestions: No blocking change to the intended clinical decision. A future precision edit should identify the molecular finding as a pathogenic activating mutation if that is what the constructed pathology record intends; have the clinician verify the sensitivity statement without inventing a specific sequence variant.
Keep the vascular supply consequence and controlled symptoms; removing either would weaken the sequencing decision against immediate surgery.

record.title: Persistent pouch symptoms after incomplete distal mucosal assessment
fairness: Normal pouch-body and afferent-limb findings do not establish normality of the obscured distal channel. Persistent bleeding and urgency justify completing site-specific mucosal evaluation before assigning the new evacuation symptoms to a primary functional disorder.

The learner must localize the limitation of the available observations and biopsy, then rank mucosal reassessment against physiology testing prompted by genuine straining and incomplete evacuation. Manometry is a credible near-miss, making this a high-yield moderate investigation-sequencing item.

MRI for a fistula is the weakest competitor: no draining tract, focal sepsis or other specific penetrating finding is supplied. Nevertheless, it is a real alternative investigation for structural pouch complications, not a nonsensical test. It does not outrank completing the clearly limited mucosal examination in this record.

The exhibit reports actual obscuration and sampled sites rather than merely announcing that a test was omitted. Repeating pouchoscopy therefore is not a disposable already-completed-test foil. 'Pouchoscopy' appears in both the prior report and the key, but that repetition alone does not establish whether repetition is justified.

The explanation does not claim that normal pouch histology excludes all pouch disease or that evacuation dysfunction can never coexist. The standalone presentation supplies the pouch history, current symptoms and investigation limits without a prior case. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Keep persistent bleeding, the genuine evacuation symptoms and the exact sites of adequate versus obscured examination; they establish the ordering of the competing investigations.

For a future harder variant, strengthen the third investigation's patient-specific rationale only if supported observations still leave one best next test. Do not add decorative fistula symptoms or remove the necessary examination limitation.

record.title: Extent of the initial operation after failed acute UC therapy
fairness: The operation-selection task explicitly begins after colectomy has been chosen. It therefore does not require the reader to invent the duration or criteria for failure of methylprednisolone and infliximab rescue.

Total abdominal colectomy with end ileostomy is the defensible initial operation for the supplied acute, steroid-exposed, nutritionally compromised record. Immediate pouch construction is a credible but premature definitive-treatment error; proctocolectomy with end ileostomy avoids a pouch anastomosis but still adds pelvic dissection.

Two consequential judgments are needed: recognize why the current risk state changes reconstructive timing, then distinguish deferral of pelvic dissection from simply avoiding an undiverted anastomosis. The alternatives are specific operations, including a diverted pouch, so this is a high-yield moderate staging question.

Absence of neoplasm or rectal perforation supports the rectum-preserving initial strategy. These are necessary boundary observations rather than a lexical match to the key. All choices have comparable procedural specificity; the key is not the uniquely qualified cautious option.

The retrospective clinic frame and hospital-operation task agree. The update provides the decision stage and relevant patient condition without another node. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the distinction between diversion and deferral of pouch construction, and between avoiding an anastomosis and avoiding pelvic surgery.
Optional clarity addition to feedback: explicitly state that the rectum is retained at this initial stage. Do not add an unsupported fixed interval for completion surgery.

record.title: Management after complete excision of visible low-grade dysplasia
fairness: En bloc excision, negative margins and absence of dysplasia in surrounding and other sampled mucosa support endoscopic surveillance. Total proctocolectomy is a meaningful over-treatment trap in a patient with extensive UC; segmental resection lacks a remaining target in the supplied record.

The learner must integrate lesion visibility, excision adequacy and the other mucosal samples, then distinguish surveillance from the obsolete simplification that any colitis-associated dysplasia mandates colectomy. This is a high-yield, lower-moderate application item, not a hard item.

The explanation appropriately says the lesion 'can be followed endoscopically' and does not claim that colectomy is never an option or that follow-up can stop. No exact unsupported surveillance interval is introduced.

'Surveillance' appears in the complaint/presentation and in the key, but the visit is a review of a surveillance examination; that word does not establish what should happen after dysplasia is found. Margins and mucosal findings are necessary clinical evidence, not gratuitous exclusions.
This is a standalone case in the supplied active packet. It does not expose the later invisible-high-grade candidate or its answer.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve complete excision and assessment of other mucosa; those facts distinguish this case from a biopsy-only or incompletely resected lesion.
Keep the teaching point conditional on the supplied findings rather than teaching surveillance for all UC-associated low-grade dysplasia.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At admission she had fever and focal right lower abdominal tenderness. decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment best fit {patientName}'s outside-hospital findings at this point?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous antibiotics with percutaneous abscess drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The contained accessible collection and maintained physiology support infection control by drainage and antibiotics before reassessment of bowel treatment.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous antibiotics with immediate ileocecal resection
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate resection can be required with uncontrolled sepsis or generalized contamination; the stated localized accessible process permits an initial drainage strategy.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous antibiotics with infliximab induction
answerChoices.rationale: Antibiotics do not make the undrained collection an appropriate setting for immediate immunosuppressive induction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the rim-enhancing collection as a localized penetrating complication, then combine its access anatomy with the patient's stability. Antibiotics plus image-guided drainage fit this initial phase. Generalized peritonitis, shock or failed source control would change the surgical priority.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Later records show resolution of the collection and fever. A drain study continues to opacify ileum from the skin tract. Meals provoke pain and vomiting; enterography shows a fixed ileal narrowing with upstream dilation. These findings persist despite optimized IBD therapy and nutritional recovery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which bowel treatment best fit {patientName}'s later record after the infection had been controlled?

answerChoices.label: Limited resection of the fistulizing stenotic ileum
answerChoices.rationale: Controlled infection does not resolve the persistent fistula and symptomatic fixed narrowing. Resection addresses the structural diseased segment.

answerChoices.label: Strictureplasty across the fistulizing ileal segment
answerChoices.rationale: Strictureplasty conserves bowel in selected uncomplicated strictures, but the persistent penetrating tract makes this site a poor target.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic balloon dilation of the ileal narrowing
answerChoices.rationale: A persistent fistulizing segment after optimized therapy needs more than relief of luminal narrowing.

decisionNodes.explanation: The resolved abscess establishes control of the immediate infection, not resolution of the fistulizing stenotic segment. Persistent enteric drainage and meal-related obstructive symptoms after optimization support limited diseased-bowel resection. Bowel-preserving repairs remain useful for appropriately selected uncomplicated strictures.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative strategy best fit {patientName}'s documented small-bowel findings?

answerChoices.label: Strictureplasty at the three narrowed segments
answerChoices.rationale: The separated uncomplicated lesions and limited remaining bowel favor widening the strictures while retaining the intervening intestine.

answerChoices.label: Separate resections of the three narrowed segments

question.stem: Which operative strategy best fit {patientName}'s documented small-bowel findings?

question.explanation: Read the spatial distribution and prior resection history together. Multiple uncomplicated small-bowel strictures separated by healthy bowel are a setting for strictureplasty, particularly when further bowel loss matters. A fistula, collection, perforation or suspicious mass at a site would change that site's treatment.
