record.title: Bowel preservation for separated uncomplicated Crohn strictures
fairness: The short, separated jejunal strictures, prior bowel loss, inaccessible endoscopic sites and absence of penetrating or suspicious findings support strictureplasty. Separate resections remain a credible operative alternative, but would remove additional bowel; en bloc resection would also sacrifice the intervening supple segments.

The two consequential judgments are whether these sites are suitable for strictureplasty and how distribution plus remaining bowel changes the choice versus resection. This is a core operative principle and moderate predicted difficulty, not a complex strictureplasty-technique question.
The 140 cm finding is patient anatomy, not a stated universal intestinal-failure threshold. The explanation appropriately avoids promising parenteral-nutrition independence or asserting a cutoff.

The negative findings are a conspicuous eligibility checklist, but they supply genuine contraindication information rather than quote the answer. 'Three narrowed segments' occurs in two options, and the options remain parallel operations. No decisive nonmedical cue was identified.
The retrospective operative task is complete and standalone. The patient, age and sex are explicit.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Do not make the item harder by withholding fistula, collection or mass findings that determine eligibility.
If a later, harder variant is desired, use a clinician-supported site-specific finding that changes the treatment of one stricture; preserve this exact reviewed version separately.

record.title: Management after complete excision of visible low-grade dysplasia
fairness: En bloc excision, negative margins and absence of dysplasia in surrounding and other sampled mucosa support endoscopic surveillance. Total proctocolectomy is a meaningful over-treatment trap in a patient with extensive UC; segmental resection lacks a remaining target in the supplied record.

The learner must integrate lesion visibility, excision adequacy and the other mucosal samples, then distinguish surveillance from the obsolete simplification that any colitis-associated dysplasia mandates colectomy. This is a high-yield, lower-moderate application item, not a hard item.

The explanation appropriately says the lesion 'can be followed endoscopically' and does not claim that colectomy is never an option or that follow-up can stop. No exact unsupported surveillance interval is introduced.

'Surveillance' appears in the complaint/presentation and in the key, but the visit is a review of a surveillance examination; that word does not establish what should happen after dysplasia is found. Margins and mucosal findings are necessary clinical evidence, not gratuitous exclusions.
This is a standalone case in the supplied active packet. It does not expose the later invisible-high-grade candidate or its answer.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve complete excision and assessment of other mucosa; those facts distinguish this case from a biopsy-only or incompletely resected lesion.
Keep the teaching point conditional on the supplied findings rather than teaching surveillance for all UC-associated low-grade dysplasia.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next plan best fits {patientName}'s postoperative Crohn record?

answerChoices.label: Obtain ileocolonoscopy to reassess disease activity
answerChoices.rationale: The apparently normal procedure assessed distal colon. The raised stool marker remains discordant with clinical remission and needs endoscopic clarification before empiric treatment change.

answerChoices.label: Intensify infliximab maintenance treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The stool findings raise concern, but do not establish the site or severity of recurrence. In symptomatic remission, the AGA favors endoscopic confirmation over empiric treatment adjustment.

answerChoices.label: Continue treatment with biomarker-only monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Normal CRP and absent symptoms do not resolve repeated stool-marker elevation or the limited procedural coverage. Biomarker-only strategies have conditional roles, rather than being interchangeable with this incomplete assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The normal summary describes distal colon, not the ileocolic postoperative sites. Repeated fecal-calprotectin elevation remains unexplained by that examination despite symptom control and normal CRP. Complete endoscopic assessment should clarify activity before changing infliximab. Biomarker-only postoperative monitoring is supported in selected low-calprotectin settings, so a universal endoscopy-for-every-normal-marker rule is withheld.

record.title: Discordant postoperative markers and an incomplete endoscopic examination

cues.phrase: Continue treatment with biomarker-only monitoring
cues.why: The '-only' qualifier makes this option sound less comprehensive than the key. This is a minor stylistic cue, not a decisive shortcut: surveillance without endoscopy is an actual competing strategy, and the reader must still interpret the raised markers and examination coverage.

fairness: A distal examination ending at the splenic flexure has not assessed the ileocolic postoperative site. Repeatedly elevated stool markers despite symptomatic remission and normal CRP support completing endoscopic assessment before empiric infliximab escalation. The displayed record resolves why repeating an apparently normal examination is appropriate.

Two consequential steps remain: reject whole-disease reassurance from limited specimen/visual coverage, then choose confirmation rather than symptom-based monitoring or treatment escalation based on a nonspecific marker. Both competing plans represent plausible clinical errors. This is high-yield and moderate.

The incomplete examination is actual acquisition information, not merely a statement that a desired test has not been done. The key is allowed to be an investigation against management alternatives because the record supplies a real unresolved discrepancy.

The explanation explicitly limits its postoperative monitoring claim. I cannot independently verify the exact scope of the conditional low-calprotectin guidance offline; I identify no confident contradiction in this high-marker, incompletely assessed case and do not endorse a universal rule.
The standalone update supplies the resection, timing, treatment and current condition without requiring the earlier Crohn case. The exhibit is labeled constructed and the task is complete.
suggestions: Optional wording cleanup: name the monitoring plan concretely, such as continuing infliximab with repeat fecal calprotectin assessment, rather than advertising '-only'. Do not introduce an unsupported interval.

Remove the editorial phrase 'a universal endoscopy-for-every-normal-marker rule is withheld' from learner feedback in a future revision; state the clinical limitation directly. Retain clinician verification of the conditional guideline boundary.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Core biopsy confirms GIST with a KIT exon 11 variant. Staging CT shows no distant metastases. Two mesenteric arterial arcades course through the mass. their branches supply a long adjacent length of otherwise uninvolved small bowel. The mass and those vessels have no separable plane on the reviewed images. His bleeding is controlled and oral intake is maintained.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s jejunal GIST record?

answerChoices.label: Begin neoadjuvant imatinib therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The arterial anatomy threatens substantial functional bowel loss from immediate resection. KIT exon 11 supports imatinib sensitivity, making preoperative cytoreduction an appropriate initial strategy for specialist planning.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with definitive en bloc resection
answerChoices.rationale: Complete surgery remains the goal, but immediate sacrifice of the incorporated vascular arcades risks unnecessary major bowel loss when a supported cytoreductive approach is available.

answerChoices.label: Begin neoadjuvant sunitinib therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Sunitinib has an established role after imatinib resistance or intolerance. The supplied untreated KIT exon 11 tumor does not provide that premise for bypassing imatinib.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the vascular map before equating localized disease with low-morbidity resectability. Immediate en bloc vascular resection would sacrifice blood supply to additional bowel. Preoperative imatinib can make surgery less morbid in appropriately selected GIST, and the KIT exon 11 result supports sensitivity. Sunitinib is a later-line choice for imatinib resistance or intolerance. Subsequent surgery still aims at complete removal with the capsule intact.

concept.displayName: jejunal gist resection
concept.learningObjective: Interpret operative anatomy and molecular findings to choose the initial treatment stage for a localized jejunal GIST.
concept.conceptVersionReason: Changes from routine local resection extent to selecting initial neoadjuvant therapy for molecularly characterized GIST with mesenteric involvement threatening major bowel loss. Do not transfer resection-extent history.
concept.identityDecision: Changes from routine local resection extent to selecting initial neoadjuvant therapy for molecularly characterized GIST with mesenteric involvement threatening major bowel loss. Do not transfer resection-extent history.

record.title: Initial therapy for localized GIST threatening major bowel loss
fairness: Localized disease does not by itself make immediate surgery the best initial plan when inseparable arterial arcades supply a long length of uninvolved bowel. Controlled bleeding and maintained intake permit a neoadjuvant strategy; the KIT exon 11 result supports the conventional imatinib choice over sunitinib.

The learner must infer the functional consequence of en bloc vascular resection, then combine that consequence with molecular sensitivity and the absence of an urgent symptom driver to choose initial therapy. Immediate surgery is a credible error, and sunitinib tests treatment-line confusion. This is high-yield and moderate, not merely diagnosis recognition.

The known GIST diagnosis is appropriate for a management question. Two choices share 'Begin neoadjuvant ... therapy', so that phrasing does not uniquely identify imatinib. The vascular description supplies operative consequences without directly stating 'unresectable' or naming a desired drug.

The word 'variant' is less precise than an activating pathogenic KIT mutation. I have not verified the particular molecular result offline and am not treating every possible exon 11 variant as sensitive. This is a precision limitation, not a confident claim that the conventional keyed answer is clinically wrong.
The named patient, staging, bleeding status and vascular anatomy make the task standalone. No later surgical result is needed.
suggestions: No blocking change to the intended clinical decision. A future precision edit should identify the molecular finding as a pathogenic activating mutation if that is what the constructed pathology record intends; have the clinician verify the sensitivity statement without inventing a specific sequence variant.
Keep the vascular supply consequence and controlled symptoms; removing either would weaken the sequencing decision against immediate surgery.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial operation best fit {patientName}'s hospital record when surgery was chosen?

answerChoices.label: Total abdominal colectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: Removing the colon controls the acute disease while retaining the rectum for later reassessment. It avoids adding pelvic dissection or pouch construction during severe illness and steroid exposure.

answerChoices.label: Total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
answerChoices.rationale: This avoids a pouch anastomosis but still adds definitive pelvic dissection during the high-risk acute operation. No current rectal perforation or malignancy requires that extra extent.

answerChoices.label: Restorative proctocolectomy with diverted ileal pouch
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary diversion does not eliminate the risks of immediate pelvic pouch construction during ongoing severe disease and systemic steroid exposure.

Total proctocolectomy with a permanent stoma avoids a pouch anastomosis but still adds pelvic surgery now. Diversion also does not remove the risks of immediate pouch construction.

record.title: Persistent pouch symptoms after incomplete distal mucosal assessment
fairness: Normal pouch-body and afferent-limb findings do not establish normality of the obscured distal channel. Persistent bleeding and urgency justify completing site-specific mucosal evaluation before assigning the new evacuation symptoms to a primary functional disorder.

The learner must localize the limitation of the available observations and biopsy, then rank mucosal reassessment against physiology testing prompted by genuine straining and incomplete evacuation. Manometry is a credible near-miss, making this a high-yield moderate investigation-sequencing item.

MRI for a fistula is the weakest competitor: no draining tract, focal sepsis or other specific penetrating finding is supplied. Nevertheless, it is a real alternative investigation for structural pouch complications, not a nonsensical test. It does not outrank completing the clearly limited mucosal examination in this record.

The exhibit reports actual obscuration and sampled sites rather than merely announcing that a test was omitted. Repeating pouchoscopy therefore is not a disposable already-completed-test foil. 'Pouchoscopy' appears in both the prior report and the key, but that repetition alone does not establish whether repetition is justified.

The explanation does not claim that normal pouch histology excludes all pouch disease or that evacuation dysfunction can never coexist. The standalone presentation supplies the pouch history, current symptoms and investigation limits without a prior case. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Keep persistent bleeding, the genuine evacuation symptoms and the exact sites of adequate versus obscured examination; they establish the ordering of the competing investigations.

For a future harder variant, strengthen the third investigation's patient-specific rationale only if supported observations still leave one best next test. Do not add decorative fistula symptoms or remove the necessary examination limitation.

record.title: Albumin-adjusted gap and the next cause-directed panel
fairness: Independent calculation gives AG 140 - 112 - 16 = 12 and adjustment 0.25 * (40 - 16) = 6, yielding 18 mmol/L against the supplied upper reference of 16. The pH/PCO2/bicarbonate combination is internally coherent.

The resident must recognize a concealed elevated-gap component despite diarrhoea and then select plasma lactate and beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than characterize stool losses or pursue renal acidification first. Those alternatives answer the same diagnostic-stage task. The small adjusted elevation warrants investigation; it does not establish a particular acid or exclude concurrent gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss.

The formula is a legitimate calculation aid, not a worked answer or a named keyed investigation. Persistent low albumin and simultaneous sampling give a coherent standalone record. The task does not require information from an earlier part. The concept is high-yield acid-base evaluation, with moderate application difficulty.

record.title: Unresolved ketoacidosis with treatment-emergent hypokalaemia
fairness: Current glucose 9 does not establish DKA resolution: beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.6, pH 7.29 and bicarbonate 14 indicate persistent metabolic disease. Current potassium 3.2 is below the explicitly supplied insulin safety condition. Potassium correction and a confirming recheck before resuming IV insulin are the best offered sequence.

The supplied potassium condition deliberately reduces recall burden and narrows the timing dimension, but does not identify which of the two potassium-first choices is correct. The resident must still integrate persistent ketosis despite glucose improvement and apply the potassium constraint. Unlike a complete regimen sentence, the aid does not name the answer's insulin route or transition decision.

The two-by-two option components are balanced: first versus concurrent potassium and IV versus maintenance basal-bolus each occur twice. There is no majority-component convergence. The two closest errors are premature transition after glucose improvement and continuing insulin despite the current potassium result.

This high-yield sequence has moderate difficulty. The current and pretreatment record, ongoing dextrose and kidney/urine context make the question standalone. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified; the item does not claim that all DKA in every setting requires an IV route.

record.title: DKA resolution despite urine ketones and low bicarbonate
fairness: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.4 and venous pH 7.34 support the resolution relation described in the explanation despite bicarbonate 17 and positive urine ketones. The sodium/chloride/bicarbonate values give a gap of 9, consistent with the proposed non-gap residual acid-base pattern. Basal-bolus insulin with IV overlap is the best offered transition for the eating, stable patient who has not received basal insulin.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish biochemical resolution from misleading residual markers, then choose a transition that preserves insulin coverage. Continuing IV treatment is a credible error if bicarbonate or urine ketones are over-weighted; correction-scale insulin misses basal coverage. This is high-yield and moderately difficult.

The medication-sheet omission is decision-critical rather than sufficient by itself to answer: it does not establish whether the metabolic episode has resolved. Likewise, DKA in the exhibit caption is an appropriate known diagnosis for this management task.

The currently standalone wrapper is coherent. Later in that outside admission refers to the admission already named in the presentation, and the exhibit and medication record provide the needed reassessment without the earlier potassium question or its explanation. This verdict does not approve future recombination into a multi-part case.

record.title: Persistent alkalosis after gastric drainage ends
fairness: The pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate are internally consistent with metabolic alkalosis. Low pretreatment urine chloride despite higher urine sodium supports a chloride-depleted maintaining process after the initiating gastric loss ends. Sodium chloride replacement with continued potassium chloride is the best offered addition.

The resident must distinguish the maintaining physiology from the ended loss and from an inference based on urine sodium, then select replacement instead of pharmacologic bicarbonate loss or mineralocorticoid blockade. Acetazolamide is particularly unattractive with current hypokalaemia, while spironolactone does not address the demonstrated chloride-depletion pattern. These are recognizable neighboring management errors.

The no-fluid/no-diuretic sampling context and absence of oedema are relevant to interpreting urine chloride and choosing replacement, not gratuitous feasibility permissions. The choices have different routes but comparable specificity and all answer the addition-to-potassium task. The classic mechanism remains high-yield and moderately difficult, rather than a hard stretch item.
The standalone historical reassessment is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy, unique wording-match shortcut or preceding-feedback dependence was identified.

record.title: HHS fluid composition during falling osmolality
fairness: Independent arithmetic confirms glucose falls 8 mmol/L over two hours, or 4 per hour, and measured osmolality falls 6 mOsm/kg, or 3 per hour. Sodium rises only 1 mmol/L while glucose falls. The improving circulation, remaining depletion and falling osmolality support the offered 0.9% sodium chloride composition with ongoing rate reassessment.

The two consequential steps are interpreting the coupled glucose/sodium/osmolality trajectory and applying it to fluid composition. Moving to 0.45% saline because sodium rises or selecting free water prematurely are recognizable errors. The existing saline treatment is relevant baseline information, not an instruction to keep it regardless of response.

Separating composition from infusion rate prevents the key from authorizing an unchanged rate. The named HHS diagnosis is appropriate for a treatment-response task. This is high-yield metabolic fluid management with moderate difficulty; the exact response limits and eventual rate require clinician verification rather than inference of a universal regimen.
The historical two-hour record stands alone and options are parallel fluid compositions. No confident clinical inaccuracy or material nonmedical cue was identified.

record.title: Thiazide-confounded urine sodium and initial replacement
fairness: Hypotonic hyponatraemia, recent thiazide exposure and substantial postural pressure/pulse changes make assessed 0.9% saline replacement the best offered initial fluid plan. High urine sodium does not establish SIAD in this medication context. Alertness without new confusion or seizure helps distinguish the offered hypertonic strategy.

Two consequential steps are present: qualify the urine finding using medication exposure and infer a depletion component, then choose replacement rather than restriction or symptom-driven hypertonic treatment. Fluid restriction remains a recognizable error for someone anchoring on the concentrated sodium-containing urine. This is high-yield surgical fluid management.

Withholding the thiazide, collecting urine before fluids and specifying the historical hospital stage make the standalone chronology coherent. The explanation appropriately requires close monitoring; it does not imply an unrestricted saline infusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical answer cue was identified.

record.title: Current potassium result after an earlier specimen-related elevation
fairness: Current plasma potassium 6.7, rather than the prior serum-plasma discrepancy, supports immediate monitored hospital assessment. Repeating the artifact explanation or choosing an outpatient binder would miss the current escalation decision. A reassuring ECG does not settle the potassium risk.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish the earlier specimen effect from the current paired elevation, then choose the appropriate disposition. The platelet count and ECG provide credible competing information. This is high-yield perioperative electrolyte reasoning.

record.title: Postoperative hypotonic hyponatraemia and initial ongoing fluids
fairness: The combined hypotonic serum, concentrated sodium-containing urine, examination and stated endocrine/renal/diuretic exclusions support inappropriate water retention. Initial total-fluid restriction is the best offered plan; the record does not establish failure of restriction that would justify selecting the salt/loop alternative first.

The resident must interpret the mechanism and then place the treatment in the correct sequence. This is a high-yield, moderately difficult distinction from postoperative volume depletion and premature second-line treatment. The task and options are clear and comparable.

The change from 125 to 124 occurred with both 2.8 L oral intake and saline. It cannot isolate a causal effect of saline itself. The explanation's overall inference is supported by the other findings and does not require that causal claim.

The standalone record supplies the necessary context, age and sex. Necessary exclusions are not diagnosis labels naming the key, and the post-answer explanation does not leak into another active node. No material nonmedical cue was identified.

fairness: The combined hypotonic serum, concentrated sodium-containing urine, examination and stated endocrine/renal/diuretic exclusions support inappropriate water retention. Initial total-fluid restriction is the best offered plan; the record does not establish failure of restriction that would justify selecting the salt/loop alternative first.

The resident must interpret the mechanism and then place the treatment in the correct sequence. This is a high-yield, moderately difficult distinction from postoperative volume depletion and premature second-line treatment. The task and options are clear and comparable.

suggestions: If polishing this version, label the exhibit row as the sodium course during the recorded total intake rather than implying an isolated saline challenge. Preserve the distinction in later feedback. This is a precision improvement, not a prerequisite for the current best answer.

decisionNodes.stem: Which addition to potassium chloride best addresses {patientName}'s persisting acid-base problem at that reassessment?

answerChoices.label: IV 0.9% sodium chloride
answerChoices.rationale: The gas supports metabolic alkalosis. The low pretreatment urine chloride supports chloride depletion despite the higher urinary sodium, which can accompany bicarbonate excretion. Chloride-containing volume replacement addresses that maintaining factor while potassium chloride continues.

answerChoices.label: Oral acetazolamide
answerChoices.rationale: A bicarbonaturic drug may seem attractive after gastric drainage stops, but the urine chloride shows that replacement of a maintaining chloride deficit remains relevant. Acetazolamide can also increase potassium loss.

answerChoices.label: Oral spironolactone
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent potassium loss and alkalosis can suggest an aldosterone-related process. This low urine chloride pattern is not evidence of chloride-resistant mineralocorticoid excess and does not make blockade the best offered addition.

concept.learningObjective: Use urine chloride rather than urine sodium alone to select replacement during gastric-loss alkalosis.

record.title: Persistent alkalosis after gastric drainage ends
fairness: The pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate are internally consistent with metabolic alkalosis. Low pretreatment urine chloride despite higher urine sodium supports a chloride-depleted maintaining process after the initiating gastric loss ends. Sodium chloride replacement with continued potassium chloride is the best offered addition.

The resident must distinguish the maintaining physiology from the ended loss and from an inference based on urine sodium, then select replacement instead of pharmacologic bicarbonate loss or mineralocorticoid blockade. Acetazolamide is particularly unattractive with current hypokalaemia, while spironolactone does not address the demonstrated chloride-depletion pattern. These are recognizable neighboring management errors.

The no-fluid/no-diuretic sampling context and absence of oedema are relevant to interpreting urine chloride and choosing replacement, not gratuitous feasibility permissions. The choices have different routes but comparable specificity and all answer the addition-to-potassium task. The classic mechanism remains high-yield and moderately difficult, rather than a hard stretch item.
The standalone historical reassessment is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy, unique wording-match shortcut or preceding-feedback dependence was identified.

decisionNodes.stem: Which insulin-and-potassium sequence should the hospital team have selected for {patientName} at this order review?

answerChoices.label: Replace potassium first; resume IV insulin after recheck
answerChoices.rationale: Glucose has improved but ketonaemia and acidemia remain, so the metabolic infusion course is still needed rather than transition to maintenance dosing. Current potassium 3.2 is below the supplied safety boundary: replace it and confirm a repeat value above 3.5 before resuming that IV insulin plan.

answerChoices.label: Replace potassium first; start maintenance basal-bolus after recheck
answerChoices.rationale: This respects potassium safety but treats glucose improvement as completion of the metabolic course. Current ketones and pH do not support a maintenance transition.

answerChoices.label: Continue IV insulin with concurrent potassium replacement
answerChoices.rationale: This recognizes the continuing metabolic need but gives insulin before the low potassium has been corrected and rechecked above the supplied boundary.

record.title: Unresolved ketoacidosis with treatment-emergent hypokalaemia
fairness: Current glucose 9 does not establish DKA resolution: beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.6, pH 7.29 and bicarbonate 14 indicate persistent metabolic disease. Current potassium 3.2 is below the explicitly supplied insulin safety condition. Potassium correction and a confirming recheck before resuming IV insulin are the best offered sequence.

The supplied potassium condition deliberately reduces recall burden and narrows the timing dimension, but does not identify which of the two potassium-first choices is correct. The resident must still integrate persistent ketosis despite glucose improvement and apply the potassium constraint. Unlike a complete regimen sentence, the aid does not name the answer's insulin route or transition decision.

The two-by-two option components are balanced: first versus concurrent potassium and IV versus maintenance basal-bolus each occur twice. There is no majority-component convergence. The two closest errors are premature transition after glucose improvement and continuing insulin despite the current potassium result.

This high-yield sequence has moderate difficulty. The current and pretreatment record, ongoing dextrose and kidney/urine context make the question standalone. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified; the item does not claim that all DKA in every setting requires an IV route.

concept.displayName: Use ketone/pH resolution rather than urine ketones or chloride-related bicarbonate to choose the insulin transition stage.
concept.learningObjective: Use ketone/pH resolution rather than urine ketones or chloride-related bicarbonate to choose the insulin transition stage.

record.title: DKA resolution despite urine ketones and low bicarbonate
fairness: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.4 and venous pH 7.34 support the resolution relation described in the explanation despite bicarbonate 17 and positive urine ketones. The sodium/chloride/bicarbonate values give a gap of 9, consistent with the proposed non-gap residual acid-base pattern. Basal-bolus insulin with IV overlap is the best offered transition for the eating, stable patient who has not received basal insulin.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish biochemical resolution from misleading residual markers, then choose a transition that preserves insulin coverage. Continuing IV treatment is a credible error if bicarbonate or urine ketones are over-weighted; correction-scale insulin misses basal coverage. This is high-yield and moderately difficult.

The medication-sheet omission is decision-critical rather than sufficient by itself to answer: it does not establish whether the metabolic episode has resolved. Likewise, DKA in the exhibit caption is an appropriate known diagnosis for this management task.

The currently standalone wrapper is coherent. Later in that outside admission refers to the admission already named in the presentation, and the exhibit and medication record provide the needed reassessment without the earlier potassium question or its explanation. This verdict does not approve future recombination into a multi-part case.

decisionNodes.stem: Which fluid composition best fits {patientName}'s recorded two-hour response?

answerChoices.label: Sodium chloride 0.9%
answerChoices.rationale: Glucose falls 4 mmol/L/hour and measured osmolality 3 mOsm/kg/hour while circulation improves and depletion remains. The sodium rise does not itself call for hypotonic fluid. Retain isotonic composition within a separately reassessed rate plan; this does not authorize an unchanged pump rate.

answerChoices.label: Sodium chloride 0.45%
answerChoices.rationale: A hypotonic formulation may be considered when osmolality fails to decline despite adequate balance and appropriate treatment. That failure is not shown by this measured response.

answerChoices.rationale: Free water may be needed at another stage, but the still-marked hyperglycaemia, residual depletion and appropriate measured response do not justify replacing the isotonic composition merely because sodium rose.

concept.displayName: Select fluid composition from the joint HHS treatment response while treating infusion rate as a separate reassessment.
concept.learningObjective: Select fluid composition from the joint HHS treatment response while treating infusion rate as a separate reassessment.

record.title: HHS fluid composition during falling osmolality
fairness: Independent arithmetic confirms glucose falls 8 mmol/L over two hours, or 4 per hour, and measured osmolality falls 6 mOsm/kg, or 3 per hour. Sodium rises only 1 mmol/L while glucose falls. The improving circulation, remaining depletion and falling osmolality support the offered 0.9% sodium chloride composition with ongoing rate reassessment.

The two consequential steps are interpreting the coupled glucose/sodium/osmolality trajectory and applying it to fluid composition. Moving to 0.45% saline because sodium rises or selecting free water prematurely are recognizable errors. The existing saline treatment is relevant baseline information, not an instruction to keep it regardless of response.

Separating composition from infusion rate prevents the key from authorizing an unchanged rate. The named HHS diagnosis is appropriate for a treatment-response task. This is high-yield metabolic fluid management with moderate difficulty; the exact response limits and eventual rate require clinician verification rather than inference of a universal regimen.
The historical two-hour record stands alone and options are parallel fluid compositions. No confident clinical inaccuracy or material nonmedical cue was identified.

record.title: GI investigation after confirmed iron deficiency
fairness: Bidirectional endoscopy is the best offered initial plan for this adult man with unexplained iron-deficiency anemia. Improvement with iron and stopping naproxen does not establish an adequate etiologic explanation or remove the need to assess the lower GI tract.

The upper-endoscopy competitor is credible because of the upper-GI symptoms. The learner must separate symptomatic/hematologic response from etiologic investigation and select its scope. Capsule examination is premature before the stated unperformed initial evaluations.
The standalone case supplies the original symptoms, actual iron results and interval course; the return-visit wording does not require a missing scored companion.

record.title: RBC compatibility despite an evanescent historical antibody
fairness: The historical clinically significant anti-Jka must inform donor antigen selection despite a negative current screen. The same history also affects eligibility for electronic issue, making serologic antiglobulin crossmatching the defensible plan.

The two-by-two option matrix balances both components. Neither component frequency nor length identifies the key. Mentioning the actual antibody is necessary evidence, not an unfair diagnosis cue for this compatibility task.
The stable nonemergency setting resolves the emergency-release exception. The previous antibody and current screening results are fully restated, so the later-admission node stands alone.

record.title: Vitamin K correction before a nonurgent biliary procedure
fairness: Obstruction and the selective factor pattern support a vitamin K-related component; ongoing impaired enteral absorption distinguishes parenteral from oral replacement, while the absence of major bleeding or immediate procedural urgency distinguishes replacement/reassessment from plasma.

IV phytonadione is defensible among the offered plans. Preserved factor V is supportive rather than definitive evidence against synthetic dysfunction, as the explanation states. The draft does not prescribe an invented dose, response interval or universal procedural INR.

The named obstruction is legitimate background for choosing a correction strategy. All options include repeat assessment, so that phrase does not uniquely cue the key. The current record is self-contained.

record.title: Revising suspected-HIT management after functional testing
fairness: The weak-positive binding assay and valid negative functional assay make discontinuation of empiric argatroban and resumption of indicated heparin prophylaxis defensible. The learner must revise an initially reasonable diagnosis/treatment rather than simply follow the earlier platelet trend.

The explanation preserves the possibility of false-negative functional testing, especially with high clinical probability and a strongly positive immunoassay; it does not claim that a negative test universally excludes HIT. Exact assay behavior and patient-level application remain clinician-review matters.
Continuing argatroban is the meaningful close alternative. Warfarin is a weaker distractor and should not be justified by an invented current platelet count, which is not supplied.
Original trajectory, both assays, empiric treatment and continuing prophylaxis indication are all restated; no prior scored answer is needed.

record.title: Empiric anticoagulation after a biphasic platelet decline
fairness: Recovery after the initial postoperative fall followed by a new substantial fall during heparin exposure supports suspected HIT rather than simply attributing the count to surgery. Absence of detected thrombosis does not justify waiting untreated for antibody results.

Stopping heparin and initiating an appropriate nonheparin anticoagulant is the best offered plan. LMWH substitution and withholding all anticoagulation represent credible distinct errors. Normal stated organ function supports argatroban without claiming it is uniquely superior to every unlisted agent.

The platelet chronology, medication exposures, bleeding assessment and organ function are present in the standalone record. The explanation does not overstate a precise score or prescribe an unsupported universal intensity.

record.title: New multilineage cytopenias after a prior platelet response
fairness: The prior steroid-responsive isolated platelet problem creates a credible anchor. New low-production multilineage cytopenias with abnormal granulocyte morphology require reassessment of that mechanism before another empiric platelet-directed course.

Integrated marrow sampling with cytogenetics is the best offered investigation; peripheral molecular testing can contribute but does not replace morphology and tissue assessment. Lymphoid flow is the weaker competitor, yet the marrow-versus-myeloid-panel distinction remains meaningful.

Normal B12/folate do not exclude all mimics; the explanation explicitly acknowledges this and does not claim a proven marrow diagnosis. The standalone presentation and exhibit provide the old and new patterns without requiring earlier serology or another node.

record.title: Platelet support with enlarging traumatic intracranial bleeding
fairness: The platelet option is defensible under the explicitly scoped European trauma guidance: the intracranial injury changes the platelet target compared with uncomplicated ongoing traumatic bleeding. The learner must interpret the count in its injury-specific context rather than apply a generic threshold.

The explanation states the weak/low-certainty nature of the recommendation and does not promise improved outcomes or assert a universal target. Current exact guidance was not newly verified offline; clinician verification remains necessary.
The correction of fibrinogen and the enlarging contusion are restated within this standalone node, so it does not depend on the former component companion.
suggestions: For traceability, identify the precise guideline/version in the eventual accessible source display; retain the current low-certainty and injury-specific wording. This is not a demand to invent a new threshold.

record.title: RBC prescription after a prior volume-related reaction
fairness: Severe symptomatic anemia supports renewed RBC treatment despite the previous reaction. Prior congestion and LV systolic dysfunction then affect the amount/rate and reassessment plan. These are consequential competing risks rather than a supplied diagnosis followed by its usual drug.
One slowly administered unit with reassessment is the best offered plan. Neither withholding needed support nor precommitting to two units is preferable under the stated nonemergency circumstances.

The prior event and current recovered volume examination are both supplied, so this later assessment stands alone. The explanation avoids an invented rate or unsupported universal prophylactic-diuretic regimen.

record.title: Calcium replacement during transfusion with peripheral access
fairness: Severe measured ionized hypocalcemia during repeated component exposure supports IV calcium. Choosing the formulation also requires applying the actual access constraint; QT prolongation alone could otherwise tempt magnesium.

Calcium gluconate is a defensible preferred peripheral option. Calcium chloride is not absolutely impossible through every peripheral line, so the explanation must retain its current comparative language and must not become a universal contraindication claim. No dose equivalence is asserted.
Access-site monitoring, ionized calcium and ongoing ECG assessment are acknowledged. This standalone record supplies the necessary result and access information.

record.title: Warfarin reversal with a product-specific HIT contraindication
fairness: Active arterial bleeding requires rapid factor replacement despite concurrent vitamin K and source-control planning. Among the named available products, plasma is defensible when Kcentra is contraindicated by the documented HIT history.

The named HIT diagnosis is legitimate prior history for a different management decision; it does not announce which product contains heparin. The learner must identify the usual reversal need and then revise the usual PCC choice for the product-specific contraindication.

The brand restriction matters: the explanation does not generalize the Kcentra contraindication to every conceivable PCC formulation. Exact product-label applicability was not independently reverified offline and remains a clinician/source-verification boundary.
The episode, prior HIT evidence, already-administered vitamin K and product stock are all present in this standalone case.

record.title: Dental hemostasis after a short-lived desmopressin response
fairness: The learner must distinguish a brisk initial laboratory response from persistence of that response, then select a procedural hemostatic plan in light of low baseline activity and prior extraction bleeding. The desmopressin-plus-tranexamic-acid option is a credible near-miss.

VWF-containing concentrate plus tranexamic acid is defensible among the listed plans; monotherapy is not supported by the supplied low-baseline, significant-bleeding profile. The explanation leaves specific targets, product and monitoring to the actual hematology plan.

Established type 1 VWD is legitimate background for this management task, not a giveaway diagnosis. The exact measured trial, previous bleeding and local measures are self-contained. The node key contains major-plan, but the visible task correctly concerns dental extractions; that internal label was not used to infer major surgery.

record.title: GI investigation after confirmed iron deficiency
fairness: Bidirectional endoscopy is the best offered initial plan for this adult man with unexplained iron-deficiency anemia. Improvement with iron and stopping naproxen does not establish an adequate etiologic explanation or remove the need to assess the lower GI tract.

The upper-endoscopy competitor is credible because of the upper-GI symptoms. The learner must separate symptomatic/hematologic response from etiologic investigation and select its scope. Capsule examination is premature before the stated unperformed initial evaluations.
The standalone case supplies the original symptoms, actual iron results and interval course; the return-visit wording does not require a missing scored companion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which available factor product best fits Philip Vance's urgent warfarin-reversal record?

answerChoices.label: Thawed plasma
answerChoices.rationale: Major warfarin-associated bleeding requires rapid replacement of deficient factors while source control and vitamin K proceed. Kcentra is generally useful for this purpose, but its label contraindicates it in known heparin-induced thrombocytopenia because it contains heparin. Among these stated products, plasma provides the needed broad factor replacement without that product-specific contraindication.

answerChoices.label: Four-factor PCC (Kcentra)
answerChoices.rationale: Four-factor PCC is a close and normally favored reversal choice. This specific product contains heparin and is contraindicated with the established HIT history in this record.

answerChoices.label: Recombinant activated factor VII
answerChoices.rationale: An activated single-factor product is not a comprehensive replacement for the warfarin-reduced vitamin K-dependent factors. Its use in selected inhibitor-associated bleeding is a different indication.

record.title: Warfarin reversal with a product-specific HIT contraindication
fairness: Active arterial bleeding requires rapid factor replacement despite concurrent vitamin K and source-control planning. Among the named available products, plasma is defensible when Kcentra is contraindicated by the documented HIT history.

The named HIT diagnosis is legitimate prior history for a different management decision; it does not announce which product contains heparin. The learner must identify the usual reversal need and then revise the usual PCC choice for the product-specific contraindication.

The brand restriction matters: the explanation does not generalize the Kcentra contraindication to every conceivable PCC formulation. Exact product-label applicability was not independently reverified offline and remains a clinician/source-verification boundary.
The episode, prior HIT evidence, already-administered vitamin K and product stock are all present in this standalone case.

decisionNodes.stem: Which electrolyte prescription best fits Daniel Price's transfusion findings using his current vascular access?

answerChoices.label: Calcium gluconate through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: Large citrate exposure can lower ionized calcium, impairing coagulation and cardiovascular function. The measured deficit requires IV calcium; with peripheral access, calcium gluconate is the better fit among these prescriptions. Calcium chloride is more irritating and is generally reserved for central administration. Continue ECG, access-site and ionized-calcium monitoring; these formulations are not dose-for-dose interchangeable.

answerChoices.label: Calcium chloride through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: This supplies calcium, but the proposed peripheral route creates an avoidable tissue-injury concern compared with calcium gluconate. The objection is the actual prescription and access, not failure of chloride to correct hypocalcemia.

answerChoices.label: Magnesium sulfate through a monitored peripheral IV
answerChoices.rationale: Magnesium can be used for a demonstrated magnesium deficit and some arrhythmias, but it does not replace the directly measured severe ionized-calcium deficit in this transfusion record. A longer QT does not establish magnesium deficiency.

record.title: Calcium replacement during transfusion with peripheral access
fairness: Severe measured ionized hypocalcemia during repeated component exposure supports IV calcium. Choosing the formulation also requires applying the actual access constraint; QT prolongation alone could otherwise tempt magnesium.

Calcium gluconate is a defensible preferred peripheral option. Calcium chloride is not absolutely impossible through every peripheral line, so the explanation must retain its current comparative language and must not become a universal contraindication claim. No dose equivalence is asserted.
Access-site monitoring, ionized calcium and ongoing ECG assessment are acknowledged. This standalone record supplies the necessary result and access information.

case.presentation: Laura Bennett, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after discharge from hospital treatment of abdominal and head trauma. The founder reviews the platelet decision during the outside admission.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: Laura Bennett, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after discharge from hospital treatment of abdominal and head trauma. The founder reviews the platelet decision during the outside admission.

sourceLabels: The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition
Patient blood management guideline for adults with critical bleeding

decisionNodes.stem: Which component action best fits Laura Bennett's later traumatic-bleeding record under the cited European trauma guidance?

answerChoices.label: Give a platelet component now
answerChoices.rationale: The fibrinogen response does not resolve the platelet decision. A count of 78 x 10^9/L exceeds the usual ongoing-bleeding trauma target of 50, but the cited European guidance suggests a target above 100 with traumatic brain injury. The enlarging intracranial injury therefore changes the ranking toward platelets. This is a weak, low-certainty recommendation, not proof of outcome benefit from a universal TBI threshold; specialist reassessment remains essential.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the count before adding a platelet component
answerChoices.rationale: Serial reassessment is necessary, and 78 is above the guideline target for general ongoing traumatic bleeding. Waiting on that general target overlooks the simultaneously enlarging intracranial injury and the cited higher TBI target.

answerChoices.label: Give another cryoprecipitate component now
answerChoices.rationale: The fibrinogen concentration has responded. Further cryoprecipitate does not address the platelet target relevant to the enlarging traumatic intracranial injury.

decisionNodes.stem: Which RBC prescription best fits Evelyn Moore's later hospital assessment?

answerChoices.label: Give one RBC unit slowly; reassess before prescribing more
answerChoices.rationale: The current severe symptomatic anemia supports RBC transfusion despite the earlier reaction. The previous pressure/volume response and LV dysfunction argue for limiting volume exposure, using a slower controlled administration and reassessing after one unit. This avoids both withholding needed support and precommitting to a larger course. No exact rate or routine prophylactic-diuretic efficacy is assumed.

answerChoices.label: Give no RBCs now; reassess symptoms and hemoglobin
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding exposure is tempting after a respiratory reaction, but it leaves severe symptomatic anemia untreated in the stated later stable assessment. The prior event should inform administration rather than automatically prohibit necessary RBC support.

answerChoices.label: Give two RBC units slowly; reassess after the course
answerChoices.rationale: Slowing administration addresses one risk, but a planned two-unit course adds volume before learning the response to the first unit in a patient with a prior congestion event. Single-unit reassessment is the better fit here.

decisionNodes.stem: Which donor-selection and compatibility plan best fits Nora Hayes's later hospital RBC requirement?

answerChoices.label: Jka-negative RBCs with an antiglobulin serologic crossmatch
answerChoices.rationale: The negative current screen does not erase the clinically significant antibody history. Select donor cells lacking Jka and use serologic antiglobulin compatibility testing. This addresses the historical antibody as well as current compatibility; routine electronic issue is inappropriate with this history. The stable nonemergency setting allows that workup rather than importing an emergency-release exception.

answerChoices.label: Jka-negative RBCs with an electronic crossmatch

answerChoices.label: Jka-positive RBCs with an antiglobulin serologic crossmatch
answerChoices.rationale: A serologic crossmatch does not justify deliberately disregarding the corresponding donor antigen after a clinically significant anti-Jka history. Current weak or absent antibody detection can make that shortcut tempting.

answerChoices.label: Jka-positive RBCs with an electronic crossmatch
answerChoices.rationale: This overlooks both the donor-antigen requirement and the historical-antibody restriction on electronic issue. A current negative screen is insufficient to justify this routine plan.

decisionNodes.stem: Which anticoagulant action best fits Owen Reed's hospital platelet record while antibody testing is pending?

answerChoices.label: Stop heparin and start argatroban
answerChoices.rationale: The initial postoperative fall recovered before a new fall exceeding half the recovery count during the characteristic delayed heparin-exposure period. That trajectory warrants suspected-HIT management despite no detected thrombosis. Stop heparin and use an appropriate nonheparin anticoagulant while testing proceeds; argatroban is one supported option with the stated organ-function context. These observations do not exclude every alternative cause, and this item does not prescribe a universal intensity or claim agent superiority.

answerChoices.label: Replace unfractionated heparin with enoxaparin
answerChoices.rationale: Changing to low-molecular-weight heparin does not remove heparin exposure in suspected HIT. A different heparin formulation is not the protective substitution needed for this delayed pattern.

answerChoices.label: Withhold anticoagulants until antibody results return
answerChoices.rationale: The low platelet count does not eliminate the thrombotic risk of a credible HIT syndrome. In the supplied record there is no active bleeding to support simply leaving suspected HIT without an alternative anticoagulant while testing is pending.

answerChoices.label: Stop argatroban and resume UFH prophylaxis
answerChoices.rationale: The delayed platelet course justified initial suspected-HIT treatment, but weak binding positivity does not establish pathogenic HIT antibodies. A valid negative functional result changes that assessment: most such patients do not have HIT and can be managed accordingly, including heparin if it remains indicated. Functional tests can be falsely negative, especially with a high-probability course and strongly positive immunoassay. The weak binding result here does not supply that strong-immunoassay conflict; clinical reassessment remains necessary.

answerChoices.label: Continue argatroban for presumed HIT
answerChoices.rationale: Interim argatroban was reasonable before confirmation. Continuing it as presumed HIT solely because of weak binding positivity disregards the valid negative functional assay. A strong immunoassay result with high clinical probability or concern about functional-assay validity would create a different conflict requiring specialist reconciliation.

answerChoices.label: Replace argatroban with warfarin for presumed HIT
answerChoices.rationale: This both carries forward an insufficiently supported HIT diagnosis and starts a VKA before platelet recovery. The question is the revised diagnostic basis for the anticoagulant, not convenience of an oral agent.

record.title: Revising suspected-HIT management after functional testing
fairness: The weak-positive binding assay and valid negative functional assay make discontinuation of empiric argatroban and resumption of indicated heparin prophylaxis defensible. The learner must revise an initially reasonable diagnosis/treatment rather than simply follow the earlier platelet trend.

The explanation preserves the possibility of false-negative functional testing, especially with high clinical probability and a strongly positive immunoassay; it does not claim that a negative test universally excludes HIT. Exact assay behavior and patient-level application remain clinician-review matters.
Continuing argatroban is the meaningful close alternative. Warfarin is a weaker distractor and should not be justified by an invented current platelet count, which is not supplied.
Original trajectory, both assays, empiric treatment and continuing prophylaxis indication are all restated; no prior scored answer is needed.

decisionNodes.stem: Which hemostatic plan best fits Alicia Grant's planned oral procedure in the reviewed record?

answerChoices.label: VWF-containing concentrate with tranexamic acid
answerChoices.rationale: The initial VWF rise does not persist on the actual four-hour sample, so it does not establish a sustained useful desmopressin response for this procedure. The low baseline activity and prior significant dental bleeding also do not fit the mild, higher-baseline group for tranexamic acid monotherapy. VWF replacement with an antifibrinolytic adjunct is the best of these plans; the hematology plan must define product, targets and monitoring.

answerChoices.label: IV desmopressin with tranexamic acid
answerChoices.rationale: The early trial rise makes this a credible option, but the four-hour VWF result has returned near baseline despite a preserved factor VIII activity. Initial response is not the same as sustained VWF coverage.

answerChoices.label: Tranexamic acid monotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: This can be appropriate for selected minor mucosal procedures in patients with a mild phenotype and higher baseline VWF activity. The baseline 0.18 and prior persistent dental bleeding do not fit that narrower group. Local hemostasis remains common care but does not remove the systemic coverage decision.

fairness: The learner must distinguish a brisk initial laboratory response from persistence of that response, then select a procedural hemostatic plan in light of low baseline activity and prior extraction bleeding. The desmopressin-plus-tranexamic-acid option is a credible near-miss.

VWF-containing concentrate plus tranexamic acid is defensible among the listed plans; monotherapy is not supported by the supplied low-baseline, significant-bleeding profile. The explanation leaves specific targets, product and monitoring to the actual hematology plan.

Established type 1 VWD is legitimate background for this management task, not a giveaway diagnosis. The exact measured trial, previous bleeding and local measures are self-contained. The node key contains major-plan, but the visible task correctly concerns dental extractions; that internal label was not used to infer major surgery.

case.presentation: June Carter, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic for reassessment of a previous isolated platelet problem before another empiric treatment. Initially her hemoglobin, neutrophil count and red-cell appearance had been within the laboratory ranges.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should precede another platelet-directed corticosteroid course for June Carter?

answerChoices.label: Marrow aspirate/core biopsy with cytogenetics
answerChoices.rationale: A prior temporary platelet response does not establish that new multilineage cytopenias share the original peripheral mechanism. Low production and abnormal neutrophil morphology warrant integrated marrow assessment, including architecture and cytogenetics, before repeating platelet-directed treatment. Nutritional, medication and other mimics still require assessment; normal B12/folate do not exclude all reversible causes and no marrow diagnosis is proved by this record.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood myeloid gene-panel sequencing
answerChoices.rationale: A clonal molecular finding can be useful, but a blood sequencing panel cannot substitute for the marrow morphology, architecture and integrated evaluation needed for this changed production pattern.

answerChoices.label: Peripheral-blood lymphoid flow cytometry
answerChoices.rationale: This is useful for a circulating lymphoid population, but the new low-production multilineage pattern with abnormal neutrophil morphology calls for marrow assessment rather than a blood lymphoid panel as its replacement.

record.title: New multilineage cytopenias after a prior platelet response
fairness: The prior steroid-responsive isolated platelet problem creates a credible anchor. New low-production multilineage cytopenias with abnormal granulocyte morphology require reassessment of that mechanism before another empiric platelet-directed course.

Integrated marrow sampling with cytogenetics is the best offered investigation; peripheral molecular testing can contribute but does not replace morphology and tissue assessment. Lymphoid flow is the weaker competitor, yet the marrow-versus-myeloid-panel distinction remains meaningful.

Normal B12/folate do not exclude all mimics; the explanation explicitly acknowledges this and does not claim a proven marrow diagnosis. The standalone presentation and exhibit provide the old and new patterns without requiring earlier serology or another node.

answerChoices.label: IV phytonadione followed by repeat coagulation testing
answerChoices.rationale: Obstruction with the selective factor pattern supports a vitamin K-related component. A parenteral route avoids relying on impaired enteral absorption, and the absence of major bleeding or an immediate procedure allows replacement and reassessment rather than automatic plasma. Preserved factor V is supportive, not proof that hepatic synthetic dysfunction is absent. Give IV phytonadione under the applicable monitored protocol; dose, rate, response interval and procedural INR requirement are not scored here.

answerChoices.label: Oral phytonadione followed by repeat coagulation testing
answerChoices.rationale: This addresses vitamin K but relies on absorption through an obstructed-bile context. A parenteral route is the better of the offered replacement plans for this record.

answerChoices.label: Plasma infusion followed by repeat coagulation testing
answerChoices.rationale: Plasma can replace factors promptly, but the current stable nonurgent phase supports trying the likely correctable vitamin K component and measuring the response first. The observation is not a universal prohibition on plasma in jaundice.

record.title: Vitamin K correction before a nonurgent biliary procedure
fairness: Obstruction and the selective factor pattern support a vitamin K-related component; ongoing impaired enteral absorption distinguishes parenteral from oral replacement, while the absence of major bleeding or immediate procedural urgency distinguishes replacement/reassessment from plasma.

IV phytonadione is defensible among the offered plans. Preserved factor V is supportive rather than definitive evidence against synthetic dysfunction, as the explanation states. The draft does not prescribe an invented dose, response interval or universal procedural INR.

The named obstruction is legitimate background for choosing a correction strategy. All options include repeat assessment, so that phrase does not uniquely cue the key. The current record is self-contained.

record.title: Familial calcium pattern after a negative genetic panel

cues.phrase: Retrieved records show mild hypercalcemia in her mother since early adulthood and similar findings in a maternal uncle
cues.why: There is some family-word overlap with 'first-degree-relative calcium testing', but these are necessary clinical observations. They do not by themselves establish whether a negative panel permits operative localization; this is an acceptable overlap, not a decisive nonmedical shortcut.

fairness: The persistent biochemical/familial pattern is not excluded by the negative panel; continued longitudinal and family evaluation is the best offered pathway. The error is treating a negative genetic panel as proof of sporadic PHPT.
Interpret the negative panel's limits, then select diagnostic clarification rather than surgical localization. PTHrP is a weaker competitor, but localization is a credible consequential error.
The update refers to a ratio 'again' and to withdrawal, but supplies the current ratio, preparation and family evidence. It is sufficiently self-contained; no prior scored answer is necessary.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Genetic-test sensitivity and current pathways were not independently reverified.
suggestions: For cleaner singleton prose, replace 'again gives a ratio' with the full calcium-to-creatinine clearance-ratio name. This is an optional clarity improvement, not a second required test.

record.title: Isolated radial osteoporosis and PHPT surgery assessment
fairness: The distal one-third-radius T-score supplies the operative skeletal indication despite reassuring axial sites and only mild hypercalcemia. Parathyroidectomy assessment is the best offered pathway.

The resident must interpret the site-specific density results, then distinguish a skeletal operative indication from calcium control or surveillance. This is moderate, familiar board content rather than a hard stretch item.
Known PHPT is a legitimate prerequisite for this management task, not diagnosis leakage. The table and parallel options do not reveal the key through wording or component convergence.
Standalone case is complete; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Preserve the discordant density sites and the distinction between calcium lowering and the skeletal treatment objective.

record.title: Surgical indication despite nonlocalizing studies
fairness: Confirmed PHPT with a low-trauma vertebral fracture supports endocrine-surgery referral despite nonlocalizing ultrasound and sestamibi. The key is assessment, not a prematurely specified operation.

The learner must identify skeletal operative relevance and then avoid treating localization failure as removal of the operative indication. Medication and surveillance are credible errors when negative imaging is overinterpreted.
Supplying the established diagnosis is appropriate for the management objective. No nonmedical wording shortcut or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This singleton contains all necessary clinical and imaging context; no companion question is needed.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between whether surgery is indicated and how an experienced surgeon plans it.

record.title: Elevated PTH with sustained postoperative normocalcemia
fairness: The supplied normocalcemia does not establish recurrent hypercalcemic PHPT. Continued calcium surveillance is the best offered strategy rather than localization based on isolated PTH elevation.

The resident must interpret the postoperative discordance and then choose the informative surveillance target rather than repeatedly pursue the abnormal PTH number. Serial PTH is a plausible closer alternative than CT.

The explanation's statement concerns routine surveillance in this setting; it should not be read as forbidding PTH testing if a new clinical question develops. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the exact follow-up recommendation was not independently reverified.
Standalone timing and reassessment of common secondary factors are coherent. No decisive wording, length or diagnosis-label cue identified.
suggestions: Keep the recommendation scoped to routine follow-up of this normocalcemic record, with clinical reassessment if the calcium pattern changes.

record.title: Progressive renal hyperparathyroidism with treatment-limiting toxicity
fairness: Progressive severe symptomatic hyperparathyroidism despite documented care and dose-limiting toxicity supports parathyroidectomy assessment while nephrology care continues.

The resident must interpret the longitudinal failure/limited tolerability, then distinguish actual medication-class constraints from an apparently helpful route or agent substitution. This is the strongest competing-management reasoning in the packet.

The below-range corrected calcium is directly relevant to etelcalcetide initiation; changing route does not remove calcimimetic hypocalcemia risk. Paricalcitol remains a credible alternative requiring clinician judgment, but its possibility need not postpone a surgical assessment.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The relative merits of a paricalcitol trial and exact medication labeling were not reverified; this PASS supports referral for assessment, not a claim that every medical option is exhausted or surgery must occur now.
The six-month trend and current update form a complete singleton. The serial values are constructed observations, not universal operative thresholds.
suggestions: Retain 'assessment' and parallel nephrology care. Preserve the feedback's distinction between a supported referral and a mandatory immediate operation.

record.title: Bone-directed treatment under competing PHPT and esophageal constraints
fairness: Denosumab is the best offered bone-directed medicine given osteoporosis, an established nonsurgical PHPT pathway and achalasia with delayed emptying. Oral alendronate and teriparatide create clinically meaningful eligibility errors.

The resident must separate calcium control from skeletal treatment, then select a medicine accounting for both esophageal disease and persistent underlying PHPT. The diagnosis is appropriately provided for this management task.
The clinical constraints are necessary to distinguish the medicines. 'Oral alendronate' has a route qualifier because the route matters; it is not an arbitrary grammatical key cue.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Denosumab still requires calcium monitoring, especially with calcium-lowering therapy; the explanation acknowledges monitoring without inventing a schedule.
The age, menopausal status, operative-risk history and current measurements are coherent without another node.
suggestions: Retain the monitoring caveat and avoid equating cinacalcet-normalized calcium with cure of PHPT.

record.title: Competing intraoperative PTH baselines and the Miami endpoint
fairness: The higher baseline is 180; half is 90, and the 10-minute value of 80 represents a greater-than-half decline. Concluding exploration matches the named conventional Miami criterion despite the above-reference final PTH.

Selecting the correct baseline and interpreting the decline, then applying the operative consequence rather than requiring laboratory normalization, are substantive linked steps. This is surgical protocol reasoning, not a statistics exercise.

Extended exploration and continued sampling encode credible wrong-baseline and wrong-endpoint errors. The normalization option is somewhat longer but does not reveal the key without knowing the protocol.
The retrospective operative record and constructed exhibit stand alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; meeting the criterion is not a guarantee of cure.
suggestions: Preserve the two different baselines, reference interval and named conventional protocol; these resolve the competing interpretations.

record.title: Invasive parathyroid-region mass and operative extent
fairness: The described gross extension and inability to separate the mass from ipsilateral thyroid support suspicion for carcinoma and an en bloc oncologic approach. The explanation appropriately does not claim histologic proof.

The resident must interpret local behavior, then choose an oncologic field rather than focused capsular excision or an operation for multigland hyperplasia. Focused excision is the more credible competing error.
References to adjacent thyroid are necessary anatomical observations for choosing the operative extent; they are not merely a repeated diagnosis label or a removable wording hint.

This is high-yield surgical principle testing with moderate rather than hard difficulty. The stopped exploration and later specialist review are coherent and self-contained. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between suspected invasive disease and confirmed histology; do not convert the case into an unsupported universal operation for every firm parathyroid lesion.

record.title: Stone-associated PHPT with reference-range PTH
fairness: Repeated hypercalcemia with nonsuppressed PTH, evaluated mimics and recurrent documented stones makes parathyroidectomy assessment the best offered pathway. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The resident must interpret a PTH value within its reference interval in the context of hypercalcemia, then apply the renal indication. Cinacalcet and surveillance represent credible stage-of-care errors, although this is not a hard item.
The delayed update supplies its own repeated measurements and completed evaluation; the singleton is understandable without R01. The name, age and sex remain consistent.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between operative assessment and automatic operation; PASS is editorial, not clinical approval.

record.title: Age-based surgery assessment despite reassuring organ studies
fairness: The biochemical pattern supports PHPT after the supplied mimic evaluation; age 44 supports operative assessment despite reassuring skeletal and renal findings. Surveillance is possible when surgery is not selected, but is not the strongest recommendation among these choices.

The two steps are recognizing inappropriate nonsuppression of PTH and applying the age criterion despite negative target-organ studies. The normal studies create a credible surveillance error rather than a linguistic shortcut.
Standalone presentation/update are coherent and sufficient. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical key cue identified.
suggestions: Preserve the normal organ findings: they are the competing consideration, not dispensable distractor exclusions.

concept.learningObjective: Use relative hypocalciuria, family context, and appropriate genetic evaluation without treating a low clearance ratio as independently diagnostic.

record.title: Familial calcium pattern after a negative genetic panel

cues.phrase: Retrieved records show mild hypercalcemia in her mother since early adulthood and similar findings in a maternal uncle
cues.why: There is some family-word overlap with 'first-degree-relative calcium testing', but these are necessary clinical observations. They do not by themselves establish whether a negative panel permits operative localization; this is an acceptable overlap, not a decisive nonmedical shortcut.

fairness: The persistent biochemical/familial pattern is not excluded by the negative panel; continued longitudinal and family evaluation is the best offered pathway. The error is treating a negative genetic panel as proof of sporadic PHPT.
Interpret the negative panel's limits, then select diagnostic clarification rather than surgical localization. PTHrP is a weaker competitor, but localization is a credible consequential error.
The update refers to a ratio 'again' and to withdrawal, but supplies the current ratio, preparation and family evidence. It is sufficiently self-contained; no prior scored answer is necessary.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Genetic-test sensitivity and current pathways were not independently reverified.
suggestions: For cleaner singleton prose, replace 'again gives a ratio' with the full calcium-to-creatinine clearance-ratio name. This is an optional clarity improvement, not a second required test.

suggestions: Preserve the discordant density sites and the distinction between calcium lowering and the skeletal treatment objective.

fairness: Confirmed PHPT with a low-trauma vertebral fracture supports endocrine-surgery referral despite nonlocalizing ultrasound and sestamibi. The key is assessment, not a prematurely specified operation.

The learner must identify skeletal operative relevance and then avoid treating localization failure as removal of the operative indication. Medication and surveillance are credible errors when negative imaging is overinterpreted.
Supplying the established diagnosis is appropriate for the management objective. No nonmedical wording shortcut or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This singleton contains all necessary clinical and imaging context; no companion question is needed.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between whether surgery is indicated and how an experienced surgeon plans it.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative strategy should be proposed at {patientName}'s specialist review?

answerChoices.label: En bloc parathyroidectomy and ipsilateral thyroid lobectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The infiltrative operative behavior raises concern for parathyroid carcinoma and supports an oncologic en bloc approach rather than dissecting the mass out of involved adjacent tissue. Histology has not yet been proved by these observations.

answerChoices.label: Focused capsular excision of the parathyroid mass
answerChoices.rationale: Shelling out a potentially invasive tumor risks violating the required oncologic plane instead of removing involved adjacent tissue together.

answerChoices.label: Bilateral exploration with subtotal parathyroidectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A multigland hyperplasia operation does not address the locally invasive behavior of this mass.

concept.displayName: Choose an oncologic surgical extent when operative behavior raises carcinoma concern.
concept.learningObjective: Choose an oncologic surgical extent when operative behavior raises carcinoma concern.

record.title: Invasive parathyroid-region mass and operative extent
fairness: The described gross extension and inability to separate the mass from ipsilateral thyroid support suspicion for carcinoma and an en bloc oncologic approach. The explanation appropriately does not claim histologic proof.

The resident must interpret local behavior, then choose an oncologic field rather than focused capsular excision or an operation for multigland hyperplasia. Focused excision is the more credible competing error.
References to adjacent thyroid are necessary anatomical observations for choosing the operative extent; they are not merely a repeated diagnosis label or a removable wording hint.

This is high-yield surgical principle testing with moderate rather than hard difficulty. The stopped exploration and later specialist review are coherent and self-contained. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between suspected invasive disease and confirmed histology; do not convert the case into an unsupported universal operation for every firm parathyroid lesion.
