record.title: Benign biopsy that missed an additional MRI focus
fairness: Interpret the sampling notch/marker in posterior fat plus the adipose specimen as failure to represent the persistent irregular focus; then choose repeat representative sampling before dismissing the site or escalating to mastectomy. The observations support that inference without a pre-answer 'discordant' label.

The alternatives reflect actual competing errors: accepting a benign report for surveillance versus treating imaging suspicion as proven multicentric malignancy. The key is not identifiable through a unique location phrase because the task and competing plans address the same additional finding.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Repeat sampling is best among the choices; the presentation establishes that the focus is targetable, so this is not a demand to repeat an inherently inaccessible biopsy.

The standalone update explicitly records the intervening biopsy and its acquisition details. It requires no prior task or explanation and preserves the 10-o'clock primary/4-o'clock additional-site relationship. Imaging-pathology concordance is high yield.
suggestions: No required revision. Keep the acquisition evidence and persistent target; a benign pathology label without those observations would make the ranking less secure.

record.title: Positive external cavity-shave margin despite clear main specimen
fairness: Resolve which specimen surface defines the final lateral boundary, then choose directed re-excision before radiation. Clear main-specimen margins compete meaningfully with the involved external surface of the separately oriented shave.

The external-surface marking, remaining radial parenchyma, and non-diffuse extent are needed to distinguish a true residual breast margin from an inner surface or an anatomic boundary without remaining breast tissue. The conservation preference is relevant to the mastectomy alternative and does not remove the radiation-versus-re-excision decision.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Radiation is not an equivalent substitute for clearing the represented involved margin; the supplied record does not require completion mastectomy.

This first node stands alone. Its explanation teaches specimen orientation and involved-edge management but does not disclose the next node's changed invasive-with-DCIS margin framework. Margin management is high yield.
suggestions: No required revision. Retain the external-surface orientation and residual parenchyma, which make the positive-margin inference fair.

record.title: Breast operation after treatment with diffuse biopsy-proven DCIS
fairness: The first inference is that the small enhancing invasive remnant does not define the full malignant field: mapped tissue establishes DCIS across the continuous calcification distribution. The second is choosing an operation that addresses that field rather than applying focal or oncoplastic conservation to it.

The extensive distribution makes the eventual surgical choice straightforward once interpreted; this is moderate, not a hard item. Both conservation alternatives are concrete operations rather than explanatory caricatures. No reliable nonmedical wording-overlap, convergence, or absolute-word shortcut identified.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The item does not assume that every post-treatment calcification is malignant: it supplies multiple mapped positive samples. Diffuse continuous central and all-quadrant involvement reaching the periphery supports mastectomy among the offered operations without an invented numerical size cutoff.
The case is standalone and tests high-yield conservation eligibility and response-assessment limits.
suggestions: No required revision. Preserve the mapped pathology and continuous distribution; do not generalize the explanation to unsampled residual calcifications or all multifocal disease.

record.title: Sequencing systemic therapy and surgery for node-positive HER2 disease
fairness: Interpret the size and biopsy-proven mobile nodal disease in the nonmetastatic setting, then select combined chemotherapy/HER2-directed treatment before surgery rather than surgery first or incomplete preoperative systemic treatment. The HER2 result identifies the treatment family, but that family is present in every option.

No unique drug-name overlap or component-majority cue selects the key: all options contain chemotherapy, trastuzumab/pertuzumab, and surgery. The third sequence tests separating HER2 blockade from the chemotherapy component; it is the weaker competitor but is a recognizable de-escalation/sequencing error.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The broad sequence is fair for the supplied substantial node-positive disease; the item is not asking for a regimen dose, chemotherapy backbone, or cardiac-safety decision for which additional details would be necessary.
This standalone initial-planning case is complete and does not borrow later response data. Stage/biology-dependent neoadjuvant sequencing is high yield. Difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
suggestions: No required revision. The explanation could more explicitly connect preoperative treatment to assessing response and subsequent treatment planning, using verified claims, rather than chiefly restating the sequence.

record.title: Initial treatment sequence for inflammatory breast cancer
fairness: Interpret rapid extensive erythema/pitting with confirmed invasive carcinoma as a clinical inflammatory presentation despite a nondiagnostic skin punch; then choose systemic treatment before surgery and radiation. The update supplies invasive tissue confirmation, nodal involvement, absence of distant metastasis, and treatment-naive status.

The same three treatment modalities occur in every option, avoiding a unique treatment-name or component-frequency cue. Upfront surgery is the main credible error; initial radiation is a weaker alternative.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The biopsy wording does not falsely make dermal lymphatic tumor identification mandatory. Receptor values are unnecessary for the broad sequence asked, since no option specifies a subtype-dependent regimen.

This is now standalone: the current update explicitly supplies the core result and staging, so it does not require a removed earlier biopsy question. The historical presentation and update remain chronologically intelligible. The sequence is a high-yield resident concept.
suggestions: No required revision. Preserve the clinical skin findings, invasive confirmation, and nonmetastatic status; do not replace them with the diagnosis label before the decision.

record.title: Pretreatment fixed axillary disease despite apparent response
fairness: The consequential steps are to interpret the pretreatment fixed cluster as a higher initial nodal burden, then determine why current clinical improvement does not establish eligibility for the usual lower-burden targeted-staging pathway. The clipped node and response make dual-tracer mapping with clipped-node retrieval a credible competing decision.

The key is not selected by wording overlap, an option-length outlier, or a majority-component pattern. Single-tracer staging is the weaker distractor but represents a recognizable staging-quality error.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The exact contemporary recommendation for initially fixed/high-burden nodes is guideline-sensitive and was not source-verified under the no-network restriction; this is editorial PASS, not independent confirmation of the cited current guidance.
The standalone presentation contains both baseline and post-treatment observations. Axillary staging after neoadjuvant therapy is high yield.
suggestions: Retain the explicit pretreatment fixed-cluster documentation and the apparent current response; both are needed to defeat the strongest alternative. Preserve clinician review of the current high-burden axillary pathway.

record.title: Final close DCIS margin when invasive carcinoma is identified
fairness: Recognize that the combined definitive specimens now establish invasive carcinoma with associated DCIS, then apply the invasive-conservation margin framework to the close but ink-negative edge. The closest error is carrying the pure-DCIS margin rule forward from the initial diagnosis.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The update supplies no tumor on ink, clear other edges, no residual suspicious calcifications, and planned whole-breast irradiation, making no additional breast excision the best offered margin-directed action. The task is limited to the lateral breast margin; it does not imply that newly identified invasion needs no other staging or treatment assessment.

The sequence is coherent: the initial specimen report was pure DCIS, re-excision occurred, and combined review newly identifies invasion. The update contains the decision-critical facts even when encountered without the first question. Prior feedback explains positive shave margins but does not give this changed-framework answer.
The absence of tumor on ink is necessary clinical evidence rather than a prohibited teaching cue. Changing definitive pathology before deciding on another operation is high yield.
suggestions: No required revision. Preserve the explicit combined-specimen chronology and the task's limitation to additional breast surgery for the margin.

record.title: Missing biopsy marker with documented calcification-target removal
clarityIssues: Minor presentation friction: 'reviews outside operating-room records in clinic' alongside 'undergoing' surgery and a request 'before closure' leaves the live-versus-retrospective consultation frame implicit. The operative decision itself is clear.
fairness: First reconcile the marker's pre-existing displacement from the calcification target; then determine whether the absent marker warrants more excision when the mapped target has been removed. Chasing the marker is a credible error, and the permanent-margin qualification prevents radiographic clearance from being equated with histologic clearance.

The exhibit's complete target retrieval and absence of residual target calcifications are decision-critical observations, not a diagnosis label or a uniquely repeated answer phrase. Additional specimen views are less compelling once the stated views answer the target question.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Closure is the best offered plan for the constructed record; the explanation appropriately leaves microscopic margins to histology.
This is a standalone operative consultation with an interpretable constructed text exhibit. Specimen-target reconciliation is a high-yield practical breast-surgery concept.
suggestions: Optional presentation improvement: explicitly call this a real-time outside-surgeon consultation before closure, or frame the entire question consistently as retrospective operative-record review. No clinical or option revision is required.

record.title: Adjuvant systemic escalation after residual invasive HER2 disease
fairness: Distinguish residual invasive carcinoma from DCIS-only residual disease or a complete invasive response, then use the stated taxane/trastuzumab exposure to choose postoperative escalation. Clear nodes and margins do not erase the residual invasive focus. Continuation of trastuzumab is the closest credible error.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the offered ranking: ado-trastuzumab emtansine is the established response-adapted choice among these alternatives. Extended neratinib is a weaker distractor at this immediate postoperative decision stage and with the supplied hormone-receptor-negative tumor.

Current systemic-therapy standards are time-sensitive. This offline review cannot establish whether newer evidence changes the best contemporary regimen outside this option set; preserve clinician verification rather than interpreting PASS as a current-guideline audit.

The split standalone case supplies the original biology, preoperative exposure, operation, and residual pathology in its own presentation/update. It does not depend on answering the separate initial-sequence item. Response-adapted HER2 treatment is high yield.
suggestions: No required editorial revision. Preserve the explicit residual invasive component and preoperative taxane/trastuzumab history; obtain exact-version clinician confirmation of the contemporary systemic-treatment ranking.

case.displayName: Clinic chart review: Axillary response review
case.presentation: {patientName}, a 50-year-old woman, attends clinic after neoadjuvant treatment for noninflammatory breast cancer. The pretreatment surgeon documented a fixed cluster of axillary nodes, and a core contained metastatic carcinoma. A node was clipped. The cluster is no longer palpable, and current ultrasound shows smaller nodes. Definitive breast surgery is planned.

answerChoices.rationale: It imports a selected initially cN1 de-escalation strategy into a pretreatment fixed-cluster presentation with less established sentinel performance.

The same three treatment modalities occur in every option, avoiding a unique treatment-name or component-frequency cue. Upfront surgery is the main credible error; initial radiation is a weaker alternative.

This is now standalone: the current update explicitly supplies the core result and staging, so it does not require a removed earlier biopsy question. The historical presentation and update remain chronologically intelligible. The sequence is a high-yield resident concept.
suggestions: No required revision. Preserve the clinical skin findings, invasive confirmation, and nonmetastatic status; do not replace them with the diagnosis label before the decision.

concept.learningObjective: Reconcile the documented marker-to-lesion relation with specimen imaging before deciding whether more tissue should be removed.

record.title: Missing biopsy marker with documented calcification-target removal
clarityIssues: Minor presentation friction: 'reviews outside operating-room records in clinic' alongside 'undergoing' surgery and a request 'before closure' leaves the live-versus-retrospective consultation frame implicit. The operative decision itself is clear.
fairness: First reconcile the marker's pre-existing displacement from the calcification target; then determine whether the absent marker warrants more excision when the mapped target has been removed. Chasing the marker is a credible error, and the permanent-margin qualification prevents radiographic clearance from being equated with histologic clearance.

The exhibit's complete target retrieval and absence of residual target calcifications are decision-critical observations, not a diagnosis label or a uniquely repeated answer phrase. Additional specimen views are less compelling once the stated views answer the target question.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Closure is the best offered plan for the constructed record; the explanation appropriately leaves microscopic margins to histology.
This is a standalone operative consultation with an interpretable constructed text exhibit. Specimen-target reconciliation is a high-yield practical breast-surgery concept.
suggestions: Optional presentation improvement: explicitly call this a real-time outside-surgeon consultation before closure, or frame the entire question consistently as retrospective operative-record review. No clinical or option revision is required.

case.displayName: Clinic chart review: Review breast extent
case.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic with a biopsy-proven left invasive carcinoma at 10 o'clock. Mammography and ultrasound show one localized lesion. MRI also shows a separate irregular enhancing focus at 4 o'clock. The radiologist can target both findings; only the 10-o'clock lesion has been sampled. The additional focus would change the planned breast resection.
sourceLabels: Clinical guidance for breast cancer screening assessment — GOV.UK
ASBrS breast conserving surgery resource guide, February 2026

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The 4-o'clock focus is sampled. Pathology shows mature adipose tissue and scant stroma. Archived needle images put the sampling notch posterior to the enhancing focus, and the postprocedure marker is in that same fat plane. Repeat targeted imaging still shows the irregular focus. {patientName}'s primary remains localized at 10 o'clock.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan should {patientName} receive for the 4-o'clock finding?

answerChoices.label: Repeat image-guided sampling of the 4-o'clock focus
answerChoices.rationale: The sample's location and contents do not represent the persisting target, so its benign result cannot settle that focus.

answerChoices.label: Interval breast imaging after the primary resection
answerChoices.rationale: The nonrepresentative sample has not resolved the additional suspicious focus before surgery is finalized.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to mastectomy for both mapped breast sites
answerChoices.rationale: The additional focus remains unproven, so this would treat uncertain extent as established separate malignancy.

record.title: Benign biopsy that missed an additional MRI focus
fairness: Interpret the sampling notch/marker in posterior fat plus the adipose specimen as failure to represent the persistent irregular focus; then choose repeat representative sampling before dismissing the site or escalating to mastectomy. The observations support that inference without a pre-answer 'discordant' label.

The alternatives reflect actual competing errors: accepting a benign report for surveillance versus treating imaging suspicion as proven multicentric malignancy. The key is not identifiable through a unique location phrase because the task and competing plans address the same additional finding.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Repeat sampling is best among the choices; the presentation establishes that the focus is targetable, so this is not a demand to repeat an inherently inaccessible biopsy.

The standalone update explicitly records the intervening biopsy and its acquisition details. It requires no prior task or explanation and preserves the 10-o'clock primary/4-o'clock additional-site relationship. Imaging-pathology concordance is high yield.
suggestions: No required revision. Keep the acquisition evidence and persistent target; a benign pathology label without those observations would make the ranking less secure.

concept.learningObjective: Select the invasive-cancer margin framework when an excision contains invasive carcinoma with associated DCIS.

record.title: Final close DCIS margin when invasive carcinoma is identified
fairness: Recognize that the combined definitive specimens now establish invasive carcinoma with associated DCIS, then apply the invasive-conservation margin framework to the close but ink-negative edge. The closest error is carrying the pure-DCIS margin rule forward from the initial diagnosis.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The update supplies no tumor on ink, clear other edges, no residual suspicious calcifications, and planned whole-breast irradiation, making no additional breast excision the best offered margin-directed action. The task is limited to the lateral breast margin; it does not imply that newly identified invasion needs no other staging or treatment assessment.

The sequence is coherent: the initial specimen report was pure DCIS, re-excision occurred, and combined review newly identifies invasion. The update contains the decision-critical facts even when encountered without the first question. Prior feedback explains positive shave margins but does not give this changed-framework answer.
The absence of tumor on ink is necessary clinical evidence rather than a prohibited teaching cue. Changing definitive pathology before deciding on another operation is high yield.
suggestions: No required revision. Preserve the explicit combined-specimen chronology and the task's limitation to additional breast surgery for the margin.

case.displayName: Clinic chart review: Surgery after treatment
case.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman, attends clinic after neoadjuvant treatment for noninflammatory left breast cancer. The pretreatment invasive mass was localized at one marked upper-outer site. Current MRI shows a small enhancing remnant there. Mammography shows branching calcifications continuous through the central breast into all four peripheral quadrants. Separate mapped samples from the central, upper-inner, lower-inner, lower-outer and upper-outer field contain DCIS. These calcifications reach the gland periphery.
sourceLabels: ASBrS breast conserving surgery resource guide, February 2026

decisionNodes.stem: Which breast operation should be recommended for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Mastectomy of the affected breast
answerChoices.rationale: The distributed proven malignant calcification field is a conservation contraindication despite the small enhancing remnant.

answerChoices.label: Bracketed oncoplastic reduction encompassing the calcification field
answerChoices.rationale: Oncoplastic redistribution does not remove the oncologic limitation imposed by diffuse malignant calcifications across the breast.

answerChoices.label: Multiple image-localized lumpectomies across the calcified regions
answerChoices.rationale: The record is a continuous intervening malignant field, not a few discrete separable foci that can each be encompassed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the distribution across modalities and sampled sites. The enhancing invasive remnant is small, but the malignant calcification field is continuous through the central breast and all quadrants. Mastectomy addresses that diffuse extent. Neither oncoplastic rearrangement nor multiple focal resections makes diffuse malignant calcifications a routine conservation setting.

record.title: Sequencing systemic therapy and surgery for node-positive HER2 disease
fairness: Interpret the size and biopsy-proven mobile nodal disease in the nonmetastatic setting, then select combined chemotherapy/HER2-directed treatment before surgery rather than surgery first or incomplete preoperative systemic treatment. The HER2 result identifies the treatment family, but that family is present in every option.

No unique drug-name overlap or component-majority cue selects the key: all options contain chemotherapy, trastuzumab/pertuzumab, and surgery. The third sequence tests separating HER2 blockade from the chemotherapy component; it is the weaker competitor but is a recognizable de-escalation/sequencing error.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The broad sequence is fair for the supplied substantial node-positive disease; the item is not asking for a regimen dose, chemotherapy backbone, or cardiac-safety decision for which additional details would be necessary.
This standalone initial-planning case is complete and does not borrow later response data. Stage/biology-dependent neoadjuvant sequencing is high yield. Difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
suggestions: No required revision. The explanation could more explicitly connect preoperative treatment to assessing response and subsequent treatment planning, using verified claims, rather than chiefly restating the sequence.

record.title: Merkel carcinoma nodal staging and sequencing despite negative PET/CT
fairness: Negative examination and PET/CT do not exclude microscopic regional involvement. Coordinating sentinel-node mapping/biopsy before definitive wide excision and flap disruption is the defensible listed plan for this fit clinically node-negative patient.

Two consequential steps survive the options: decide whether negative macroscopic staging can replace sentinel staging, then decide when mapping must occur relative to the planned wide excision and reconstruction. Ultrasound substitution and delayed sentinel biopsy represent different credible errors.

The proposed schedule is a relevant operative constraint. The word 'before' in the task does not uniquely choose the key because an ultrasound-first strategy also fits a preoperative planning task; knowledge of microscopic staging and lymphatic disruption is still needed.

The prior narrow diagnostic excision is clearly separated from the unperformed definitive operation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation does not claim that baseline PET/CT is mandatory for every MCC patient.

MCC is less common than melanoma or keratinocyte cancers, but sentinel staging despite negative imaging is a core testable surgical principle for this disease. Standalone and coherent, with no earlier node or feedback dependency.

record.title: Regional management after a microscopic positive melanoma sentinel node
fairness: The small sentinel-node deposit, absence of palpable regional disease and feasible follow-up support nodal ultrasound surveillance over routine completion dissection. Completion dissection is a credible historical/common-error competitor; regional irradiation is less competitive but does not create another best answer in this presentation.

The follow-up-availability sentence is a relevant surveillance constraint, not sufficient by itself to select ultrasound without knowing how microscopic sentinel-node disease differs from clinically apparent nodal disease. No decisive nonmedical wording, length, absolute or convergence shortcut identified.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the regional disease burden, then apply the surveillance-versus-completion-dissection decision with follow-up feasibility. This is a high-yield melanoma management principle.

fairness: The thickness, ulceration, negative sentinel-node biopsy and absence of distant disease support stage IIB rather than stage III. Nivolumab is the defensible listed adjuvant discussion option; the BRAF result makes dabrafenib plus trametinib a meaningful stage-indication trap.

The task asks about discussion, not mandatory treatment initiation. Lack of a complete immunotherapy screening history therefore does not defeat the key. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the supplied content; current regulatory wording was not independently verified offline.

Two consequential steps: derive the stage from the pathology and nodal findings, then distinguish stage-appropriate adjuvant therapy from mutation-driven extrapolation. Stage-dependent melanoma systemic-treatment principles are high yield.
Standalone, with coherent postoperative chronology and a complete task.

record.title: Integrating sequential melanoma specimens before selecting an excision margin
fairness: The first reliable 2.6-mm invasive measurement remains relevant despite a thinner residual focus in the completion specimen. A 2-cm clinical radial margin is the defensible listed answer for the supplied unconstrained extremity site.

Two consequential steps remain: reconcile the two samples of one primary rather than substitute the latest residual depth, then select the definitive margin. The 1-cm alternative represents using the residual 0.6-mm depth; the 0.5-cm alternative represents focusing on the surrounding in-situ component. These are recognizable clinical interpretation errors, not wording giveaways.

The explanation's warning against adding measurements does not distinguish any listed answer here: adding these particular depths still leads to the same margin category. That sentence should not be counted as an additional tested inference.

The options are parallel numeric margins with no uniquely qualified key or component-convergence shortcut. The complete separated task identifies a total radial margin and the original site. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
High-yield melanoma microstaging and definitive-margin planning. Standalone and coherent; diagnostic sampling is clearly distinguished from definitive wide excision.
suggestions: Optional feedback tightening: focus on the consequential latest-specimen-versus-greatest-reliable-depth error; the addition warning is extra teaching rather than an error the present answers discriminate.

record.title: Choose gallbladder source control during active cardiac deterioration
fairness: Immediate percutaneous gallbladder drainage is the best offered plan alongside cardiac treatment and resuscitation. Persistent gallbladder inflammation plus deterioration makes antibiotic reassessment inadequate as the preferred source-control strategy, while new ischemic findings materially change immediate operative suitability.

The resident must interpret the cardiac trajectory and integrate it with a separately persistent gallbladder source. Neither simply noticing gallstones nor recognizing myocardial injury fully answers the management question.

Both intervention options say 'Immediate', so urgency wording does not uniquely identify the key. Continued antibiotics with reassessment is a real competing plan without an 'alone' caricature. All options address the same immediate gallbladder decision.

The falling blood pressure need not be assigned exclusively to cardiac or infectious shock to rank these offered plans. No specific infarction subtype, drug regimen or post-infarction waiting interval is asserted. The standalone checkpoint is coherent.

record.title: Choose gallbladder filling rather than emptying assessment
fairness: Gallbladder-filling scintigraphy is the best offered protocol for persistent focal and systemic inflammatory findings despite an adequately visualized ultrasound lacking wall thickening or surrounding fluid.

The resident must interpret the clinical-ultrasound discrepancy and then distinguish an acute filling question from stimulated emptying or duct mapping. The two scintigraphic choices prevent generic recall of HIDA from uniquely answering the question.

The observations do not name acute cholecystitis or teach the filling rule before the choice. All options are examination protocols of comparable specificity. The recorded admission stage is clear, and this active case stands alone rather than teaching the separate incomplete-acquisition item immediately beforehand.

record.title: Reassess postoperative antibiotics after source control
fairness: Stopping routine postoperative biliary antibiotics is the best offered plan after the represented complete source control, absence of complicated or residual infection, and improving clinical course.

The resident must interpret the operative findings as adequate source control and then weigh a still-abnormal but falling white-cell count against the postoperative trajectory. Continuing oral therapy is a credible common error; ongoing intravenous treatment is less compelling but answers the same decision.

The negative operative and infection findings are necessary to establish the antibiotic boundary. They are not a reason to omit clinically important facts to increase difficulty. Stop versus continue is the decision itself, so the key's different verb is not a gratuitous style cue.

The progression from the first part's operation decision to a completed operation is coherent. The current update independently supplies the operation, source-control findings and postoperative course, so it remains answerable without the preceding question. Earlier feedback does not rehearse the antibiotic rule. Difficulty is at the lower end of moderate.

record.title: Drain an infected duct while deferring a high-risk sphincterotomy
fairness: Stenting with staged sphincterotomy/extraction is the single best offered plan for ongoing obstructive infection, excessive anticoagulation and established access across the obstruction.

The resident must balance urgent drainage against the bleeding implications of sphincterotomy, rather than treating drainage and definitive extraction as inseparable. The mechanical-valve history makes anticoagulation management consequential without requiring an invented reversal or bridging regimen.

The phrase 'before any endoscopic drainage' defines the actual delaying strategy being compared. It is broad, but not an unrelated rhetorical absolute: choosing it requires misunderstanding which part of ERCP creates the relevant bleeding risk.

Both immediate extraction and delaying decompression are credible errors. The explanation allows concurrent anticoagulation management and does not prescribe an unsupported time interval. The standalone procedural checkpoint is clear.

record.title: Select a bailout when the hilar junction remains unresolved
fairness: Subtotal cholecystectomy is the best offered completion plan for the represented fusion, traction distortion and inability to expose the lower attachment. Neither a fundus-first approach nor conversion by itself establishes safe identification for a committed total operation.

The resident must interpret the apparent funnel as potentially misleading anatomy and then choose an extent of surgery that avoids the unresolved junction. The two total-operation strategies are real operative alternatives, not unrelated foils.

Subtotal is the only limited operation, but that distinction is the actual clinical decision, not a stylistic outlier. There is no pre-answer instruction to preserve tissue or perform a bailout. The explanation appropriately allows conversion and fundus-first reassessment when they genuinely improve safety.
The clinic frame clearly concerns an earlier operative checkpoint. The item stands alone and does not require a missing earlier answer.

record.title: Confirm a suspected duct stone before invasive treatment
fairness: MRCP is the single best offered investigation: persistent cholestatic abnormalities and duct enlargement warrant duct assessment, but neither a demonstrated stone nor an infected obstruction is supplied. EUS is not offered, and the explanation appropriately acknowledges it.

The resident must localize the unresolved problem to the duct and distinguish confirmation from therapeutic ERCP. Normal bilirubin and settled pain do not automatically settle the duct question. HIDA represents a different, credible biliary-workup error.

The negative inflammatory observations are relevant to the competing HIDA path rather than a nonmedical answer shortcut. The full investigation names have comparable grammar and specificity. The standalone task is complete.

Review scope for this report: all 18 current proposals, comprising seven rewrites and eleven new items, including the eleven pass-preserved proposals, were independently assessed from their after fields. Six kept inventory records, 42 historical retirement/replacement proposals, 16 parked attempts and the recorded held/unkeyed material were noted but not scored. Archived v1 candidates and author verdicts did not determine these judgments.

All difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative editorial estimates. This is an offline content review, not fresh guideline/source verification, runtime wait/randomization validation or clinical approval. Every draft still requires Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical sign-off. These limitations apply to every entry.

record.title: Reassess duct-stone suspicion after a negative MRCP
fairness: EUS is the best offered test for renewed suspicion after a negative interval MRCP. Recurrence and new cholestatic abnormalities make the prior negative result insufficient to close the question, while the current comfortable, afebrile state and lack of a demonstrated stone do not establish a therapeutic ERCP indication.

Two consequential judgments remain: reassess the meaning of the earlier negative study in light of the later episode, then choose a confirmatory rather than invasive therapeutic pathway. The task identifies a duct question but does not supply either judgment.

HIDA is the weaker competitor because the task is already duct-focused; ERCP remains a credible close error. There is no key-only wording overlap or length outlier. The standalone chronology is coherent, and the explanation does not claim that every negative MRCP requires EUS.

record.title: Distinguish failed extraction from failed endoscopic drainage access
fairness: A transpapillary plastic stent is the best offered drainage route when extraction has failed but a wire crosses the obstruction, contrast remains upstream, and the patient is deteriorating.

The resident must distinguish retained obstruction from achieved access, then decide whether to use that access for a bridge or abandon it for percutaneous or operative drainage. Failed extraction does not establish failure of the endoscopic route.

Wire position is a legitimate procedural discriminator, not a statement that stent deployment is guaranteed. Actual inability to pass or deploy a drainage device would change the route decision; the explanation does not promise universal technical success.

All three options are actual drainage routes with comparable specificity. The task does not restrict the answer to endoscopy. The standalone sequence is clear, and planned definitive clearance and device removal/exchange are appropriately kept in feedback.

record.title: Distinguish chronic operative risk from current unsuitability
fairness: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the best offered plan for the represented acute gallbladder process with preserved pre-illness function and no new organ instability. Neither age and remote infarction nor antibiotic improvement independently establishes a reason for drainage or interval surgery.

The case requires weighing chronic risk against current fitness and applying that assessment to definitive-treatment timing despite improvement on antibiotics. These are consequential competing considerations, not two successive diagnosis labels.

The actual severity of chronic kidney disease and full anesthetic assessment are not supplied; the item supports a best plan among these choices, not a declaration of universal operative eligibility. No confident clinical error is identified. The options are parallel treatment plans.
This first part is coherent. Its feedback explains the timing/source-control decision but does not disclose the later postoperative antibiotic answer.

record.title: Let distal duct anatomy change difficult-stone treatment
fairness: Cholangioscopy-guided fragmentation is the best offered stone-directed strategy after failed standard extraction with a fixed distal duct stricture. Treating proximal duct caliber as permission to dilate the narrowed distal segment is the consequential competing error.

The resident must interpret the caliber/stricture relationship and choose a clearance technique that addresses the stone without applying the inappropriate dilation strategy. Repeat conventional sweeps are a weaker foil, but the large-balloon competitor is clinically relevant.

The pre-existing drainage stent and separate stricture evaluation establish why urgent decompression or a new stricture workup is not the current task. They do not uniquely name the key. No unsupported balloon diameter or universal technical-success claim is made.

This is relevant difficult-duct-stone teaching for surgery residents, although more specialized than initial duct-risk assessment. Actual cholangioscope access and final technique depend on procedural findings; no confident inaccuracy is identified in this best-strategy formulation. The standalone task is clear.

record.title: Interpret proximal obstruction beside an impacted neck stone
fairness: MRCP is the best offered initial mapping study for this stable jaundiced patient with a neck stone and disproportionate proximal dilation. ERCP can also define anatomy and provide therapy, but the supplied setting does not establish an urgent drainage need or a routine distal extraction target.

The two consequential judgments are localization from the proximal/distal pattern and selection of anatomical mapping before a potentially misleading routine duct-stone intervention. The syndrome name is not supplied.

The explanation properly treats external compression as a supported possibility rather than proving a fistula subtype or excluding another stricture. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; this does not claim ERCP is never appropriate for this syndrome.
The longer HIDA label clarifies its actual target rather than supplying the key. The standalone clinical stage is clear, and this is a high-yield Mirizzi-pattern/safe-operative-planning concept.

record.title: Map a possible stone-bearing remnant before intervention
fairness: MRCP is the best offered next investigation to characterize the postoperative pouch and its relationship to the ducts, including the incompletely visualized distal duct. There is no demonstrated duct target or represented infection that makes therapeutic ERCP the clearly preferred immediate action.

The resident must combine the prior subtotal operation with a fluid structure containing shadowing foci, then separate anatomical planning from immediate duct intervention or gallbladder functional testing.

The missing duct-connection map is decision-critical anatomical uncertainty; it does not literally repeat the MRCP label. Normal bilirubin between attacks does not negate episodic obstruction. Options are parallel investigations, and the explanation stops short of claiming ultrasound has proved the entire cause of the pain.
The standalone history and task are coherent. This is useful tested postoperative biliary anatomy, though less common than the core acute-cholecystitis and duct-stone decisions.

record.title: Treat recurrent obstruction despite an unchanged stent position
fairness: ERCP with stent reassessment/exchange is the best offered immediate drainage plan for recurrent infection and increasing upstream dilation despite unchanged device position, with current upstream wire access achieved.

The resident must distinguish device position from drainage function and distinguish failure of the old device from failure of the current endoscopic route. Percutaneous rescue is a credible alternative if present access or deployment fails; operative exploration is a greater escalation in this represented checkpoint.

Repeating 'stent' in the history and exchange option is necessary identification of the device being managed. It is not sufficient to answer without understanding the evidence of functional obstruction and the available route. The task does not grammatically require an endoscopic answer.

Occlusion is inferred rather than proved by CT. The explanation appropriately leaves the exact maneuver dependent on procedural findings and preserves later stone clearance and device follow-up. The standalone chronology is coherent, with no earlier bridge-stenting answer supplied.

record.title: Reassess early surgery despite several days of symptoms
fairness: Operating during the current admission is the best offered schedule for the supplied symptom/admission chronology and recovered physiology. A rigid early-symptom deadline or initial renal abnormality would lead to inappropriate automatic deferral.

The resident must distinguish the symptom and admission clocks, then decide whether the current physiological course still supports early surgery. The three choices compare schedules for the same operation, and the later dates are clearly constructed alternatives rather than diagnostic thresholds.

The hospital's usual biliary service is relevant feasibility context and does not say which schedule it permits. The physiological observations are concrete rather than an authored fitness conclusion.

The stated WSES timing window is consistent with recalled guidance, but its exact numbers were not freshly source-verified in this no-network review. They should retain their source mapping and clinical review. The task and standalone chronology are intelligible.

record.title: Limit an unstable ERCP to effective drainage
fairness: Drainage stenting with staged clearance is the best offered plan when physiology is worsening and a large stone above a tight distal segment requires additional manipulation for extraction.

The two decisions are to limit intervention because of the physiological trajectory and still establish drainage across the persistent obstruction. Sphincterotomy and ending the session is an anatomically relevant near-miss: it can be shorter than extraction yet need not resolve the upstream obstruction.

record.title: Confirm a suspected duct stone before invasive treatment
fairness: MRCP is the single best offered investigation: persistent cholestatic abnormalities and duct enlargement warrant duct assessment, but neither a demonstrated stone nor an infected obstruction is supplied. EUS is not offered, and the explanation appropriately acknowledges it.

The resident must localize the unresolved problem to the duct and distinguish confirmation from therapeutic ERCP. Normal bilirubin and settled pain do not automatically settle the duct question. HIDA represents a different, credible biliary-workup error.

The negative inflammatory observations are relevant to the competing HIDA path rather than a nonmedical answer shortcut. The full investigation names have comparable grammar and specificity. The standalone task is complete.

Review scope for this report: all 18 current proposals, comprising seven rewrites and eleven new items, including the eleven pass-preserved proposals, were independently assessed from their after fields. Six kept inventory records, 42 historical retirement/replacement proposals, 16 parked attempts and the recorded held/unkeyed material were noted but not scored. Archived v1 candidates and author verdicts did not determine these judgments.

All difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative editorial estimates. This is an offline content review, not fresh guideline/source verification, runtime wait/randomization validation or clinical approval. Every draft still requires Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical sign-off. These limitations apply to every entry.

record.title: Reassess duct-stone suspicion after a negative MRCP
fairness: EUS is the best offered test for renewed suspicion after a negative interval MRCP. Recurrence and new cholestatic abnormalities make the prior negative result insufficient to close the question, while the current comfortable, afebrile state and lack of a demonstrated stone do not establish a therapeutic ERCP indication.

Two consequential judgments remain: reassess the meaning of the earlier negative study in light of the later episode, then choose a confirmatory rather than invasive therapeutic pathway. The task identifies a duct question but does not supply either judgment.

HIDA is the weaker competitor because the task is already duct-focused; ERCP remains a credible close error. There is no key-only wording overlap or length outlier. The standalone chronology is coherent, and the explanation does not claim that every negative MRCP requires EUS.

record.title: Distinguish chronic operative risk from current unsuitability
fairness: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the best offered plan for the represented acute gallbladder process with preserved pre-illness function and no new organ instability. answerChoices.rationale: Initial drainage can be established without sphincterotomy while the bleeding-risk and valve-anticoagulation plan are addressed before definitive stone work.

fairness: Stenting with staged sphincterotomy/extraction is the single best offered plan for ongoing obstructive infection, excessive anticoagulation and established access across the obstruction.

The resident must balance urgent drainage against the bleeding implications of sphincterotomy, rather than treating drainage and definitive extraction as inseparable. The mechanical-valve history makes anticoagulation management consequential without requiring an invented reversal or bridging regimen.

The phrase 'before any endoscopic drainage' defines the actual delaying strategy being compared. It is broad, but not an unrelated rhetorical absolute: choosing it requires misunderstanding which part of ERCP creates the relevant bleeding risk.

Both immediate extraction and delaying decompression are credible errors. The explanation allows concurrent anticoagulation management and does not prescribe an unsupported time interval. The standalone procedural checkpoint is clear.

decisionNodes.stem: Alongside cardiac treatment and resuscitation, which immediate gallbladder plan best fit {patientName} at that checkpoint?

answerChoices.label: Immediate percutaneous gallbladder drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent gallbladder infection still needs source control while the new cardiac findings and circulatory deterioration make immediate general anesthesia hazardous. Drainage addresses that competing need.

answerChoices.label: Immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Definitive surgery is preferred for many patients with stable comorbidity, but the current dynamic ischemic findings and falling pressure are different from chronic risk.

answerChoices.label: Continued antibiotics with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Concurrent cardiac treatment is necessary, but continuing fever and focal findings despite antibiotics leave gallbladder source control unresolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: There are two simultaneous problems: persisting gallbladder infection and new active myocardial ischemic findings with circulatory deterioration. The latter changes the immediate operative choice; it does not remove the need to address the infected compartment. Gallbladder drainage provides source control while cardiac care and resuscitation continue. This does not prescribe a post-infarction waiting interval or a cardiac drug regimen.

record.title: Choose gallbladder source control during active cardiac deterioration
fairness: Immediate percutaneous gallbladder drainage is the best offered plan alongside cardiac treatment and resuscitation. Persistent gallbladder inflammation plus deterioration makes antibiotic reassessment inadequate as the preferred source-control strategy, while new ischemic findings materially change immediate operative suitability.

record.title: Distinguish failed extraction from failed endoscopic drainage access
fairness: A transpapillary plastic stent is the best offered drainage route when extraction has failed but a wire crosses the obstruction, contrast remains upstream, and the patient is deteriorating.

The resident must distinguish retained obstruction from achieved access, then decide whether to use that access for a bridge or abandon it for percutaneous or operative drainage. Failed extraction does not establish failure of the endoscopic route.

Wire position is a legitimate procedural discriminator, not a statement that stent deployment is guaranteed. Actual inability to pass or deploy a drainage device would change the route decision; the explanation does not promise universal technical success.

All three options are actual drainage routes with comparable specificity. The task does not restrict the answer to endoscopy. The standalone sequence is clear, and planned definitive clearance and device removal/exchange are appropriately kept in feedback.

concept.displayName: Recurrent obstruction despite a stent history
concept.learningObjective: Use current drainage function rather than device position to recognize a renewed source-control problem.
concept.identityDecision: Distinct scored meaning; retain predecessor definitions and cards without transferring history.

record.title: Treat recurrent obstruction despite an unchanged stent position
fairness: ERCP with stent reassessment/exchange is the best offered immediate drainage plan for recurrent infection and increasing upstream dilation despite unchanged device position, with current upstream wire access achieved.

The resident must distinguish device position from drainage function and distinguish failure of the old device from failure of the current endoscopic route. Percutaneous rescue is a credible alternative if present access or deployment fails; operative exploration is a greater escalation in this represented checkpoint.

Repeating 'stent' in the history and exchange option is necessary identification of the device being managed. It is not sufficient to answer without understanding the evidence of functional obstruction and the available route. The task does not grammatically require an endoscopic answer.

Occlusion is inferred rather than proved by CT. The explanation appropriately leaves the exact maneuver dependent on procedural findings and preserves later stone clearance and device follow-up. The standalone chronology is coherent, with no earlier bridge-stenting answer supplied.

record.title: Initial management of a recently irreducible inguinal hernia
fairness: A gentle manual reduction attempt is the best offered initial plan in the stated hospital surgical setting. The resident must recognize acute irreducibility and then use trajectory, skin, abdominal and systemic findings to distinguish it from a presentation that raises sufficient concern for strangulation to favor immediate exploration.

Exploration represents equating every acute irreducibility with suspected ischemia; CT represents routinely requiring imaging despite an established inguinal episode and a reassuring clinical course. Both are credible nearby decisions. The necessary negative findings do not literally announce the answer or constitute gratuitous exclusions.

The clock times describe onset and reassessment, not a universal safe reduction window. The explanation retains failed reduction and emerging ischemic concern as escalation triggers and does not claim viability is guaranteed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; assessment for ischemia remains a clinical judgment, not a negative-examination proof.
The hospital setting, initial decision and current findings are all supplied locally, so the node stands alone.

record.title: Posterior repair after recurrence of an anterior mesh repair
fairness: TEP is the single best offered operation. The cord, inguinal-floor mesh and external-oblique relationships establish prior anterior repair; the resident must then apply the recurrence-plane principle to the named procedures.

Lichtenstein repeats the prior compartment, and Shouldice changes the material strategy without escaping that compartment. These represent distinct credible errors. The cholecystectomy history can test overgeneralization from abdominal surgery to relevant pelvic dissection without falsely describing a scarred preperitoneal pelvis.

The explanation appropriately avoids claiming superiority of TEP over an unoffered TAPP. The symptom-related functional limitation, current recurrence, operative history and available techniques are supplied within this node. No confident clinical inaccuracy or standalone-context gap identified.

record.title: Small directly closable groin defect after gross enteric spillage
fairness: Primary tissue closure is the best offered repair for this small, directly closable defect after perforation and gross enteric contamination. The resident must distinguish this field from controlled bowel entry and then use defect size and closure feasibility to distinguish tissue closure from biologic reinforcement.

'Approximate its edges without tension' is necessary information for that comparison, not an expendable permission sentence. Removing it would weaken the ranking against biologic reconstruction. The options name actual repairs with comparable specificity.

The explanation limits the recommendation to this setting and explicitly acknowledges older, low-certainty guidance. The precise guideline boundary quoted in the explanation was not independently source-verified in this offline review; no confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted. The hospital operative-record task stands alone.

record.title: Repair and anesthesia planning after retropubic prostate surgery
fairness: Lichtenstein repair with local infiltration is a defensible favored plan among the three choices. The resident must recognize the prior pelvic/retropubic dissection from the operative description, apply it to approach selection, and distinguish local from general anesthesia for an experienced team's cooperative patient with a reducing open-repair target.

The patient is not presented as unable to tolerate general anesthesia, and the explanation correctly does not make prior prostate surgery an absolute prohibition on expert laparoscopy. The wording 'should be favored' allows a preferred plan without pretending the other techniques are universally contraindicated.

Cooperation during supine examination and experience with the offered combinations are legitimate conditions for the anesthesia comparison. They are not unique availability permissions, and the fit patient's activity makes TEP/general anesthesia a credible competing default. The key is not the most frequent combination of components: both open repair and general anesthesia appear twice.

The precise strength of the approach and anesthesia preferences has not been independently source-verified here and still requires clinician sign-off. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the candidate text. The operative history and current hernia state are supplied within this standalone node.

record.title: Elective repair of an asymptomatic marked femoral swelling
fairness: Elective groin repair is the single best offered plan. The marker identifies which of two abnormalities is being asked about. The resident must localize that sac to the femoral compartment and then reject extrapolating the minimally symptomatic male inguinal observation policy to it.

The painless, reducing examination and preference for deferral make surveillance a credible competing choice. The lack of an acute painful irreducible presentation distinguishes elective repair from emergency exploration. The marked versus cranial labels identify targets without naming the diagnosis or keyed plan.

The exhibit is explicitly constructed, internally understandable and necessary to the decision: deleting it removes the anatomy that defeats observation. The named patient, age, sex and complete task are present. No prior case part is required and no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Targeted dynamic imaging after an examination of a different site
fairness: Dynamic groin ultrasound is the best offered next investigation. The learner must establish from the acquisition record, reproduced symptom and video location that the prior study did not test the new contour, then distinguish an initial appropriately targeted study from escalation after an adequate negative study.

Dynamic MRI is a credible alternative for unresolved groin uncertainty after appropriate initial assessment. The signed worksheet and matching cine loops matter: the packet describes what was acquired rather than assuming an acquisition was omitted because exported images are missing. CT is less competitive for this intermittent, reducing contour but remains a real investigation in the same option category.

The word 'sonographer' is not an unfair instruction to repeat ultrasound: the necessary inference is whether the previous acquisition assessed the same site and provoking condition. The task is complete, the chronology is locally supplied, and no earlier node is needed. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Threatened partial bowel wall despite continued stool passage
fairness: Emergency operative exploration is the single best offered intervention. The partial-circumference anatomy explains why stool passage is not reassuring; substantially reduced enhancement and fixed tenderness then make a reduction attempt inappropriate. These are observations requiring clinical interpretation, not a pre-answer diagnosis of strangulation.

Manual reduction is a credible consequential error if the learner overweights ongoing stool passage. Elective discharge planning is a weaker distractor. The explanation appropriately distinguishes suspected ischemia from proven irreversible necrosis.

The hospital chart-review frame and hospital-directed task agree, with initial support already underway. The current record supplies the needed context independently of any later bowel-resection item. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Observation when functional limitation does not track the hernia
fairness: The best offered plan is observation with return precautions. The resident must separate the running-related adduction pain from the painless protrusion during usual warehouse lifting, then apply the selected-male observation boundary and the patient's preference.

The preference to defer is necessary decision context, not an unfair instruction to choose observation: it would not justify observing a hernia with a different risk profile or attributable functional limitation. Elective repair remains discussable, but arranging it now is less aligned with this particular record. Repeating ultrasound is the weaker distractor because a dynamic sac and reduction are already established.

The task is complete and the node stands alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This report reviews only current candidate display text, not author gates or earlier verdicts; no network or independent source verification was performed. PASS is an editorial judgment, not Melissa Rowland's clinical approval, and difficulty predictions are qualitative.

fairness: Dynamic groin ultrasound is the best offered next investigation. decisionNodes.stem: Which repair and anesthetic plan should be favored for Evan's symptomatic primary inguinal hernia?

answerChoices.label: Lichtenstein mesh repair with general anesthesia
Totally extraperitoneal mesh repair with general anesthesia

decisionNodes.explanation: The old operation used the retropubic/pelvic region, so primary-repair advice must be individualized rather than automatically applying the usual laparo-endoscopic preference. An offered anterior Lichtenstein repair is reasonable, and experienced local infiltration is favored for this cooperative reducing open-repair patient. Prior prostate surgery is not an absolute ban on expert laparoscopy, and neither general nor spinal anesthesia is universally contraindicated.

record.title: Repair and anesthesia planning after retropubic prostate surgery
fairness: Lichtenstein repair with local infiltration is a defensible favored plan among the three choices. The resident must recognize the prior pelvic/retropubic dissection from the operative description, apply it to approach selection, and distinguish local from general anesthesia for an experienced team's cooperative patient with a reducing open-repair target.

The patient is not presented as unable to tolerate general anesthesia, and the explanation correctly does not make prior prostate surgery an absolute prohibition on expert laparoscopy. The wording 'should be favored' allows a preferred plan without pretending the other techniques are universally contraindicated.

Cooperation during supine examination and experience with the offered combinations are legitimate conditions for the anesthesia comparison. They are not unique availability permissions, and the fit patient's activity makes TEP/general anesthesia a credible competing default. The key is not the most frequent combination of components: both open repair and general anesthesia appear twice.

The precise strength of the approach and anesthesia preferences has not been independently source-verified here and still requires clinician sign-off. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified from the candidate text. The operative history and current hernia state are supplied within this standalone node.

record.title: Extubation strategy after recovery to chronic hypercapnic baseline
fairness: Scope: independent review of the four status=salvage candidate contexts in salvageRound, using their presentation, current update, exhibit, task, options and explanation. Kept-unchanged, retired, parked, held and other non-salvage records are outside this review; their presence does not confer acceptance. Earlier reviewer verdicts and author self-checks were not used as evidence of correctness. No network or fresh source verification was performed. PASS is editorial only; every reviewed draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval.

The standalone presentation identifies Robert, age 70, male, and the COPD admission. The update supplies the invasive-support history, successful breathing trial, airway function and both baseline and current gases. 'Later hospital entry' refers intelligibly to that admission; no prior scored answer or explanation is needed. The complete task asks for an airway plan at the documented recovery stage, rather than an intervention in today's clinic.

The resident must recognize that a normal pH with PaCO2 near the pre-illness value does not require continued intubation, then distinguish readiness for tube removal from the need for preventive support afterward. COPD, age and persistent hypercapnia make immediate bilevel support the best offered plan. Ordinary nasal oxygen is a credible competing plan after a successful trial, but omits the preventive ventilatory strategy for this risk profile.

Cue attack: 'tolerates an SBT' and 'Low-flow oxygen maintains the trial’s oxygenation' establish relevant observations, but neither identifies bilevel support without clinical knowledge; the latter could tempt the oxygen distractor. 'Continue intubation until PaCO2 normalizes' is a concrete, clinically familiar normalization error rather than a rhetorical 'always/never' foil. The two extubation options have parallel wording and comparable length. No unique wording match, teaching sentence, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut selects the key.

Predicted moderate: baseline-versus-normal interpretation changes whether the tube stays, and risk assessment changes support after removal. Both distinctions are high-yield ventilator-liberation decisions. This is not a hard item: the successful trial and preserved clearance deliberately resolve basic readiness uncertainty.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. 'Low-flow oxygen' is less specific than a recorded oxygen setting, but the stated tolerated trial and maintained oxygenation suffice to rank these options; the task does not ask for an exact oxygen prescription. The explanation appropriately confines preventive NIV to a selected profile and does not claim superiority over every alternative post-extubation regimen. Its exact guideline support was not newly verified offline.

record.title: Proceeding to an SBT despite a concerning isolated RSBI
fairness: Sarah's named age/sex presentation and current update supply the illness trajectory, spontaneous effort, oxygen requirement, hemodynamics and observed breathing behavior. The index measurement is explicitly complete rather than terminated for distress. This distinction makes the record intelligible without a preceding question or an invented trial-duration rule. The task is complete and all options address the present liberation pathway.

A monitored SBT is the best offered next step after integrating the improving illness, oxygenation on modest support and cardiovascular stability. The discordant RSBI is a reason to examine readiness carefully, not proof that an SBT has failed. Continuing assist-control or requiring a pressure-support taper treats the isolated index as a barrier despite the other supplied findings. Those are plausible resident errors, not equally supported necessities in this record.

Cue attack: 'she remains comfortable, with no accessory-muscle use' and 'The measurement ends when its scheduled recording is complete' favor proceeding, but they distinguish an isolated concerning measurement from actual intolerance and are needed for fairness. They do not state that RSBI can be bypassed. 'breathing trial' occurs in both the key and taper option, and the task's 'liberation plan' does not uniquely match the key. No option is conspicuously longer, uniquely comprehensive or qualified with an explanatory criticism of itself.

Predicted moderate: infer readiness from several clinical domains, reconcile that inference with the concerning index, and choose direct monitored testing rather than a delay or unnecessary taper. Removing the index would make the item substantially easier. SBT readiness and misuse of a single weaning parameter are high-yield concepts; difficulty here depends partly on familiarity with evolving liberation recommendations, not on a novel physiologic puzzle.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation properly distinguishes an index from demonstrated clinical intolerance and does not infer extubation readiness from this assessment alone. Exact AARC wording and currency were not freshly verified; the numerical observation should not be promoted into a new universal cutoff. Editorial PASS does not constitute clinical approval.

record.title: Interpreting a tolerated breathing trial performed at increased FiO2
fairness: The exhibit contains its own before-trial and during-trial support, FiO2, saturation and respiratory-rate observations. Sarah's presentation establishes the intubated pneumonia recovery context. 'Next hospital entry' is a minor chronological remnant, but no unseen earlier entry is needed to understand or solve this single-node case. The table is clearly labelled fictional, and the task asks for a specific liberation plan.

The learner must distinguish removal of ventilatory assistance from increased oxygen supplementation, then choose a reassessment that tests the unresolved oxygenation condition. The higher saturation cannot establish tolerance at FiO2 0.35 when it was measured at 0.60. Repeating an unassisted trial at the earlier concentration is the best offered way to resolve that uncertainty; adding support while retaining 0.60 changes the wrong variable, and extubating at 0.60 accepts the incomplete assessment.

Cue attack: 'The trial is recorded as tolerated' supplies a report for the resident to scrutinize, not the keyed conclusion. 'Repeat an unassisted trial at FiO2 0.35' is the only option with 0.35, but the number also occurs in the actual baseline and is decision-critical. Choosing the lone lower number is not justified by wording alone. 'Repeat' is shared by two options and 0.60 by two options, so majority-component convergence does not assemble the key. The caption and column labels do not explain the answer.

Predicted moderate: separate an acceptable unassisted trial method from a confounded oxygen comparison, then select the corrective assessment. The superficially reassuring saturation and reported tolerance create a consequential error opportunity. This tests a high-yield liberation principle, although the precise unchanged-FiO2 recommendation is a narrower point than basic extubation readiness.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the offered ranking. The record does not prove that Sarah failed the trial, cannot tolerate FiO2 0.35, or could never be extubated at 0.60. The reason for increasing oxygen is not stated; the key is therefore a reassessment of uncertainty, not a diagnosis of worsening lung disease. Airway-clearance and consciousness findings are also absent, so this record must not be treated as a complete extubation-clearance assessment. Those omissions do not make either alternative the better offered plan.

The explanation acknowledges conditional guidance with very low certainty. This supports a bounded best-offered-answer interpretation, not an absolute prohibition or a claim that every supported SBT is invalid. The exact recommendation was not freshly checked offline and remains subject to named clinician review. There is no later node or prior feedback in the candidate context to create a sequence cue.

record.title: Selecting initial support for acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure
fairness: Robert's age, sex, COPD admission, treatment stage, work of breathing, alertness, secretion clearance and blood pressure are explicit. The exhibit supplies both arterial-gas time points and the oxygen conditions without needing another node. 'initial hospital assessment' is compatible with an initial support decision after bronchodilator treatment; it does not imply that the current outpatient encounter is the emergency.

The change from pH 7.38/PaCO2 50 to pH 7.28/PaCO2 70 indicates an acute ventilatory deterioration on a hypercapnic baseline. Persistent respiratory effort calls for ventilatory assistance, while alertness, secretion clearance and stable blood pressure make an initial bilevel-mask strategy preferable to immediate invasive ventilation among these choices. High-flow nasal oxygen is a plausible oxygenation-focused error but is not the preferred substitute for bilevel assistance in this supplied acidotic COPD presentation.

Cue attack: 'acute COPD exacerbation' names the underlying disease appropriately for a support-selection task; it does not state whether oxygen, NIV or intubation is indicated. 'He is alert and clears oral secretions' narrows airway risk through observations rather than declaring NIV eligibility. 'Start bilevel mask ventilation', 'Start high-flow nasal oxygen' and 'Start invasive endotracheal ventilation' are parallel, similarly specific actions. No unique task-to-key phrase, length outlier, convergence, absolute or pre-answer teaching sentence identifies the key without medical reasoning.

Predicted moderate at the easier end: interpret the acute change rather than treat chronic hypercapnia in isolation, then use airway function and clinical stability to choose the support route. The oxygen-focused alternative and premature-intubation alternative represent different consequential errors. This is a core, commonly tested respiratory-support decision, but the supplied findings make the pattern relatively recognizable for a prepared resident.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The numbers are observations, not universal pH or PaCO2 thresholds for intubation. The explanation appropriately combines gas interpretation with clinical state and does not claim that alertness guarantees NIV success. No later response or escalation node remains, and no prior feedback is needed. Exact guideline currency was not newly verified offline; PASS is editorial and the draft remains needs_clinician_review.

fairness: Scope: independent review of the four status=salvage candidate contexts in salvageRound, using their presentation, current update, exhibit, task, options and explanation. Kept-unchanged, retired, parked, held and other non-salvage records are outside this review; their presence does not confer acceptance. Earlier reviewer verdicts and author self-checks were not used as evidence of correctness. No network or fresh source verification was performed. PASS is editorial only; every reviewed draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version approval.

The standalone presentation identifies Robert, age 70, male, and the COPD admission. The update supplies the invasive-support history, successful breathing trial, airway function and both baseline and current gases. 'Later hospital entry' refers intelligibly to that admission; no prior scored answer or explanation is needed. The complete task asks for an airway plan at the documented recovery stage, rather than an intervention in today's clinic.

The resident must recognize that a normal pH with PaCO2 near the pre-illness value does not require continued intubation, then distinguish readiness for tube removal from the need for preventive support afterward. COPD, age and persistent hypercapnia make immediate bilevel support the best offered plan. Ordinary nasal oxygen is a credible competing plan after a successful trial, but omits the preventive ventilatory strategy for this risk profile.

Cue attack: 'tolerates an SBT' and 'Low-flow oxygen maintains the trial’s oxygenation' establish relevant observations, but neither identifies bilevel support without clinical knowledge; the latter could tempt the oxygen distractor. 'Continue intubation until PaCO2 normalizes' is a concrete, clinically familiar normalization error rather than a rhetorical 'always/never' foil. The two extubation options have parallel wording and comparable length. No unique wording match, teaching sentence, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut selects the key.

Predicted moderate: baseline-versus-normal interpretation changes whether the tube stays, and risk assessment changes support after removal. Both distinctions are high-yield ventilator-liberation decisions. This is not a hard item: the successful trial and preserved clearance deliberately resolve basic readiness uncertainty.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. 'Low-flow oxygen' is less specific than a recorded oxygen setting, but the stated tolerated trial and maintained oxygenation suffice to rank these options; the task does not ask for an exact oxygen prescription. The explanation appropriately confines preventive NIV to a selected profile and does not claim superiority over every alternative post-extubation regimen. Its exact guideline support was not newly verified offline.

fairness: Sarah's named age/sex presentation and current update supply the illness trajectory, spontaneous effort, oxygen requirement, hemodynamics and observed breathing behavior.
